title: Life Ready
greet: Hey, I’m Lensy. 🧭 You’re about to run your own life. Know your values, decide like an adult, handle the big stuff. There’s no single ‘right’ path.

badge.title: Life Ready 🧭
badge.blurb: You know your values, can decide like an adult, handle the big stuff, work with people, and build a support network, and asking for help is strength. 🫂

helpLine: Asking for help is a strength. Talk to a trusted adult or mentor, or call Tele-MANAS 14416 or Manodarpan. (Life-skills, not therapy.)
reassure: No single ‘right’ path; asking for help is strength. If the big stuff feels heavy, lean on people: Tele-MANAS 14416 or Manodarpan. 🫂

scenarios.hook: Lensy: good adult decisions start with knowing yourself, your values and what matters. Ready to map that?
scenarios.affirm: Self-knowledge is the base every good decision is built on, you're starting in the right place.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing your values and what matters is the base of good decisions.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: what matters most to you as you head into adult life?
scenarios.affirm: Naming what matters to you is the start of living by it, whatever you chose.
scenarios.relearn: Naming what matters to you is the start of living by your values.

scenarios.hook: "There's a set of 'right' values you're supposed to have."

myth.un: There's a 'right' set of values you must have.
myth.re: There are no 'right' values to copy; the work is knowing your own.
myth.why: Self-knowledge is personal, not a template.

scenarios.relearn: There's no 'right' set of values; the work is knowing your own.

scenarios.hook: Sort: builds self-awareness, or avoids it?

items.text: Noticing how you actually feel and react
Reflecting on what matters to you
Asking yourself why a thing got to you
Numbing out so you don't have to feel it

scenarios.relearn: Noticing your feelings and reflecting builds self-awareness; pretending and just-conforming avoid it.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: knowing your strengths is as important as knowing your values. What's one of yours?
scenarios.affirm: Knowing a real strength of yours is something to build your future on.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing your strengths gives you something to build on.

scenarios.hook: Big choices are coming up, and you've never sat down to think about your values.

steps.prompt: Subject choices are due on Friday, and you're unsure what to pick. What do you do?

options.text: Take an evening to write what matters to you
options.then: Your list shows three things: helping people, learning by doing, and some freedom.

options.text: Pick on impulse and see if it fits later
options.then: The form is done in two minutes. The doubt starts the next day.

options.text: Choose whatever your best friend is choosing
options.then: Your friend is thrilled to have company. You're not sure it's yours.

options.text: Ask your parents to tell you what suits you
options.then: They have views, and you hear a lot of them. None of them are about you.

steps.why: A short list of what matters gives your choice something solid to stand on.

steps.prompt: A week later, an opportunity comes up that everyone calls a great chance. What do you do?

options.text: Check it against what matters to you and decide if it fits
options.then: It fits one thing you value and misses two. You can say why when you say no.

options.text: Take it because it sounds impressive
options.then: People congratulate you. You feel odd about it by evening.

options.text: Reject it without thinking, because it's new
options.then: It's easy to say no. You wonder later whether it would have fit.

options.text: Ask everyone you know to vote and follow the majority
options.then: The votes split three ways. You're more confused than before.

steps.why: Knowing what matters to you lets you decide quickly and explain why.

steps.prompt: Months later, you feel unsure again. What do you do?

options.text: Think again about what matters to you and update what has changed
options.then: Two things have shifted since your subject choice. The new picture feels truer.

options.text: Ignore the feeling and carry on as before
options.then: The feeling doesn't leave. It sits quietly beneath your day.

options.text: Decide your first thoughts were wrong and drop them
options.then: You've thrown away the useful parts of them too.

options.text: Compare yourself with classmates who seem certain
options.then: They look sure. You can't tell what they haven't said out loud.

steps.why: Self-knowledge keeps growing, so what matters to you is worth revisiting.

scenarios.debrief: A little self-reflection makes every choice that follows truer to you.
scenarios.relearn: Figure out your values first; choices then fit who you are.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: what do you want your life to stand for?
scenarios.affirm: A sense of what you want to stand for is a compass for the years ahead.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing what you want your life to stand for is a compass.

scenarios.hook: "By now you should have your whole self and future figured out."

myth.un: By now you should have yourself and your future all figured out.
myth.re: Self-knowledge unfolds for life; you only need to start, not finish.
myth.why: No one has it all worked out, at any age.

scenarios.relearn: You don't need yourself all figured out; self-knowledge unfolds for life.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a healthy way to know yourself, or a trap?

items.text: Treating a mistake as a thing you did, not who you are
Calling yourself useless when you slip

scenarios.relearn: Kind, honest reflection builds self-knowledge; harsh self-criticism and comparison don't.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: emotional self-awareness, noticing how you feel and why, helps you handle whatever comes. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Noticing your feelings and their causes is the start of handling them well.
scenarios.relearn: Emotional self-awareness helps you handle whatever comes.

scenarios.hook: Match the self-knowledge to what it guides.
scenarios.relearn: Values guide decisions, strengths guide building, feelings guide coping.

scenarios.hook: People around you have strong opinions about who you should be.

steps.prompt: At a family function, an uncle tells you what you ought to become. What do you do?

options.text: Hear him out and think about it later, on your own
options.then: He feels listened to. You keep what fits and leave the rest.

options.text: Nod along and promise to do what he says
options.then: He's delighted. You feel a weight settle in your chest.

options.text: Argue loudly that he doesn't know you at all
options.then: The room goes quiet. Your mother quickly changes the subject.

options.text: Say nothing and stay upset for the whole evening
options.then: The party carries on around you. You go home with a knot in your stomach.

steps.why: Hearing others out is fine, and the final word on who you are is yours.

steps.prompt: A few weeks later, a friend says you seem different lately. What do you do?

options.text: Say you've been thinking about what matters to you
options.then: She nods slowly. "You do seem more thoughtful lately," she says.

options.text: Apologise and say you'll go back to how you were
options.then: She smiles. You miss the person you were starting to be.

options.text: Tell her she's just jealous
options.then: She goes quiet. The chat ends sooner than usual.

options.text: Say nothing and slowly drift away from her
options.then: The messages thin out. Neither of you says why.

steps.why: You can explain your growth calmly without owing anyone your old self.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks you to describe yourself in three words for a form. What do you write?

options.text: Words that come from your own values and strengths
options.then: You write three words that surprise you a little. They feel like yours.

options.text: The words your relatives would pick for you
options.then: The words look neat. They aren't how you'd describe yourself.

options.text: Words you think will impress the panel
options.then: The words look polished. You can't quite remember why you chose them.

options.text: Words borrowed from a classmate's form
options.then: Her words sound confident. They belong to someone else.

steps.why: Describing yourself from your own values keeps the story yours.

scenarios.debrief: Input from others is useful. The final word on who you are is yours.
scenarios.relearn: Hear others, but decide who you are by your own values.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a private 'values map' you carry, does that feel like a useful thing to have?
scenarios.affirm: A values map is a quiet compass you can return to whenever a choice is hard.
scenarios.relearn: A personal values map is a compass for hard choices.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: knowing yourself isn't about being perfect, it's about being honest with yourself. Feel that?
scenarios.affirm: Honesty with yourself, not perfection, is what real self-knowledge is.
scenarios.relearn: Self-knowledge is honesty with yourself, not perfection.

scenarios.hook: A month from now you must choose what to study after Class 12, and everyone has a view.

steps.prompt: Your head is full of opinions and worries. Where do you start?

options.text: Write what I know, what I don't, and what matters to me
options.then: Your page shows two gaps you can't fill by thinking alone. You note both.

options.text: Pick whatever feels easiest right now
options.then: The choice is quick and the weight lifts for a day. Then the doubts come back.

options.text: Ask my friends what they picked and copy them
options.then: Three friends say three different things. None of them know your marks or interests.

options.text: Ask my parents to decide so I can't get it wrong
options.then: Your parents are glad to help. You feel relief, and a small worry that it isn't yours.

steps.why: Starting with facts and your own values gives the choice a base.

steps.prompt: A week on, you still don't know enough about the courses on your list. What do you do next?

options.text: Find fees, subjects and where each course leads
options.then: A senior and a college website answer questions you hadn't thought to ask.

options.text: Pick the course that sounds most impressive
options.then: The list is long and glossy. Your own interests quietly drop off it.

options.text: Ask a teacher which one is easiest to get into
options.then: She names the easiest one. It tells you little about what you want.

options.text: Rank them by facts alone and ignore what I enjoy
options.then: The numbers point to one course. You feel nothing when you read it.

steps.why: Facts matter, and so do your own values. Good choices use both.

steps.prompt: Two options are left and each has a real cost. How do you choose between them?

options.text: Weigh each against my values and where I want to be later
options.then: One option keeps matching what matters most to you.

options.text: Toss a coin and move on
options.then: The coin lands. You feel relief for a second, then wish it had landed the other way.

options.text: Take whichever one pays more
options.then: The pay is higher. Money was only one of the things you wanted.

options.text: Take the one that disappoints the fewest people
options.then: Everyone at home nods. You aren't sure you'd have picked it alone.

steps.why: Your values and long-term goals break the tie, not luck or other people's moods.

steps.prompt: You've made your choice. A cousin says you'll regret it. What do you do?

options.text: Thank them and stay with the choice I made on purpose
options.then: Your cousin shrugs. The choice still feels like yours.

options.text: Reopen the whole decision and start the list again
options.then: The old doubts crowd back and a week goes by with no progress.

options.text: Admit I was never sure either way
options.then: Your cousin nods, and you feel less certain than a minute ago.

options.text: Argue until they agree I'm right
options.then: The talk becomes a debate. Neither of you is listening any more.

steps.why: Owning a considered choice means you can hear doubt without dropping it.

scenarios.debrief: Deciding like an adult: facts, values, consequences, the long game, then own it.
scenarios.relearn: Decide by facts, values and the long term, then own it.

scenarios.hook: Match the decision step to what it does.
scenarios.relearn: Facts, values, the long term, resisting pressure and owning it form a good decision.

scenarios.hook: "There's one right life path and you must find it."

myth.un: There's one right life path you have to find.
myth.re: There's no single 'right' path; the skill is deciding well by your own values.
myth.why: Many good lives are possible; deciding well is what counts.

scenarios.relearn: There's no single right path; decide well by your own values.

scenarios.hook: Your parents and your best friend push you toward different streams, and the deadline is close.

steps.prompt: At dinner your father lists reasons for his pick. What do you do?

options.text: Listen to all of it and say I'll think it over
options.then: He looks relieved to be heard. He asks when you'll tell him.

options.text: Agree so dinner stays calm
options.then: Dinner is peaceful. Your father tells your aunt it's settled.

options.text: Say he's pushing his own dream onto me
options.then: He goes quiet, then raises his voice. Dinner ends badly.

options.text: Say I'll follow my friend's pick instead
options.then: Your father says nothing. You haven't told your friend yet, and the pressure only moves.

steps.why: Hearing people out keeps the door open while the choice stays yours.

steps.prompt: Your best friend texts that she has chosen her stream and you should join her. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her and say I'm deciding by my own plan
options.then: She says okay but sounds a little hurt. The pressure eases.

options.text: Pick her stream so we stay together
options.then: She sends three happy emojis. You wonder if you'd have picked it alone.

options.text: Ask classmates what they're choosing
options.then: Six answers come back, all different, and you feel more tangled.

options.text: Say I haven't decided and stop replying
options.then: She sends two puzzled messages. You feel unsettled about leaving them unanswered.

steps.why: A friend's plan is input. Your own goals decide.

steps.prompt: A teacher offers to talk about your marks and interests. What do you do?

options.text: Go, and bring my goals and the facts I've gathered
options.then: She asks sharp questions and points to one fact you'd missed.

options.text: Go and ask which stream she'd pick for me
options.then: She says what she'd pick. It fits her life, and you can't tell if it fits yours.

options.text: Skip it, since everyone has already told me what to do
options.then: The week slips by and you still haven't heard an unbiased view.

options.text: Go and repeat only what my family wants
options.then: She nods and notes it down. Your own interests never come up.

steps.why: A mentor helps most when you bring your own goals and facts.

steps.prompt: Decision day. Your parents ask for your answer. What do you say?

options.text: Give my choice and my reasons, and thank them
options.then: Your mother asks one question and then nods. Your father stays quiet, then says okay.

options.text: Choose what will cause the least argument at home
options.then: Everyone relaxes. You feel a small lump in your throat.

options.text: Say I need more time, again
options.then: Your mother sighs and the deadline gets closer.

options.text: Say it's my life and end the talk
options.then: Your father is stung, and nobody hears your reasons.

steps.why: Your own decision, calmly explained, respects them and you.

scenarios.debrief: Others' input informs you; your values make the final call.
scenarios.relearn: Weigh others' input, but decide by your own values and goals.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a good basis for a big decision, or a poor one?

items.text: What you can honestly commit to

scenarios.relearn: Facts, values, consequences and honest fit are a good basis; panic, image and noise aren't.

scenarios.hook: You feel the urge to settle a big choice fast, just to end the uneasy feeling.

steps.prompt: The deadline is a month away and the choice still feels uncomfortable. What do you do?

options.text: Set aside time each week to work on it
options.then: You block two evenings. The choice feels less like a cloud and more like a task.

options.text: Choose today to be done with it
options.then: The uneasy feeling lifts for an evening, then you wonder if it was too quick. You tell nobody yet.

options.text: Ask a cousin to pick for me
options.then: She picks fast and cheerfully. You can't tell if it fits you.

options.text: Wait quietly and hope it sorts itself out
options.then: Weeks pass. The question is still there and the date is nearer.

steps.why: Giving a big decision regular time is how you decide well, not fast.

steps.prompt: A friend asks how the decision is going and says you're overthinking and should just pick. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her I'd rather decide well than fast
options.then: She shrugs and says okay. You feel steadier for saying it.

options.text: Pick right then so she stops asking
options.then: She cheers. The choice sits oddly, like a coat that doesn't fit.

options.text: Agree I'm overthinking and drop it for now
options.then: The worry goes quiet for a few days and then comes back louder.

options.text: Ask her which she'd choose and go with that
options.then: She picks in two seconds. You aren't sure why it feels borrowed.

steps.why: Other people's rush isn't your deadline. Take the time it needs.

steps.prompt: A week before the deadline, you still aren't sure about your choice. What do you do?

options.text: Check my values once more, then decide and own it
options.then: It's a little uncomfortable, but you can name why you chose it.

options.text: Switch to a new option at the last minute to be safe
options.then: The new option looks fresh for one evening, and the doubts follow it.

options.text: Flip back and forth until the last hour
options.then: The last hour arrives and you take whichever one was left.

options.text: Decide fast now so the worry ends
options.then: The worry ends for a night. The reasons stay unwritten.

steps.why: A final values check turns a worry into an owned decision.

scenarios.debrief: Important decisions are worth slowing down for.
scenarios.relearn: Take the time a big decision needs; don't rush it.

scenarios.hook: Your first scholarship instalment lands in your account, and you have to decide what to do with it.

steps.prompt: Your phone is cracked, a friend wants to go out, and fees are due. Where do you start?

options.text: List what I must pay, what I need and what I just want
options.then: The list is short and the fees are at the top. You breathe out.

options.text: Fix the phone and enjoy the outing first
options.then: The phone works again and the evening is great. The balance looks smaller.

options.text: Spend on what I feel like first, then see what's left
options.then: You spend freely for two days. The rest looks thinner than you thought.

options.text: Leave it untouched and avoid thinking about it
options.then: Nothing gets spent, and the fee date creeps closer.

steps.why: Sorting needs from wants first gives every rupee a job.

steps.prompt: A shop offers a new phone on small monthly instalments, and your friend says go for it. What do you do?

options.text: Check the full price and whether I need a new phone
options.then: The total is far bigger than the instalment suggested.

options.text: Take it, since the monthly amount looks small
options.then: The phone is shiny. You wonder how the next months will look.

options.text: Say no straight away without looking at the numbers
options.then: Your friend teases you. You never learn what the real cost was.

options.text: Take it if my friend splits the cost with me
options.then: He agrees for a moment, then gets vague. You can't rely on it.

steps.why: Checking the real total and your real need protects your money.

steps.prompt: The month ends and some money is left. What do you do?

options.text: Set a little aside as a cushion, then plan the rest
options.then: You can see where each part of the money is going.

options.text: Spend the rest to celebrate getting through the month
options.then: It's a nice evening. Next month's gap is already forming.

options.text: Lend it to a friend who asked, no questions
options.then: He says thanks and the date to repay never gets mentioned.

options.text: Keep it all in cash at home and forget about it
options.then: The cash sits in a drawer and a few notes quietly go missing.

steps.why: A small cushion comes first. Then you plan the rest.

scenarios.debrief: Money decisions use the same method: facts, values, long term.
scenarios.relearn: For money choices, weigh facts, needs vs wants, and the future.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'owning' a decision means you chose it and you'll see it through. Feel the difference from drifting?
scenarios.affirm: Owning your choices, rather than drifting into them, is what adult agency feels like.
scenarios.relearn: Owning a decision means you chose it and will see it through.

scenarios.hook: Sort: part of the adult decision method, or not?
scenarios.relearn: Facts, values and the long term are in the method; ignoring, deferring and rumour aren't.

scenarios.hook: "A good decision is one that turns out perfectly."

myth.un: A good decision is one that turns out perfectly.
myth.re: A good decision is one made well, with the facts and values you had; outcomes aren't fully in your control.
myth.why: You can decide wisely and still face an uncertain result.

scenarios.relearn: A good decision is made well, not one guaranteed to turn out perfectly.

scenarios.hook: A choice you made months ago hasn't worked out, and you can see it clearly now.

steps.prompt: You notice the choice isn't working. What is your first move?

options.text: Look at what happened and what I'd do differently
options.then: You write down two things you missed then, and one thing that did go well.

options.text: Tell myself I'm bad at decisions
options.then: The thought repeats and makes the next choice feel scarier.

options.text: Blame the people who advised me
options.then: You feel lighter for a minute. Nothing about the next choice changes.

options.text: Pretend it's fine and say nothing
options.then: You say nothing, and the problem keeps growing quietly.

steps.why: Looking at what happened turns a miss into something you can use.

steps.prompt: A friend asks how that choice went. What do you say?

options.text: Tell her what went wrong and what I've learned
options.then: She listens, then shares a time her own plan flopped.

options.text: Say it went great
options.then: She smiles and moves on. You feel a little lonely.

options.text: Make a joke about how terrible I am at this
options.then: She laughs politely. The joke hides what you actually feel.

options.text: Say I'm never deciding anything big again
options.then: She looks worried and doesn't know what to say.

steps.why: Honest talk about a miss helps you learn and lets others support you.

steps.prompt: A new decision comes up that looks a lot like the last one. What do you do?

options.text: Use what I learned and adjust how I decide
options.then: You spot the same early warning sign and ask about it first.

options.text: Avoid deciding so I can't get it wrong again
options.then: The chance passes while you stay still.

options.text: Decide exactly the same way as last time
options.then: The same gap shows up, a little later.

options.text: Ask someone else to make this one for me
options.then: They choose quickly. You miss the chance to practise your own judgement.

steps.why: Learning from a choice that didn't work is how judgement grows.

scenarios.debrief: Deciding well includes learning from the ones that don't pan out.
scenarios.relearn: Learn from a decision that didn't work; that's deciding well over time.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which part of deciding do you most want to get better at?
scenarios.affirm: Strengthening any one of those makes your decisions wiser and more yours.
scenarios.relearn: Facts, values, long-term thinking and resisting pressure are all parts of deciding well.

scenarios.hook: Both of your options for next year have real costs, and neither is painless.

steps.prompt: Your two options sit side by side on a page. What do you do?

options.text: Write what each cost means to me
options.then: You see one cost matters far more to you than the other.

options.text: Search for a third option with no costs
options.then: Days go by. Every new option has a cost of its own.

options.text: Put it away until things get clearer
options.then: Things don't get clearer, and the deadline gets closer.

options.text: Ask a friend which one would hurt less
options.then: She picks one. You can't tell if it would hurt you less.

steps.why: Naming what each cost means for you makes the trade-off visible.

steps.prompt: A relative says the right choice would be obvious to anyone sensible. What do you do?

options.text: Say it isn't obvious and I'm weighing my priorities
options.then: He raises an eyebrow, then nods and asks what your priorities are.

options.text: Agree, then wonder what I'm missing
options.then: You nod, and feel foolish for finding it hard.

options.text: Ask him to just tell me what he'd pick
options.then: He answers at once. It reflects his priorities, not yours.

options.text: Say there's no right answer so it doesn't matter
options.then: He frowns. You feel yourself drifting further from deciding.

steps.why: Hard choices aren't obvious, and your priorities are what decide them.

steps.prompt: The deadline is today and both costs are still there. What do you do?

options.text: Pick what fits my top priority, cost included
options.then: It stings a little, and it feels like a real decision.

options.text: Let the deadline pass and see what happens
options.then: The deadline passes and the choice is made for you.

options.text: Pick the one with the smaller cost, quickly
options.then: It's easy now. Your top priority gets left out of the room.

options.text: Pick one, then keep checking out the other
options.then: You can't settle into either choice. It feels like carrying two.

steps.why: Avoiding is still a choice. Priorities let you pick on purpose.

scenarios.debrief: Some decisions have no painless option; your priorities break the tie.
scenarios.relearn: For hard trade-offs, decide by your priorities; avoiding is still a choice.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two pressures that shouldn't drive a big decision.

scene.text: "Everyone's doing this course"
A clear look at your own goals
"Decide now or miss out forever"
The real facts and figures
What you can commit to long-term

scenarios.why: 'Everyone's doing it' and false urgency are pressure; goals, facts and fit are real reasons.
scenarios.relearn: Spot pressure like 'everyone's doing it' and false urgency in big decisions.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: deciding by your own values, within safety and the law, is real adult freedom. Feel it?
scenarios.affirm: Within safety and law, deciding by your own values is exactly what adult freedom is.
scenarios.relearn: Deciding by your own values, within safety and law, is adult freedom.

scenarios.hook: "Feeling stressed about exams means you're weak or not coping."

myth.un: Exam stress means you're weak or failing to cope.
myth.re: Stress at big moments is normal; tools and support help you handle it.
myth.why: Around 81% of students feel exam anxiety, you're far from alone.

scenarios.relearn: Exam stress is normal, not weakness; tools and support help.

scenarios.hook: Board exams are weeks away, and the pressure feels huge.

steps.prompt: Your timetable is blank and your chest feels tight. What do you do?

options.text: Break the syllabus into small daily chunks
options.then: The page fills with small, doable boxes. Your breathing slows a little.

options.text: Study through the night for a few days
options.then: The hours pile up. By the third night your eyes sting.

options.text: Wait until I feel calm enough to plan
options.then: The calm doesn't come. The blank page stays blank.

options.text: Copy a topper's timetable exactly
options.then: Her plan has no gaps. Yours was never going to fit it.

steps.why: Small daily chunks make a huge task feel doable.

steps.prompt: A few days in, you're worn thin and a friend invites you for a short walk. What do you do?

options.text: Go for a short walk and be back in an hour
options.then: You come back clearer. The next chapter feels lighter.

options.text: Skip it to save study time
options.then: You stay at the desk. You re-read the same page twice.

options.text: Stay up and have more coffee instead
options.then: The coffee hums. Your hands begin to shake.

options.text: Go and stay out all evening
options.then: The evening is fun. The syllabus is exactly where you left it.

steps.why: Movement and breaks keep your mind able to study.

steps.prompt: Your mother notices you skipping meals and asks if she can help. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her about the pressure and ask for help
options.then: She sits down. She offers to handle meals so you can focus.

options.text: Say I'm fine and eat later
options.then: She nods, worried. Later never quite arrives.

options.text: Say she can't help with exams
options.then: She goes quiet. You feel a little more alone.

options.text: Say I'll just eat at my desk
options.then: She leaves a plate. You eat a few bites without looking up, still tense.

steps.why: Leaning on people is part of coping well. It isn't weakness.

steps.prompt: The night before the first paper, your mind races. What do you do?

options.text: Do a light revision, then sleep on time
options.then: You fall asleep later than usual, but you do sleep.

options.text: Revise all night to be safe
options.then: The pages blur by morning. You feel dazed.

options.text: Skip revision and just worry in bed
options.then: The worry grows. You have no extra facts to calm it.

options.text: Check what everyone else is revising
options.then: Every message makes you feel further behind.

steps.why: Rest before an exam helps more than another night of cramming.

scenarios.debrief: Big stress shrinks when you break it down and keep healthy habits.
scenarios.relearn: For exam pressure: break it down, healthy routine, lean on people.

items.text: Breaking the task into small steps

myth.un: Failing at something makes you a failure.
