scenarios.hook: You're about to leave home for the first time, and you feel anxious.

steps.prompt: Your bag is half packed and your stomach feels twisted. What do you do?

options.text: Name it: this is a big change and I'm anxious
options.then: Saying it takes the knot down by a notch.

options.text: Wave it off and tell everyone I'm excited
options.then: Everyone smiles. The knot stays inside.

options.text: Pack in a rush so I can stop thinking
options.then: The bag is full by dinner. The knot is still there.

options.text: Say I feel nothing and keep going
options.then: You keep going. The feeling follows you around the room.

steps.why: Naming a big change makes it easier to prepare for.

steps.prompt: Your mother asks what you'd like help with before you go. What do you do?

options.text: Ask her to go through lists, money and contacts
options.then: You write down three things you hadn't thought of.

options.text: Say I need nothing and I'll manage
options.then: She says okay. The list stays empty.

options.text: Say I'll figure it out when I get there
options.then: She looks uneasy. The first night's problems are left for later.

options.text: Ask her to pack everything for me
options.then: The bag is packed. You don't know where anything is.

steps.why: Preparing with the people who know you makes a big change safer.

steps.prompt: Your best friend says she'll miss you and asks how to stay in touch. What do you do?

options.text: Plan a regular call time we can both keep
options.then: She picks Sunday evening. You both put it in your phones.

options.text: Say we'll just see how it goes
options.then: She nods. Both of you wonder if it'll fade.

options.text: Say we'll text only when something big happens
options.then: She looks hurt. Her small news isn't big enough.

options.text: Say staying in touch will make it harder
options.then: She goes quiet. You both feel more alone.

steps.why: A set time to talk keeps your people close as things change.

steps.prompt: On your first night in the new place, you feel lonely. What do you do?

options.text: Call someone from home and say how I feel
options.then: Your cousin picks up. She says her first night was lonely too.

options.text: Pretend I'm fine in the family chat
options.then: Everyone sends hearts. You feel more alone behind the screen.

options.text: Stay in my room and scroll
options.then: The room is quiet. Others are laughing down the corridor.

options.text: Tell myself I should be tougher
options.then: The thought makes the loneliness heavier, not smaller.

steps.why: Feeling lonely in a big change is normal. Staying connected helps.

scenarios.debrief: Naming a big transition and staying connected makes it manageable.
scenarios.relearn: For a big change like leaving home: name it, prepare, stay connected.

scenarios.hook: The future feels uncertain, and it's making you anxious.

steps.prompt: You lie awake with questions about next year. What do you do?

options.text: Write down what I can and can't control
options.then: Two short lists appear. The 'can control' list is more useful.

options.text: Keep going over every possible outcome
options.then: The outcomes multiply. Midnight passes.

options.text: Scroll to see what everyone else is planning
options.then: Everyone's plans look clearer than yours.

options.text: Ask everyone what will happen to me
options.then: Nobody knows. Each guess gets you more tangled.

steps.why: Sorting what you can and can't control gives worry somewhere to go.

steps.prompt: A cousin says you should have it all figured out by now. What do you do?

options.text: Say I'm working it out one step at a time
options.then: She shrugs. She admits she hasn't figured hers out either.

options.text: Agree and feel worse about it
options.then: The words stick. You feel behind.

options.text: Snap at her to mind her own business
options.then: She looks hurt and the talk ends there.

options.text: Make up a plan so I sound sure
options.then: The plan sounds good. You don't believe it.

steps.why: Nobody has it all figured out. Next steps matter more.

steps.prompt: A week later you're anxious again, and one small step is possible. What do you do?

options.text: Take that step today
options.then: The step takes thirty minutes. The future feels a notch closer.

options.text: Wait until I feel sure about everything
options.then: The sureness doesn't arrive. The week slips by.

options.text: Plan five steps ahead before starting
options.then: The plan grows. The first step still isn't done.

options.text: Skip it and worry about next year instead
options.then: The worry grows. The step is still waiting.

steps.why: Taking the next step you can control shrinks uncertainty.

scenarios.debrief: You can't control the future, but you can take the next right step.
scenarios.relearn: For uncertainty, focus on the next step you can control.

scenarios.hook: A close friend is drifting away as you both move on in life.

steps.prompt: You see photos of her with new friends and feel a pang. What do you do?

options.text: Let myself feel it and say it hurts
options.then: The hurt is real and sits in your chest. It's easier to carry once named.

options.text: Tell myself it doesn't matter
options.then: You say it twice. It doesn't sound true.

options.text: Message her angrily and ask why she left
options.then: She replies defensively. The distance widens.

options.text: Delete all our chats and her photos
options.then: The chats are gone. The feeling is not.

steps.why: Allowing a feeling is the first step to getting through it.

steps.prompt: Your cousin asks why you look low. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her how I'm feeling
options.then: She listens. She says she's lost a close friend once too.

options.text: Say I'm fine and change the topic
options.then: She lets it go. You feel the pressure inside.

options.text: Say I just need to push on alone
options.then: She nods but stays close for the evening.

options.text: Joke that I don't care
options.then: She laughs. The joke hides what you actually feel.

steps.why: Talking to someone who cares shrinks a hurt.

steps.prompt: A free evening comes and the old routine feels empty. What do you do?

options.text: Be kind to myself and keep a routine
options.then: A walk and a proper dinner. It isn't a cure, but it helps.

options.text: Stay busy every minute so I can't feel
options.then: You do four tasks. At night the feeling comes back.

options.text: Reread our old messages for hours
options.then: The messages hurt more. It's past midnight.

options.text: Stay in bed and skip meals
options.then: The day goes by. Your head aches by evening.

steps.why: Gentle routines help you through a change.

steps.prompt: A few weeks later, your friend sends a short message. What do you do?

options.text: Reply kindly and honestly
options.then: She writes back warmly. You both admit it's strange.

options.text: Ignore it to protect myself
options.then: The message waits. So does the hurt.

options.text: Reply as if nothing has happened
options.then: The chat is breezy. Neither of you says what you feel.

options.text: Reply with everything that hurt
options.then: The long message lands hard. She goes silent.

steps.why: Honest, kind words let a changing friendship settle.

scenarios.debrief: Changing relationships bring real feelings; healthy coping and support help.
scenarios.relearn: For a changing relationship: feel it, lean on support, be kind to yourself.

scenarios.hook: Your stress has been heavy for weeks, and it isn't easing even on days off.

steps.prompt: It's late and your mind is racing again. What do you do?

options.text: Message someone I trust right now
options.then: You send two lines to someone you trust. Your shoulders drop slightly.

options.text: Tell myself to just push through
options.then: You grit your teeth. The weight stays.

options.text: Scroll until I'm too tired to think
options.then: The scrolling works until the screen goes dark.

options.text: Wait until the exams end, then see
options.then: The exams are weeks away. The weight is heavy now.

steps.why: Stress that stays heavy is worth sharing now, not later.

steps.prompt: At school, a trusted teacher asks if you're all right. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her it's been heavy for weeks
options.then: She puts her pen down. She says, "Thank you for telling me."

options.text: Say I'm fine and smile
options.then: She nods. Her eyes stay on you a second longer.

options.text: Say it's only exam stress and will pass
options.then: She says she hopes so. The weight remains.

options.text: Say I don't want to bother her
options.then: She says you aren't bothering her.

steps.why: A trusted adult can help once they know it's heavy.

steps.prompt: Later, she mentions that the school counsellor could help too. What do you do?

options.text: Say yes and ask how to meet one
options.then: She says the school counsellor has a slot this week.

options.text: Say counsellors are for people who can't cope
options.then: She says many people see one. The thought stays.

options.text: Say I'll think about it and not go
options.then: The week passes with no appointment.

options.text: Say I'll book one after the exams
options.then: She says a slot is free this week. The appointment keeps slipping.

steps.why: Seeing a counsellor is normal, smart and strong.

steps.prompt: At home your father asks why you've been so quiet. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him it's heavy and I want help
options.then: He sits down next to you. He says he's glad you told him.

options.text: Say it's just exams and I'll be fine
options.then: He nods, unconvinced. The silence stays.

options.text: Say I'm tired and go to my room
options.then: He lets you go. He looks worried.

options.text: Say he wouldn't understand this at all
options.then: He sighs. He says he'd like to try.

steps.why: Letting family in lets them help you carry it.

steps.prompt: On a bad night, everything feels like too much. What do you do?

options.text: Reach a trusted adult or call Tele-MANAS 14416
options.then: Someone calm and kind listens. You are less alone with it tonight.

options.text: Tell myself to push through it again
options.then: The night is long and nobody knows.

options.text: Wait for morning and tell nobody at all
options.then: Morning comes. The night's weight comes with it.

options.text: Message a friend and tell no adult at all
options.then: Your friend is kind. She is worried and has no idea what to do.

steps.why: Heavy nights deserve real support. Tele-MANAS 14416 and trusted adults are there for you.

scenarios.debrief: When stress is heavy and lasting, reaching for support is the wise move.
scenarios.relearn: For heavy, persistent stress, reach support like a trusted adult or Tele-MANAS 14416.

scenarios.hook: Match the 'handle the big stuff' step to what it does.
scenarios.relearn: Name it, break it down, ask early, keep a routine and lean on people to handle big stress.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: change being hard doesn't mean you're failing at it. Hear that?
scenarios.affirm: Change is genuinely hard for everyone; finding it hard is human, not failure.
scenarios.relearn: Change being hard doesn't mean you're failing at it.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two unhealthy responses to a setback among the healthy ones.

scene.text: Taking a breath and a small next step
Harsh self-blame spirals
Asking someone for support
Telling yourself you always ruin everything
Looking at what you can learn from it

scenarios.why: Harsh self-blame and "I always ruin everything" harm you; a breath, support and learning help.
scenarios.relearn: Catch harsh self-blame and "I always ruin everything"; a small step and support are healthy.

scenarios.hook: You're carrying a lot and running on empty.

steps.prompt: It's midnight and you're hungry, with a long to-do list. What do you do?

options.text: Eat and sleep, then tackle it tomorrow
options.then: The list looks smaller after a proper meal and a night's rest.

options.text: Push on with chai and no dinner
options.then: The chai hums. By two, your head is pounding.

options.text: Add more tasks to feel productive
options.then: The list grows. Your energy shrinks.

options.text: Scroll until I fall asleep
options.then: You fall asleep on the sofa. The list is unchanged.

steps.why: Food and sleep come first. A tired mind works worse.

steps.prompt: A friend invites you for a short walk, and you feel you can't spare the time. What do you do?

options.text: Take the walk, since a break helps me work
options.then: You come back with a clearer head.

options.text: Say no since there's too much to do
options.then: You sit longer. You get less done.

options.text: Say yes but spend it on my phone
options.then: The walk is a scroll. Your head is as heavy as before.

options.text: Say I'll rest after everything is done
options.then: Everything is never done. Rest stays on tomorrow's list.

steps.why: A short break is part of the work, not a gap in it.

steps.prompt: You've had headaches and tiredness for a few days. What do you do?

options.text: Tell a parent and keep meals regular
options.then: Your mother books a check-up. She also takes over dinner.

options.text: Ignore it until the work is done
options.then: The work stretches. The headaches too.

options.text: Drink more caffeine to get through
options.then: The caffeine helps for an hour, then your hands shake.

options.text: Tell myself I'm just being lazy
options.then: The thought makes you feel worse, not better.

steps.why: Basic care is part of handling hard times, and a trusted adult can help.

scenarios.debrief: Rest, food and basic care are part of handling hard times, not a luxury.
scenarios.relearn: Build in rest and basics; you can't cope well on empty.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: adulthood has hard moments, and you can be equipped to meet them. Feel readier?
scenarios.affirm: Hard moments are part of adult life, and you're building the tools to meet them.
scenarios.relearn: Adulthood has hard moments; you can be equipped to meet them.

scenarios.hook: Sort: helps you through a transition, or makes it harder?

items.text: Asking someone who's been through it

scenarios.relearn: Preparing, leaning on support and asking help you; pretending, isolating and denial make it harder.

scenarios.hook: "You should handle big stress completely on your own now."

myth.un: You should handle big stress entirely on your own now.
myth.re: Leaning on people is part of handling stress well, at any age.
myth.why: Support multiplies your capacity to cope.

scenarios.relearn: Handling stress well includes leaning on people, not doing it alone.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which 'big stuff' tool do you most want in your pocket?
scenarios.affirm: Carry that tool, it'll meet you in exactly the hard moment you'll need it.
scenarios.relearn: Breaking it down, routine, asking early and self-kindness handle the big stuff.

scenarios.hook: You have to tell your friend Neha you won't join the group trip.
scenarios.setup: She calls tonight to settle the plan.

steps.prompt: Neha says: "So are you in for the trip? I need to book today."

options.text: "You'll honestly have more fun without me there anyway."
options.then: Neha frowns. "What does that mean? Did I do something?"

options.text: "Ugh, I'll try. Please don't count me out just yet."
options.then: "Okay, I'll hold your spot," she says, then pauses. "You sound worried."

options.text: "Can we talk? I can't come, and I'd like to explain."
options.then: Neha goes quiet, then says, "Okay. Tell me."

options.text: "Maybe. Things are a bit crazy right now, so let me see."
options.then: "Maybe? I need a yes or no today," she says, puzzled. "Is something wrong?"

steps.why: Saying it plainly and offering to explain gives her a real answer to work with.

steps.prompt: Neha says: "I'd like to understand what's going on. Is it me, or the group?"

options.text: "Not you. Money is tight and I didn't want to say."
options.then: She breathes out. "Thank you for telling me. I thought I'd upset you."

options.text: "It's complicated and awkward. Let's just drop it, okay?"
options.then: Neha lets it go, but the question hangs between you.

options.text: "You'd get upset if I told you the real reason."
options.then: "Now I'm worried. Just say it, please."

options.text: "It's nothing, really. I just can't make it this time."
options.then: "Nothing?" She sounds hurt and unsure what to think.

steps.why: Honest reasons, said calmly, let a friend understand instead of guess.

steps.prompt: A few days later Neha says: "I'm sad you won't be there. What do we do now?"

options.text: "Me too. Can we plan something small before you go?"
options.then: She brightens. "A chai evening on Saturday? Yes."

options.text: "Fine, I'll find a way to come along after all."
options.then: Neha looks unsure. "Only if it's really okay for you."

options.text: "Don't think about me at all. Just go and have fun."
options.then: "Okay," she says, but her voice has dimmed.

options.text: "It's only a trip. You'll be fine without me there."
options.then: Her smile fades. "Yeah. I guess."

steps.why: Staying kind while keeping your answer holds the friendship and your limit.

scenarios.relearn: Clear, calm, honest communication beats hinting and hoping.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Isha is upset after a fight with her cousin, and you want to really listen.
scenarios.setup: She starts telling you the story.

steps.prompt: Isha says: "She told everyone I lied, and I didn't. I'm so angry."

options.text: "Okay, okay. I know exactly what you should tell her next."
options.then: Isha pauses. "I haven't even finished."

options.text: "Mm-hm, go on." You are already planning your reply.
options.then: Isha slows down. "You seem somewhere else."

options.text: "So you feel blamed unfairly. Is that right?"
options.then: "Yes. That's exactly it." Isha's shoulders drop a little.

options.text: "Wait, but did you actually say it, though? Be honest."
options.then: She stiffens. "Of course not. You too?"

steps.why: Reflecting back what she said shows her that you heard her.

steps.prompt: Isha says: "And she did it in front of everyone. I felt so small."

options.text: "Same happened to me once. Let me tell you the whole thing."
options.then: She listens politely. Her own story gets lost under yours.

options.text: "Post a reply in the group chat so everyone sees it too."
options.then: Isha's face tightens. Your idea feels like more fuel for the fire.

options.text: "It's not that big a deal. People forget these things fast."
options.then: Isha shrugs and goes quiet. The feeling stays stuck.

options.text: "That sounds humiliating. Did I get that right?"
options.then: "Yes." Her eyes fill. "Nobody has said it like that."

steps.why: Naming the feeling and checking it keeps the focus on her.

steps.prompt: Isha says: "I don't even know what I want to do about it."

options.text: "Do you want ideas, or just to be heard?"
options.then: She smiles, tired. "Just heard, for now. Ideas tomorrow."

options.text: "Easy. Block her and move on with your life."
options.then: Isha stares. "It's my cousin. I can't just block her."

options.text: "Let's make a step-by-step plan for it right now."
options.then: She nods, but she looks more tired than before.

options.text: "Sleep on it. It will all feel different by tomorrow."
options.then: "Maybe," she says, and drops the subject.

steps.why: Asking what she needs lets her lead, and that is what listening is.

scenarios.relearn: Reflecting back what you heard is real listening.

scenarios.hook: Your group has a week to build a science model, and four different skill sets.

steps.prompt: On day one, everyone talks at once. What do you do?

options.text: Take over and make the whole plan alone
options.then: The plan is neat. Two teammates look sidelined.

options.text: Ask everyone what they're good at doing
options.then: Karan likes wiring, and others name theirs. A rough plan comes together.

options.text: Wait for the loudest person to decide
options.then: Karan's idea wins. A couple of people go quiet.

options.text: Take the easiest job and keep quiet
options.then: You finish fast, and the hard parts wait for someone else.

steps.why: Matching roles to strengths gets everyone working and included.

steps.prompt: Nisha hasn't said much, and her name isn't on the plan yet. What do you do?

options.text: Ask her what she'd like to take on
options.then: She lights up. "Actually, I'd love to do the labels and diagrams."

options.text: Give her whatever task is left over
options.then: She nods. It's the part nobody wanted.

options.text: Leave her be so she can join if she wants
options.then: She doesn't, and the group never hears her ideas.

options.text: Do her part myself to save time
options.then: You save an hour. She stops offering ideas.

steps.why: Asking someone what they'd like to do includes them for real.

steps.prompt: Two days before the deadline, Karan's part is late. What do you do?

options.text: Quietly redo his whole part myself tonight
options.then: You finish at 2 am. He isn't sure what he did wrong.

options.text: Complain about him to the teacher after class
options.then: The teacher asks the group to sort it out. Karan feels watched.

options.text: Say nothing and just hope it arrives on time
options.then: The deadline gets closer, and so does the stress.

options.text: Ask what's blocking him and offer to split it
options.then: He admits he's stuck on the wiring. You split it.

steps.why: Asking what's in the way and sharing the load keeps the team whole.

scenarios.debrief: Good collaboration shares the load by strengths and includes everyone.
scenarios.relearn: Collaborate by sharing roles and including everyone.

scenarios.hook: Your cousin Pooja has asked you to fill in her practical records for the third time.
scenarios.setup: She turns up with her notebooks again.

steps.prompt: Pooja says: "Please, just once more? Everyone helps family like this."

options.text: "Let me check my schedule and I'll tell you tomorrow."
options.then: She leaves the notebooks. The question is still open.

options.text: "Fine. Leave them here. I'll find the time somehow."
options.then: She thanks you. Your revision slips aside again.

options.text: "You always do this to me. Stop asking me for things."
options.then: Pooja flushes. "I thought we were close."

options.text: "I can't do that, but I can explain the hard parts."
options.then: Pooja sighs. "Okay. That's something."

steps.why: A clear no with something real to offer keeps the boundary and the bond.

steps.prompt: The next day Pooja says: "There are more records than I thought. Aunty will be so upset if I fail."

options.text: "I care. I can't fill them in, but I can help you plan."
options.then: She goes quiet, then nods. "Okay. Plan how?"

options.text: "That's not my problem. Go and talk to your own mother."
options.then: Pooja's eyes sting. "Wow. Okay."

options.text: "I'm sorry. I'll do half of them, and you do the rest."
options.then: "Thank you!" You feel a small, familiar resentment.

options.text: "Okay, okay. I'll do them all. Please don't be upset."
options.then: She grins and leaves. The tightness in your chest stays.

steps.why: Caring about her and holding your answer can both be true.

steps.prompt: A few weeks later Pooja shows up with the next set of notebooks. She asks: "Where do we go from here?"

options.text: "Ask someone else. I'm done with all of this now."
options.then: Pooja turns away, hurt. She has nobody else to ask.

options.text: "I'll do them, but this is honestly the last time ever."
options.then: She promises, and a month later she is back with yet another set.

options.text: "After all the records I've filled, you ask me again?"
options.then: Pooja goes red. "I didn't know you felt like that."

options.text: "Tonight I'll sit with you for an hour while you do them."
options.then: She nods. "That works. I'll bring chai."

steps.why: A clear offer of what you can do keeps the boundary respectful, not harsh.

scenarios.relearn: A clear, respectful boundary beats a resentful yes.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Zoya has been cold since you picked Mira as your project partner.

steps.prompt: Zoya answers you with one-word replies. What do you do?

options.text: Ask if we can talk, and say I want her side
options.then: She types, deletes, then says, "Okay. After class."

options.text: Ignore it until she cools down
options.then: The silence stretches. She tells a classmate you don't care.

options.text: Snap back with one-word replies
options.then: The chat goes cold. Both of you are annoyed now.

options.text: Post something vague about fake friends
options.then: Everyone guesses who it's about. Zoya sees it first.

steps.why: Asking to talk and listening opens the door without blame.

steps.prompt: Zoya says you chose Mira over her without even asking. What do you do?

options.text: Explain why it really wasn't a big deal
options.then: She goes quiet. Her face says she hasn't been heard.

options.text: Tell her she's exaggerating this a lot
options.then: She looks away. "See? This is what I mean."

options.text: Apologise for everything just so it ends
options.then: She says okay. The real issue is still untouched.

options.text: Listen to it all, then say what I heard
options.then: She nods slowly. "Yeah. That's exactly it."

steps.why: Saying back what you heard shows you listened, which calms things.

steps.prompt: Zoya asks: "So what do you want to happen now?"

options.text: Say forget it: nothing needs to change
options.then: She shrugs. The same thing could happen again.

options.text: Say she should apologise first
options.then: Her jaw tightens. The talk goes back to blame.

options.text: Suggest a fair way to pick partners
options.then: She smiles slightly. "Okay. Let's do that."

options.text: Ask her to decide everything from here
options.then: She agrees, and you lose a say in it.

steps.why: A fair plan you both agree on fixes the cause, not just the feeling.

scenarios.debrief: Conflict handled calmly and fairly can strengthen a relationship.
scenarios.relearn: Address conflict calmly, listen, and seek a fair resolution.

scenarios.hook: "Being good with people is just something you're born with."

myth.un: People skills are something you're just born with.
myth.re: Communication, listening, boundaries and conflict skills are all learnable.
myth.why: Like any skill, they grow with practice.

scenarios.relearn: People skills are learnable, not just innate.

scenarios.hook: Sort: strengthens a relationship, or strains it?
scenarios.relearn: Listening, respecting boundaries and owning mistakes strengthen a bond; talking over, resentment and scorekeeping strain it.

scenarios.hook: Your summer internship starts Monday, with people you didn't choose.

steps.prompt: Your team lead, Mr. Khan, is brisk and you clash on day one. What do you do?

options.text: Match his tone with sarcasm
options.then: He raises his voice, and the room feels tense.

options.text: Avoid him and pass messages through others
options.then: Messages get garbled. He starts to doubt you.

options.text: Stop speaking up so I don't clash
options.then: The days are calm. You share fewer ideas than you could.

options.text: Stay polite, say what I need, ask what he needs
options.then: He relaxes a little. "Fair. Let's work it out."

steps.why: Respect and clear talk can work even with people you clash with.

steps.prompt: In a meeting, a colleague presents an idea you once told him as his own. What do you do?

options.text: Say nothing and quietly fume all week
options.then: You smile through the meeting. The anger lingers all week.

options.text: Call him a thief in the team group chat
options.then: Others gasp. The chat turns into a fight.

options.text: Say calmly it was my idea, and credit both
options.then: He pauses. "Right. Sorry. We'll say both."

options.text: Stop sharing my ideas with the whole team
options.then: Nobody takes your idea again. Nobody gets the benefit either.

steps.why: Calmly claiming your work keeps the relationship and the credit.

steps.prompt: A colleague you don't like asks you to help with a task. What do you do?

options.text: Say no because we aren't really friends
options.then: They shrug. The team notices the cold shoulder.

options.text: Help clearly and kindly, within my limits
options.then: They thank you. The next meeting is easier.

options.text: Help, but make them feel small about it
options.then: The task gets done. They avoid you now.

options.text: Help, but only if they return the favour
options.then: They agree stiffly. Helping now feels like a deal, not teamwork.

steps.why: Working well with people you don't choose is part of adult life.

scenarios.debrief: Working respectfully across differences is core to adult and work life.
scenarios.relearn: Work with respect and clear communication, even with people you clash with.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Dev wants his debate topic, and you see it differently.
scenarios.setup: He turns to you for your view.

steps.prompt: Dev says: "My topic is obviously the best. You agree, right?"

options.text: "Mm, sure." Smile, then complain about him to the others later
options.then: By lunch half the group knows. Dev notices the whispers and gets defensive.

options.text: "I see it differently. Can I explain, then hear yours?"
options.then: Dev shrugs. "Okay. Go on."

options.text: "Sure, whatever you think is best."
options.then: Dev grins and tells the others. Your own idea stays unsaid until he asks about it.

options.text: "You're just wrong. Yours is the weakest topic."
options.then: Dev's jaw sets. "Excuse me? Fine, we'll vote."

steps.why: Saying you see it differently, and offering to listen too, keeps it respectful.

steps.prompt: Dev says: "My reasons are solid. What's your topic, and why would it be better?"

options.text: "Let me share mine, then tell me what I'm missing."
options.then: He listens, then nods slowly. "The examples part is good, actually."

options.text: "You never listen anyway, so I didn't bother explaining."
options.then: He goes red. "That's not fair. You never even tried."

options.text: "Because mine is. I shouldn't have to prove it to you."
options.then: Dev folds his arms. "Then there's nothing to talk about."

options.text: "Forget it. We'll do yours. It's not worth the fight."
options.then: He relaxes, but the others grumble, and you can feel the thing you didn't say.

steps.why: Sharing your reasons and asking what you missed makes it a conversation, not a contest.

steps.prompt: The teacher wants the topic by evening. The team is still unsure, and Dev says: "We should settle this properly."

options.text: "Mine wins, since I spoke up about it first."
options.then: Dev stares. "That's not how it works."

options.text: "Let's ask the teacher to pick. No more talking about it."
options.then: The teacher says to decide yourselves. The group is back where it started.

options.text: "I'll vote for yours so this ends today."
options.then: "Great," he says, and the vote ends in a minute. You feel flat.

options.text: "Let's list pros and cons for each and then vote."
options.then: Dev agrees. The list shows both topics have real strengths.

steps.why: A fair way of deciding keeps the disagreement from becoming a fight.

scenarios.relearn: Respectful disagreement explains and listens, rather than attacks.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: half of adult life is other people, so people skills are worth real practice. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Investing in people skills pays off in nearly every part of adult life.
scenarios.relearn: People skills are half of adult life and worth real practice.

scenarios.hook: You asked your cousin Vikram not to read your phone, and he has done it again.

steps.prompt: You catch Vikram scrolling your phone. What do you do?

options.text: Tell myself it's only a phone and let it slide
options.then: He keeps the phone and sees you hesitate. Nothing changes.

options.text: Shout that he can never be trusted with anything
options.then: He yells back. The whole house hears.

options.text: Say calmly I asked him not to, and take it back
options.then: He grumbles but hands it over. "Fine. Sorry."

options.text: Start hiding the phone without telling him why
options.then: He's confused. The issue stays unspoken.

steps.why: Restating the line calmly shows it's real without a fight.

steps.prompt: Later, Vikram reaches for your phone again. He says it's just a phone and you're overreacting. What do you do?

options.text: Apologise for overreacting just so it ends
options.then: He's relieved. You feel your own line sliding.

options.text: Repeat that it's private, without a debate
options.then: He rolls his eyes. "Okay, okay." He doesn't touch it again.

options.text: Argue until he finally admits he was wrong
options.then: The argument goes on an hour. He never admits anything.

options.text: Let him look if he promises to tell nobody
options.then: He shrugs and scrolls happily. He'll ask again next week.

steps.why: Holding the same calm line, without arguing, is what makes it stick.

steps.prompt: At dinner, your aunt says family shouldn't have secrets. What do you do?

options.text: Say privacy isn't secrets, then talk to Mummy afterwards
options.then: Aunty pauses. Vikram mutters, "Fair enough." Later your mother listens and says she'll speak to him.

options.text: Say you're right and I'll let them look whenever
options.then: You hand your phone over. Your stomach clenches.

options.text: Say it's Vikram who actually has the secrets
options.then: The table turns on him. The talk turns into a fight.

options.text: Tell myself I'm making a fuss over nothing
options.then: The talk moves on. You wonder whether your line was ever fair.

steps.why: A boundary is about privacy, not secrets, and a parent can back you up.

scenarios.debrief: A boundary only works if you hold it, calmly and consistently.
scenarios.relearn: If a boundary is crossed, restate it calmly and hold it.

scenarios.hook: Sort: emotional intelligence with others, or the opposite?

items.text: Bottling it up till you snap

scenarios.relearn: Noticing feelings, clear talk and naming your own feeling are EQ; ignoring, assuming and bottling up aren't.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which people skill do you most want to grow?
scenarios.affirm: Growing that skill will improve your friendships, family and future work.
scenarios.relearn: Listening, boundaries, conflict and clear talk are people skills to grow.

scenarios.hook: You joked about a friend's accent in front of others, and she went quiet.

steps.prompt: Priya hasn't replied to your messages since the joke. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for her to bring it up first
options.then: Days pass. The silence feels worse each day, until she stops you in the corridor.

options.text: Message that I'd like to listen and say sorry
options.then: She replies after an hour. "Okay. Can we talk tomorrow?"

options.text: Send "It was only a joke. Don't be sensitive."
options.then: She reads it and doesn't reply. Days later she stops you in the corridor, hurt.

options.text: Ask our friends to tell her I'm sorry
options.then: She hears it second-hand and wonders why you didn't come yourself. Then she asks to talk.

steps.why: Reaching out and offering to listen puts the repair first.

steps.prompt: Priya says she's been teased about her accent for years. What do you do?

options.text: Listen, and say sorry for the hurt without excuses
options.then: Her shoulders loosen. "Thank you for hearing it."

options.text: Say I didn't mean it, so it's fine
options.then: She stares at you. "That's not how it landed."

options.text: Say other people joke about it too
options.then: She goes quiet and looks away.

options.text: Promise never to joke again so she forgives me
options.then: She nods, unsure, and you feel the pressure to be forgiven.

steps.why: Listening without excuses is how trust gets repaired.

steps.prompt: Priya is still wary and asks what happens now. What do you do?

options.text: Ask her to forgive me properly today
options.then: She says she needs time, and you feel rejected.

options.text: Buy her a gift and treat it as sorted
options.then: She thanks you politely. She's still wary.

options.text: Say I've apologised enough now
options.then: Her face closes. "Okay."

options.text: Change how I joke, and give her time
options.then: You stop the accent jokes. She gives a small, careful smile.

steps.why: Changing what you do, and giving time, is what rebuilds trust.

scenarios.debrief: Owning your impact and repairing it is a mature people skill.
scenarios.relearn: If you hurt someone, listen, take responsibility, and make it right.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: being good with people isn't about being liked by all, it's about respect both ways. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Mutual respect, not universal popularity, is the heart of real people skills.
scenarios.relearn: People skills are about mutual respect, not being liked by everyone.

scenarios.hook: "Asking for help means you've failed at being an adult."

myth.un: Asking for help means you've failed at adulting.
myth.re: Help-seeking is a lifelong strength; capable adults lean on people too.
myth.why: No one does adult life entirely alone.

scenarios.relearn: Asking for help is a lifelong strength, not a failure.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: who's in your support network, the people you can lean on?
scenarios.affirm: Knowing who you can lean on means you're never truly facing things alone.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing your support network means you're never facing things alone.

scenarios.hook: "Once you turn 18 you stop needing support."

myth.un: Once you're 18 you stop needing support.
myth.re: Needing people never expires; help-seeking continues for life.
myth.why: Adults rely on networks throughout their lives.

scenarios.relearn: Needing support never expires; it continues for life.

scenarios.hook: Match the support to what it's good for.

pairs.right: Support right when you need it

scenarios.relearn: Different supports, friends, mentors, professionals, suit different needs.

scenarios.hook: You have felt weighed down all month, but you don't want to burden anyone.

steps.prompt: Your cousin Meera asks how you are, and she looks free to talk. What do you do?

options.text: Wait until you've fixed it, then mention it later
options.then: Weeks pass. The heaviness doesn't move, and you carry it alone.

options.text: Say you're fine, so she doesn't worry
options.then: She smiles and chats about her day. You feel lonelier.

options.text: Sigh loudly and hope she asks again
options.then: She misses it and sends a thumbs-up on the way out.

options.text: Tell her it has been a heavy month and ask to talk
options.then: Meera puts her phone away. "Of course. Tell me."

steps.why: Reaching out when it is heavy lets the people who care show up.

steps.prompt: A week later Meera says you've seemed tired and that she is there. What do you say?

options.text: "Maybe later. I'm still trying to work it out on my own."
options.then: She says okay. Later never quite arrives.

options.text: "Sorry, I'm always complaining. Please forget I said anything."
options.then: Meera shakes her head. "You aren't complaining."

options.text: "Thanks. I'd like to talk more, if you can."
options.then: She sits down. "I've got all evening."

options.text: "No, no. I really don't want to waste your time."
options.then: She nods, but she looks a little hurt.

steps.why: Accepting the offer shows you can lean on someone who cares.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says everyone needs support sometimes. Who do you name as people you can lean on?

options.text: "I'll just push harder and not think about it."
options.then: He hesitates. "Not thinking about it usually just postpones it."

options.text: "Only Meera. I don't want to bother more people."
options.then: He nods. "More people would carry less each."

options.text: "Meera, my mother, and you, sir."
options.then: He smiles. "That's a good circle to have."

options.text: "Nobody. I'll manage on my own."
options.then: He frowns gently. "Managing alone is tiring."

steps.why: More than one person to lean on makes the load lighter, and it is never a burden.

scenarios.debrief: Letting people support you isn't a burden; it's how connection works.
scenarios.relearn: Reach out when struggling; you're not a burden to people who care.

scenarios.hook: Weeks have passed, and the heaviness hasn't lifted, even though friends and family listen.

steps.prompt: Another week goes by and it still feels heavy. What do you do?

options.text: Keep leaning only on friends and hope it eases
options.then: Your friends keep trying. The heaviness stays exactly the same.

options.text: Call Tele-MANAS 14416 or tell a trusted adult
options.then: Someone listens and helps you work out the next step.

options.text: Fill every evening with games until it fades
options.then: The hours pass quickly. The heaviness is waiting when you stop.

options.text: Decide it's just a phase and you are overreacting
options.then: You brush it aside again. Another week goes by, still heavy.

steps.why: Bigger struggles need the right level of help, and a trusted adult is a good start.

steps.prompt: Your school counsellor, Mr. Reddy, says he has a free slot this week. What do you do?

options.text: Wait to see if you feel better first, then decide
options.then: The slot passes. The heaviness is still there next week.

options.text: Book the slot and tell a parent you are going
options.then: Mr. Reddy confirms Thursday. Your mother says she's glad you told her.

options.text: Go once, then stop if it feels awkward
options.then: The first talk is awkward. You don't go back, and nothing changes.

options.text: Skip it, because counselling is for people who can't cope
options.then: You tell yourself you're fine. The heaviness doesn't shift.

steps.why: Taking the slot and telling a parent means more people can support you.

steps.prompt: Mr. Reddy checks in again and says this kind of heaviness is common and can ease with support. What do you do next?

options.text: Tell a parent or carer, and keep Tele-MANAS 14416 handy
options.then: Your mother holds your hand. "We'll work through this together."

options.text: Keep it secret so your family doesn't worry
options.then: You carry it alone. Mr. Reddy gently says he'd like your family involved.

options.text: Wait until exams are over, then think about it
options.then: Exams pass. You are more tired and still carrying it.

options.text: Rely only on friends and a self-help video
options.then: The video helps for a day. The heaviness comes back.

steps.why: You didn't cause this and need not carry it alone, so more help is wise.

scenarios.debrief: Matching the help to the size of the struggle is wise self-care.
scenarios.relearn: For bigger struggles, reach a professional or Tele-MANAS 14416.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: building your network before you need it means it's there when you do. See the value?
scenarios.affirm: A network built early is a safety net that's there the moment you need it.
scenarios.relearn: Build your support network before you need it.

scenarios.hook: You want to reach out to your older cousin Karan for support.
scenarios.setup: He is free this evening, playing a game.

steps.prompt: Karan says: "Hey, you look quiet. Everything okay?"

options.text: "It's a long story. Forget it, honestly."
options.then: He shrugs and goes back to the screen. A moment later he looks over again.

options.text: "I'm going through something. Could I talk to you?"
options.then: He pauses the game. "Yes. I've got all evening."

options.text: "Nothing, I'm fine. Just tired. That's all."
options.then: He nods. "Okay. Sleep well." Then he hesitates, still watching you.

options.text: "Oh, you know. Life." Sigh and hope he asks more.
options.then: He laughs. "Same, same." Then he puts the controller down and looks at you.

steps.why: Asking plainly is the clearest way to open real support.

steps.prompt: Karan turns to you and says: "I'm here if you want to tell me what's going on." You feel nervous.

options.text: "Actually, it's silly. Never mind about it."
options.then: He shrugs. "If you say so." He waits, and a little more comes out.

options.text: "It's just exam stuff. Don't worry about me."
options.then: He nods, relieved, then gently asks again. A little more comes out.

options.text: "I don't know where to start. Can I just talk?"
options.then: "Take your time. I'm not going anywhere."

options.text: "Can you promise not to tell anyone at all?"
options.then: He pauses. "I'll listen. If it's big, I may need to bring someone in."

steps.why: Not having perfect words is fine, because starting is the hard part.

steps.prompt: After you talk, Karan says: "Thanks for telling me. Is there anyone else we should bring in?"

options.text: "No one else. It's just you I trust with this."
options.then: He nods, but he looks a bit worried.

options.text: "I'll think about it a bit later on, maybe."
options.then: "Okay," he says gently. Later never has a date.

options.text: "Nobody. I only wanted to vent for a bit."
options.then: He nods. You both feel the weight is still there.

options.text: "Maybe my mother. Will you sit with me?"
options.then: "Absolutely. Let's do it tonight."

steps.why: Bringing in a trusted adult adds support, and none of this is your fault.

steps.prompt: A week later Karan texts: "How are you doing? Want to talk again?"

options.text: "Let's not make a big thing of it, okay?"
options.then: He says okay. The door feels a little more closed.

options.text: "I'm okay now. No need to check in again."
options.then: He replies "alright" and stays quiet. The offer stays.

options.text: "Maybe. I don't want to be a bother."
options.then: "You're not," he writes, but he can't make you answer.

options.text: "Yes please. That helped me a lot."
options.then: "Good. Evening call?"

steps.why: Saying yes again shows needing support isn't a one-time thing.

scenarios.relearn: A simple, direct 'I could use someone to talk to' opens real support.

scenarios.hook: Sort: builds a support network, or isolates you?

items.text: Insisting on doing it all alone
Checking in on the people you care about

scenarios.relearn: Staying in touch and asking early build support; cutting off and going solo isolate you.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Rohan has been quiet, and tonight he texts that things are hard.

steps.prompt: Rohan texts that he's had a rough few weeks and wants to talk. You have an exam tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: Send a quick "Stay strong!" and go back to studying
options.then: He sends a thumbs-up. He doesn't say more.

options.text: Reply "Busy, talk later" and forget about it
options.then: He replies "ok" and the chat goes quiet for a while.

options.text: Tell him it's just exam stress and he'll be fine
options.then: He types and deletes. He says "maybe" and logs off.

options.text: Reply that you're here and call him for a short while
options.then: He picks up. His voice is shaky, but he starts to talk.

steps.why: Making time for even a short call shows him he is not alone.

steps.prompt: Later, Rohan reaches out again and says everything feels heavy and he doesn't know why. What do you do?

options.text: Give him a list of fixes: sleep early, run, stop worrying
options.then: He nods politely. He doesn't say anything more that night.

options.text: Say everyone feels like this, so it's no big deal
options.then: He gives a small laugh. "Yeah. Okay," he says.

options.text: Say you're glad he told you and ask what would help
options.then: He breathes out. "I just needed someone to hear it."

options.text: Tell him about your own bad month instead
options.then: He listens kindly. His own words stay unspoken.

steps.why: Listening first and asking what helps lets him say what he needs.

steps.prompt: A few days on, Rohan is still low and says he wants no one else to know. What do you do?

options.text: Drop it, because he asked you not to push
options.then: He thanks you. The heaviness stays his alone.

options.text: Offer to go with him to a trusted adult or Tele-MANAS 14416
options.then: He is quiet, then says, "Okay. Can you come with me?"

options.text: Promise to be his only support and tell no one else at all
options.then: You check on him daily. You start to feel worn thin.

options.text: Tell the class group so everyone can help him
options.then: Rohan feels exposed and stops answering your texts.

steps.why: Going with him to a trusted adult gets help in place, and none of this is his fault.

scenarios.debrief: Support networks work both ways, being there for others too.
scenarios.relearn: Be a support for others: listen and help them find help if it's big.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: self-care habits, sleep, movement, downtime, keep you able to cope. Worth building now?
scenarios.affirm: Self-care habits built now will steady you through all of adult life.
scenarios.relearn: Self-care habits like sleep and downtime keep you able to cope.

scenarios.hook: "Reaching out for mental-health support is shameful."

myth.un: Reaching out for mental-health support is shameful.
myth.re: It's a normal, smart, strong thing to do, just like any other health care.
myth.why: Stigma is the only thing that makes it feel otherwise.

scenarios.relearn: Reaching out for mental-health support is normal, smart and strong.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'you don't have to do adulthood alone', does that land as a relief?
scenarios.affirm: You really don't have to do it alone, that's the most important message here.
scenarios.relearn: You don't have to do adulthood alone.
