scenarios.hook: Match each habit to the toolkit part it keeps strong.
Lensy: the toolkit you've carried since you were small is now ready for adult life. Feel equipped?
scenarios.affirm: Everything you've built since the start is now a toolkit for your whole adult life.
scenarios.relearn: Your life-skills toolkit is now ready for adult life.

scenarios.hook: You've read the whole toolkit and want to actually use it.

steps.prompt: It's Monday and the toolkit is still just notes. What do you do?

options.text: Keep it as nice to know for now
options.then: The notes stay in your bag. The week fills up with other things.

options.text: Pick one tool and decide when I'll use it
options.then: You choose break-it-into-days and write it on your timetable.

options.text: Try all six tools at once
options.then: By Wednesday you're tired and have dropped every one.

options.text: Wait for a very stressful day to start
options.then: A calm week goes by. You think of the toolkit once.

steps.why: One tool with a time attached is easier to start than six at once.

steps.prompt: A test is announced and your stomach tightens. What do you do?

options.text: Pick a small tool that fits and use it now
options.then: You split the syllabus across five days. The test feels less huge.

options.text: Tell myself I'll start after the test
options.then: The test passes. The tool is still in the notes.

options.text: Decide the toolkit isn't for me
options.then: You close the notes and feel a little flat.

options.text: Push through the old way, no tool
options.then: You cram the night before and feel wrung out.

steps.why: A tool used under real pressure is how it becomes a habit.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, a friend asks how you're handling the tests. What do you do?

options.text: Say I'm fine and leave it there
options.then: She shrugs. You lose the chance to keep it real.

options.text: Explain every tool until her eyes glaze over
options.then: She nods politely and forgets all of it.

options.text: Say it's all sorted now
options.then: She's impressed. You feel pressure to look perfect.

options.text: Tell her honestly what I've tried and how it went
options.then: She says she'd like to try something too and asks what.

steps.why: Telling someone makes it real, and an honest story helps them more.

scenarios.debrief: A tool used once becomes a habit you keep.
scenarios.relearn: Put one tool into practice this week to make it real.
Values, a network and asking early are in the toolkit; going solo, suppressing and proving you never struggle aren't.
scenarios.hook: Sort: in your Life-Ready toolkit, or not?
Lensy: being 'life ready' isn't having it all figured out, it's having the tools and your people. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Life-ready means equipped and supported, not having every answer, and you are.
scenarios.relearn: Being life-ready is having the tools and your people, not all the answers.

scenarios.hook: A friend is anxious about adulting and feels alone in it.

steps.prompt: Kabir sighs and says everyone else seems ready. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him to just figure it out
options.then: He goes quiet and turns back to his phone.

options.text: Say everyone feels it, so it's no big deal
options.then: He nods, but the heaviness stays on his face.

options.text: Change the subject to something fun
options.then: He laughs along. The worry is still there when you part.

options.text: Say I feel unsure sometimes too
options.then: He looks up. "Really? You always seem sorted."

steps.why: Saying you've felt it too is how someone learns they aren't alone.

steps.prompt: Kabir asks what actually helps with all of it. What do you do?

options.text: Send him a long list of everything I know
options.then: He opens it, feels more buried, and doesn't reply.

options.text: Say it's different for everyone
options.then: He nods. He still has nothing to try.

options.text: Share one or two tools that worked for me
options.then: He writes down the one-next-step idea and tries it that evening.

options.text: Offer to handle his forms for him
options.then: He's relieved today. He's no more ready next month.

steps.why: A tool or two that he can try is more useful than everything at once.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, Kabir says he's still struggling to get started. What do you say?

options.text: Tell him to just push through
options.then: He nods tightly. Trying starts to feel like homework.

options.text: Say a small step counts, and ask what he'd try next
options.then: He says he'll ask his cousin to be his go-to person.

options.text: Pick his next step for him
options.then: He agrees to everything. It stays your plan, not his.

options.text: Say it's just not for everyone
options.then: He shrugs. He stops trying and goes back to worrying alone.

steps.why: Counting a small step as progress and asking keeps the next step his own.

scenarios.debrief: Passing on the toolkit and reassurance is real support.
scenarios.relearn: Share the toolkit and remind a friend they're not alone.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: biggest take-away from Life Ready?
scenarios.affirm: Any of those, carried forward, makes you genuinely ready for the life ahead.
scenarios.relearn: Know yourself, decide well, handle the big stuff, don't go it alone.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: you've grown from naming feelings as a kid to running your own life. Feel how far that is?
scenarios.affirm: From a small friend naming feelings to a near-adult ready for life, that's real growth.
scenarios.relearn: You've grown from naming feelings to being ready to run your own life.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: whatever the future holds, you have a toolkit and people, and that's enough to start. Believe it?
scenarios.affirm: A toolkit and your people is genuinely enough to step into adulthood, you're ready.
scenarios.relearn: A toolkit and your people is enough to step into adulthood.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: stepping into adult life equipped and not alone, worth carrying that forward?
scenarios.affirm: Equipped and not alone, that's exactly how to step into the life ahead.
scenarios.relearn: Step into adult life equipped, and never alone.

scenarios.hook: It's stream-choosing time. Relatives all push commerce, but you love biology.

steps.prompt: An aunty phones to say commerce is the only sensible choice. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her and ask what facts she's basing that on
options.then: She goes quiet, then talks about a neighbour's son and his steady salary.

options.text: Say yes so the calls stop
options.then: The calls stop. You feel quietly squeezed.

options.text: Say biology is what I love and nothing else counts
options.then: She is offended and tells your mother. The calls get louder.

options.text: Say my father will handle it
options.then: She phones him. Now the argument is his and yours is still unanswered.

steps.why: Asking for the facts behind advice separates input from pressure.

steps.prompt: That evening you sit down to look at your stream choice properly. What do you do?

options.text: List subjects, costs, jobs and interest for both
options.then: Biology has a long road and a real pull. Commerce has clear steps and a steady start.

options.text: Ask three aunties which stream earns more
options.then: Each says a different answer, with full confidence.

options.text: Look up which stream the top scorers chose
options.then: Their choices fit their strengths, which aren't yours.

options.text: List only biology's good points and best colleges
options.then: The list is long and cheerful. It skips the hard parts.

steps.why: A fair list covers facts, costs and your interests for both options.

steps.prompt: A senior says biology means a longer, costlier road. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what the longer road involves for me
options.then: He lays out the years, the fees and where help is available.

options.text: Ask my aunty if the cost makes biology a bad idea
options.then: She says yes at once. Your question about the real cost goes unanswered.

options.text: Ignore him and keep biology no matter what
options.then: You feel sure and then caught out when fees come up.

options.text: Take commerce so nobody has to worry
options.then: The calls stop. You think about biology more than you expected.

steps.why: Hard facts about a path are worth hearing before you commit to it.

scenarios.debrief: Use the method: facts, your values, the long term, then own it.
scenarios.relearn: Decide a stream by facts and your own values, not relatives' pressure.

scenarios.hook: A coaching centre tells you seats fill today, so pay the full fee now or lose your place.

steps.prompt: The woman at the desk taps the fee form and says only two seats are left. What do you do?

options.text: Say I'll check the details first, in writing
options.then: Her smile tightens. She says the offer may not last.

options.text: Pay a booking amount now so I don't lose the seat
options.then: The receipt is printed in a minute. The rest is still due, and you feel a flutter of worry.

options.text: Say yes and promise to pay the full fee by evening
options.then: She says the seat is held only until you pay.

options.text: Walk out quietly without asking any questions
options.then: You feel relieved and a bit rude. The questions stay unasked.

steps.why: A big payment is never due in one minute. Ask for the details in writing.

steps.prompt: Back home, your father asks what the centre said. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him all of it, including the pressure to pay
options.then: He listens and asks to see the form.

options.text: Say it went fine and not mention the deadline
options.then: He nods. You carry the pressure alone.

options.text: Say they were rude and I'll never go back
options.then: He wonders what happened, and the facts stay unclear.

options.text: Say I'll sort it out myself and not worry him
options.then: He looks relieved. You are less sure than you sound.

steps.why: A trusted adult can help check a big money decision.

steps.prompt: A few days later, you start comparing two other centres. What do you do?

options.text: Check fees, result claims and refund rules for each
options.then: One centre won't put refunds in writing. That helps narrow it down.

options.text: Pick the one with the biggest ad
options.then: The ad is shiny. The details are thin.

options.text: Pick the cheapest one without reading anything
options.then: The price is low and the fine print is hidden.

options.text: Ask the first centre which other one is better
options.then: She names a friend's centre with a smile.

steps.why: Compare facts across options instead of trusting a single seller.

steps.prompt: The first centre calls again and says the seat goes to someone else tonight. What do you do?

options.text: Say I'll pass, since a fair seat can wait
options.then: She pauses, then says goodbye politely.

options.text: Pay today to keep the seat
options.then: The payment is non-refundable. You wonder about that detail.

options.text: Ask whether they'll hold the seat a few days
options.then: She says maybe, if you pay today.

options.text: Shout that they cheated me and hang up
options.then: You feel a flash of power and shake afterwards.

steps.why: False urgency is a sales tactic. A real seat can wait for a fair look.

scenarios.debrief: False urgency is a pressure tactic, not a fact about your timeline.
scenarios.relearn: Resist false 'decide now or lose it' urgency on big money choices.

scenarios.hook: An online 'mentor' you don't know DMs you a paid course that promises a top rank.

steps.prompt: His message says only five seats are left and the rank is guaranteed. What do you do?

options.text: Hold off paying and check who he really is
options.then: You close the chat. A small fear of missing out tugs at you.

options.text: Say yes, since a guarantee means it works
options.then: He sends a payment link and a warm message within seconds.

options.text: Ask for a discount and pay if he agrees
options.then: He offers a discount in seconds. The speed feels odd.

options.text: Ask him for a free demo, then decide
options.then: He sends a short clip and pushes you to pay before you've seen anything real.

steps.why: A guarantee of results is a warning sign. Check first.

steps.prompt: You look him up and find only his own page and his own ads. What do you do?

options.text: Show a parent or teacher and check it together
options.then: Your teacher says she'll look at it with you. You aren't alone with it.

options.text: Decide that no reviews doesn't matter and go ahead
options.then: His page looks professional. Nothing outside it backs it up.

options.text: Message him to ask him to prove the rank claim
options.then: He replies with screenshots that can't be checked.

options.text: Ask the comments on his page if it works
options.then: Everyone there praises him. Several accounts look brand new.

steps.why: A trusted adult helps check a claim. Being targeted is never your fault.

steps.prompt: A classmate says she paid and got the notes, and tells you to hurry. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what she got and if her marks have changed
options.then: She admits the notes are copied pages and it's too soon to tell.

options.text: Decide to pay too so I don't fall behind her
options.then: Your fear of being behind makes the amount feel small, and you open the payment link.

options.text: Trust her because she's a friend
options.then: She sounds sure. She is repeating what she was told.

options.text: Ask her to cover my payment and I'll repay later
options.then: She frowns. Now there's money between you and the same doubt.

steps.why: A friend's word isn't proof. Ask what she actually got.

steps.prompt: The mentor writes again: 'Last chance, or your rank is gone.' What do you do?

options.text: Let it go and show the message to a trusted adult
options.then: Your mother reads it, thanks you for showing her, and says she'll look into it.

options.text: Pay half to be safe
options.then: Half the money is gone, and the pressure doubles.

options.text: Reply with angry abuse
options.then: He screenshots your reply. Now it's a messy back and forth.

options.text: Ask him for a day to arrange the money
options.then: He agrees warmly and sends a new payment link. The pressure carries on.

steps.why: Pressure to pay now is a tactic. Sharing it with an adult keeps you safe.

scenarios.debrief: A good decision weighs facts; 'guaranteed results' is a warning sign.
scenarios.relearn: Distrust guaranteed-outcome promises; verify before you pay.

scenarios.hook: Your friends all plan a gap year of travel and say you're boring if you don't join.

steps.prompt: They send a group poll and everyone is waiting for your vote. What do you do?

options.text: Say I'll think about my goals and reply tomorrow
options.then: Someone sends a groan emoji. Your phone goes quiet for a while.

options.text: Vote yes right now so nobody calls me boring
options.then: Your vote shows up with a row of hearts. Your stomach drops a little.

options.text: Vote no and say their plan is silly
options.then: Two friends reply with annoyed faces and the chat turns tense.

options.text: Leave the poll and mute the chat
options.then: The chat fills up without you. You feel left out and relieved.

steps.why: A group poll is not a deadline. Taking time to think is allowed.

steps.prompt: The next day a friend messages you directly to ask where you really stand on the trip. What do you do?

options.text: Say I'm still checking my goals
options.then: She says okay, a bit stiffly. You feel steadier.

options.text: Agree to come along to keep the friendship
options.then: She cheers. You feel pulled along, not chosen.

options.text: Say they were never real friends anyway
options.then: The chat goes silent and you replay it all evening.

options.text: Change the topic and say nothing about it
options.then: The topic changes. The question follows you around all day.

steps.why: You can value friends and still weigh your own goals.

steps.prompt: Time to give the group your final answer. How do you tell them?

options.text: Tell them my answer and why, kindly
options.then: They ask a few questions. Your reasons are out in the open.

options.text: Say nothing and just stop replying in the chat
options.then: The chat drifts on. They find out from someone else.

options.text: Joke that I'm too boring to travel anyway
options.then: A few friends laugh. Your real reasons never come out.

options.text: Say yes without explaining my reasons
options.then: The group celebrates. Nobody knows why you agreed, or whether you wanted to.

steps.why: Share your answer and reasons kindly, whichever way you decide.

scenarios.debrief: Weigh the group's input, then decide by your own goals.
scenarios.relearn: 'Everyone's doing it' isn't a reason; decide by your own goals.

scenarios.hook: You have one week to make a big choice, and your mind keeps spinning.

steps.prompt: It's Sunday night, the first evening of your week. What do you do?

options.text: Write it down: facts, values, then outcomes
options.then: The mess becomes three short lists. It's still hard, but less foggy.

options.text: Stay up thinking until I feel sure
options.then: It's past midnight and you aren't any surer.

options.text: Scroll my phone to forget about it for now
options.then: The evening goes by. The choice is waiting for you in the morning.

options.text: Ask everyone I know what they would do
options.then: Seven messages come back, and no two say the same thing.

steps.why: Breaking a big choice into steps turns a spin into a plan.

steps.prompt: Midweek, you realise you don't know one key fact about the choice. What do you do?

options.text: Find that fact or ask for it this week
options.then: A teacher gives you the missing detail in two minutes.

options.text: Guess what it probably is and move on
options.then: The guess feels fine. You can't tell if it's right.

options.text: Leave it and hope it won't matter
options.then: The gap sits there like a loose step on a staircase.

options.text: Ask a friend who sounds sure about it
options.then: She sounds sure. She's guessing too.

steps.why: A missing fact is worth finding before you decide.

steps.prompt: It's the last day and you still feel nervous. What do you do?

options.text: Go through facts and values once, then decide
options.then: You still feel nervous. You also know why you chose.

options.text: Wait for the nerves to go before deciding
options.then: The nerves don't leave, and the deadline arrives anyway.

options.text: Choose the first option I thought of on Sunday
options.then: It feels quick. You skip everything you learned this week.

options.text: Let a coin decide
options.then: The coin picks one. You feel oddly unconvinced.

steps.why: Steps and facts let you decide even when you're nervous.

scenarios.debrief: A big choice feels lighter when you break it into the method's steps.
scenarios.relearn: Break a hard choice into facts, values and consequences.

scenarios.hook: At a cousin's wedding, a relative offers a 'great match' and says deciding right now shows maturity.

steps.prompt: She adds that the family is waiting and wants your answer today. What do you do?

options.text: Say I need time and I'll talk with my parents
options.then: She pauses. "Well, don't take too long." The room is awkward.

options.text: Wonder if I'm being childish for not agreeing
options.then: She nods as if that settles it. Your question is still unanswered, and the doubt follows you around.

options.text: Snap in front of everyone that it's my life
options.then: The room goes silent. Your mother looks at you with a worried face.

options.text: Ask a cousin whether I should just say yes
options.then: Your cousin shrugs. "Everyone gets married, no? Why fuss." It doesn't help.

steps.why: No answer is due today, and marriage under 18 isn't allowed. Take time and bring in your parents.

steps.prompt: That night at home, your mother asks about the relative's offer. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her what was said and that I need time
options.then: She sits down. She says she wants to hear more.

options.text: Say a friend told me it's just talk and to ignore it
options.then: She nods, unsure. The question stays on your own shoulders.

options.text: Say I'm probably overreacting and drop it
options.then: She says maybe so. You aren't sure you believe it.

options.text: Say people at the wedding think I should just agree
options.then: She raises her eyebrows. Now other people's views are in the room too.

steps.why: A parent can help once they know what was said. Needing time is fair.

steps.prompt: A cousin warns that good proposals don't wait. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what she's worried about, then share mine
options.then: She admits she's worried for you. You start to hear each other.

options.text: Start to believe good proposals really don't wait
options.then: The worry grows. Your own questions start to fade.

options.text: Tell her she's being old-fashioned about it
options.then: She laughs, hurt. The talk stops there.

options.text: Ask her to decide for me
options.then: She says no and looks uneasy. She doesn't want to carry it either.

steps.why: People's worries are worth hearing. Your own timeline still comes first.

steps.prompt: A week later the relative phones again for your answer. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her, say I'm not ready, tell my mother
options.then: She sounds a little cool. Your mother says she'll speak to her.

options.text: Tell myself it's rude to refuse an elder
options.then: She says elders know best, and names another day to call.

options.text: Say a sharp no and snap that she should stop
options.then: She sounds hurt and says she only meant well. The line goes quiet.

options.text: Tell myself a no needs a reason she will accept
options.then: You search for words that will satisfy her. She says she'll call again when you have them.

steps.why: Never your fault. Marriage under 18 isn't allowed. Parents, a teacher or Childline 1098 can help.

scenarios.debrief: Maturity is deciding well, not deciding fastest.
scenarios.relearn: A life decision is yours to take on your own timeline.

scenarios.hook: Two people you trust give you advice that completely contradicts each other.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says one thing and your uncle says the opposite. What do you do first?

options.text: Ask each of them why they think so
options.then: Your teacher gives data and your uncle shares his own past. Both are useful.

options.text: Follow whoever I spoke to last
options.then: It's an easy rule. The earlier advice slips out of your mind.

options.text: Follow the one I like more
options.then: You feel comfortable. You haven't tested anything yet.

options.text: Ask a third person to settle it
options.then: A cousin picks a side in a second. Now there are three opinions.

steps.why: Asking for reasons turns two opinions into material you can use.

steps.prompt: Both of them now explain their reasons to you in full. What do you do?

options.text: Check each against facts and my values
options.then: One reason fails the facts. One fits your values well.

options.text: Count who has more reasons and pick them
options.then: One side has more reasons, but they're weaker ones.

options.text: Go with the one who sounded more confident
options.then: His voice was sure. His facts were thin.

options.text: Take half of each so nobody is upset
options.then: The mix suits neither plan. It leaves you with half of everything.

steps.why: Advice is input. Facts and your values do the deciding.

steps.prompt: You've decided, and one of them is disappointed with your choice. What do you do?

options.text: Thank them both and explain my reasons calmly
options.then: He frowns, then says he understands your reasons even if he disagrees.

options.text: Apologise and change my choice to please them
options.then: The mood lifts. The choice is no longer yours.

options.text: Tell them I won't ask either of them again
options.then: They both look hurt. You've closed two doors.

options.text: Avoid them both for a while
options.then: The silence grows and your reasons never get shared.

steps.why: Explaining your choice calmly keeps relationships and your decision.

scenarios.debrief: Conflicting advice is normal; your values break the tie.
scenarios.relearn: Test advice against facts and your values, then decide.

scenarios.hook: A part-time job clashes with your study hours, and the rent is due.

steps.prompt: The shop owner offers extra evening shifts for better pay. What do you do?

options.text: Ask for a day to weigh the pay against study
options.then: He says fine, but the shifts won't stay open for long.

options.text: Say yes at once because the rent is due
options.then: The pay will help. Your textbooks stay shut the next evening.

options.text: Say yes to every shift and study later
options.then: Your week fills up. Study turns into 'someday'.

options.text: Say no, since studying is all that matters
options.then: He shrugs and gives the shifts to someone else. The rent is still due.

steps.why: Weighing pay against study time keeps both needs in sight.

steps.prompt: Your mother says the rent is short by a week's pay. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with her and list needs, goals and costs
options.then: You both see the real gap is smaller than the fear.

options.text: Take every extra shift without telling her
options.then: The money comes in. You get very tired, very quickly.

options.text: Offer to stop school until money is better
options.then: She is torn and very sad. Nothing is settled.

options.text: Borrow from a friend and tell nobody
options.then: The gap closes for now. You owe someone and she doesn't know.

steps.why: Money choices work best when you list needs, goals and costs together.

steps.prompt: A teacher notices you look tired and asks what's going on. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her about the job, the rent and the exams
options.then: She listens and tells you about a small fund for students.

options.text: Say it's nothing and keep going
options.then: She nods, unconvinced. The tiredness stays.

options.text: Say I'll drop the exams to work more
options.then: She looks worried and asks you to think again.

options.text: Say it's all my family's fault
options.then: She sees how hard it is. The talk turns to blame, not options.

steps.why: Telling a trusted adult opens options you can't see alone.

scenarios.debrief: Money choices use the same method: facts, needs vs wants, the long term.
scenarios.relearn: For money, weigh needs, goals and the long term together.

scenarios.hook: An app pushes a loan for a new phone with easy EMIs and a 'decide now' timer.

steps.prompt: A countdown shows ten minutes left on the offer. What do you do?

options.text: Close the app and look at the full cost
options.then: The timer disappears from the screen. So does the pressure.

options.text: Tap accept because the EMI looks small
options.then: A small number flashes on screen. A form asks for more details.

options.text: Take just a small loan so it's not much debt
options.then: The app suggests a bigger amount 'for your convenience'.

options.text: Ask a friend whether it's worth it first
options.then: She says everyone does it. She hasn't read the terms either.

steps.why: A countdown is pressure. The full cost is the fact.

steps.prompt: You open the full terms and the total is far above the phone's price. What do you do?

options.text: Show a parent the terms and ask what they think
options.then: Your father reads it twice and sighs. He's glad you showed him.

options.text: Decide the phone is worth it anyway
options.then: You feel a rush. The total doesn't go away.

options.text: Look for another app with a smaller EMI
options.then: The next app has the same trick in a different place.

options.text: Close the terms since they're too long to read
options.then: The terms disappear. They still apply to you.

steps.why: Debt deserves the whole picture and a trusted adult's eyes.

steps.prompt: A friend says everyone gets phones on EMI and the terms are nothing to worry about. What do you do?

options.text: Say I read the total, and it's far above the price
options.then: She rolls her eyes, but asks what the total was.

options.text: Say she's right and keep the offer in mind
options.then: She smiles. Your worry is still there, quieter.

options.text: Argue that all EMIs are a trick
options.then: She gets defensive. You both stop listening.

options.text: Say nothing and let it pass
options.then: You change the topic. The doubt stays with you.

steps.why: You can ask about cost without judging anyone else's choice.

steps.prompt: A month later, a shop has the phone you wanted at a lower price. What do you do?

options.text: Compare price and need, and wait until I truly need one
options.then: The cost is clearer now. The want has cooled a little.

options.text: Buy it now before the price changes
options.then: It's yours by evening. Your savings take a hit.

options.text: Take a new loan to buy it at once
options.then: A new app agrees in minutes. The debt grows.

options.text: Stop looking, since I missed the chance anyway
options.then: The want turns sour. You still don't know what you need.

steps.why: Need versus want, and the real cost, keep money decisions steady.

scenarios.debrief: A 'need vs want' check and the real cost guard money decisions.
scenarios.relearn: Check real cost and need vs want before taking on debt.

scenarios.hook: You're choosing between a safe, known option and a riskier one you really want.

steps.prompt: A friend says the risky one is obviously better because you want it. What do you do?

options.text: List what I could gain and lose with each
options.then: Both columns have real entries. Neither option wins on paper yet.

options.text: Agree that wanting it is reason enough
options.then: It feels thrilling. Nothing is on paper yet.

options.text: Lean towards the safe one so nobody says I took a chance
options.then: Everyone relaxes. A little of your excitement leaves with them, and nothing is final yet.

options.text: Ask her to promise it will work out
options.then: She laughs and promises. A promise can't hold the risk for you.

steps.why: Listing real gains and losses shows what each option costs.

steps.prompt: Looking again at the risky option, you notice downsides you hadn't counted. What do you do?

options.text: Check how bad each downside could get
options.then: The worst case is hard but not unbearable. One downside stays unclear.

options.text: Hope they won't happen
options.then: The downsides sit in the corner of every plan.

options.text: Ignore them so I can stay excited
options.then: The excitement stays. The downsides stay with it.

options.text: Put the whole decision off until next month
options.then: You feel relief, then a pang of 'what if'. The decision is still waiting.

steps.why: Honest trade-offs mean looking at downsides, not hiding from them.

steps.prompt: It's time to choose. Part of you is still scared. What do you do?

options.text: Choose by my priorities, with a plan either way
options.then: Fear is still there. So is a clear plan.

options.text: Wait until the fear disappears
options.then: The fear stays, and the chance closes.

options.text: Pick the safe one just to stop being scared
options.then: The fear fades for now. The wondering doesn't.

options.text: Choose the risky one and not think about it
options.then: You commit with a flourish. The plan is missing.

steps.why: Fear doesn't need to vanish. A choice made on priorities, with a plan, is enough.

scenarios.debrief: Hard choices have real costs; your priorities break the tie.
scenarios.relearn: Name the trade-offs honestly, then choose by your priorities.

scenarios.hook: Your family expects engineering, but you're drawn to design and afraid to say so.

steps.prompt: A relative asks at a family function what you'll study. What do you say?

options.text: Say I'm deciding and will talk it over at home
options.then: She nods and passes you a plate. Nothing explodes.

options.text: Say engineering, as everyone expects
options.then: The room approves. Your stomach knots.

options.text: Say design loudly so everyone hears
options.then: The room goes quiet, then louder. Your parents stare.

options.text: Make a joke and change the topic
options.then: People laugh. The question is only delayed.

steps.why: You don't have to announce anything. You can simply say you are deciding.

steps.prompt: Later that night you can't sleep, thinking about it. What do you do?

options.text: Write what draws me to design and what worries me
options.then: Your page shows more interest than fear, and some real worries.

options.text: Tell myself it doesn't matter and try to sleep
options.then: You lie awake until two. The question is still there.

options.text: Decide to forget design since it'll cause trouble
options.then: The idea fades. A dull ache replaces it.

options.text: Post about it online to see what people say
options.then: Strangers argue in the replies. None of them know you.

steps.why: Writing it down turns a vague worry into things you can look at.

steps.prompt: A few days on, design is still in the back of your mind. What do you do?

options.text: Look up courses, costs and jobs, and ask a teacher
options.then: You find real paths and one useful question for your parents.

options.text: Read only the success stories about designers
options.then: The stories are exciting. They skip the hard years.

options.text: Skip research and trust my gut completely
options.then: Your gut is loud. It has no facts to share.

options.text: Compare design to engineering on pay alone
options.then: One number wins, and it says nothing about what you enjoy.

steps.why: Facts about courses, costs and jobs make a values-based choice solid.

steps.prompt: Your father notices you've been quiet and asks what's on your mind. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him calmly what I'm drawn to and why
options.then: He is quiet, then asks what made you interested.

options.text: Say it's just exams and nothing else
options.then: He nods, unconvinced. Then he says your mother mentioned you've been looking at design.

options.text: Say I'll do engineering to keep him happy
options.then: He looks relieved. Then he says your mother mentioned you've been looking at design.

options.text: Say he never listens to me
options.then: He stiffens. Then he says your mother mentioned you've been looking at design.

steps.why: A calm, honest reason lets a parent hear your values, not a fight.

steps.prompt: He says design isn't a career. What do you do?

options.text: Say I respect his worry, and show him what I found
options.then: He reads your notes without a word, then asks about fees.

options.text: Drop the subject and promise to take engineering
options.then: He relaxes. You feel your plan slide away.

options.text: Say I'll leave home if he won't agree
options.then: The room freezes. A threat shuts down the talk.

options.text: Wait for my mother to speak up for me
options.then: She tries. He hears her as taking your side.

steps.why: Within safety and law, your future is yours to decide. Explain it calmly.

scenarios.debrief: Within safety and law, your future is yours to decide by your values.
scenarios.relearn: Decide your path by your own values, and explain it calmly.

scenarios.hook: A 'sure-shot' investment tip is going round your class group chat.

steps.prompt: A classmate posts the tip with screenshots of big profits. What do you do?

options.text: Check where the tip came from and how it works
options.then: The screenshots can't be traced to anyone. The tip has no source at all.

options.text: Plan to put in my savings so I don't miss it
options.then: You open the payment page and refresh it all evening, finger hovering.

options.text: Ask the group who else is putting money in
options.then: Eight people say yes, and not one has read anything about it.

options.text: Tell everyone in the chat it's a scam
options.then: Your classmate is furious. Others join in on both sides.

steps.why: Check a tip's source and how it works before you trust it.

steps.prompt: You find that nobody in the chat can explain how the money is made. What do you do?

options.text: Ask a parent or teacher what they make of it
options.then: Your teacher says unexplained returns are a reason for caution.

options.text: Assume someone else has already checked
options.then: The tip keeps rolling. Everyone assumes that someone has.

options.text: Put in a small amount just to test it
options.then: A small amount goes in. A bigger ask follows.

options.text: Ask the classmate to show proof of her profit
options.then: She sends another screenshot. It proves nothing new.

steps.why: A trusted adult can spot what a crowd misses.

steps.prompt: Your friend says the tip closes tonight and urges you to put in real money now. What do you do?

options.text: Hold back, since a real chance can wait
options.then: Your friend sulks. Your savings stay where they are.

options.text: Put in my pocket money so I won't regret it
options.then: The pocket money is gone, and your heart is thudding.

options.text: Borrow from my sister to put money in
options.then: She hands it over, worried. Now two people are exposed.

options.text: Put money in if my friend promises to cover any loss
options.then: Your friend agrees quickly. A promise like that has nothing behind it.

steps.why: A crowd's excitement isn't evidence. Facts protect you.

scenarios.debrief: Decide on facts, not rumour or the crowd's excitement.
scenarios.relearn: Verify a 'sure-shot' tip's facts and risk before you act.

scenarios.hook: You chose a path months ago, and now a small setback makes you want to scrap it all.

steps.prompt: Your first test on this path goes badly. What do you do?

options.text: Check what went wrong and if it's fixable
options.then: The gaps are specific, and two of them look fixable.

options.text: Quit the whole plan right now
options.then: The tension drops for a day. The empty space after it is large.

options.text: Blame the path and look for a new one
options.then: A new path looks bright. It has bumps of its own.

options.text: Hide the result and hope it won't matter
options.then: The result stays in your bag. The next test is closer.

steps.why: A bad result is information about what to adjust.

steps.prompt: A friend on another path says you should switch to hers. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what suits her, then weigh my reasons
options.then: Her path fits her. Your original reasons still hold up.

options.text: Switch since hers looks easier
options.then: The new path looks smooth for a week. Then the bumps appear.

options.text: Tell her she's wrong to suggest it
options.then: She is hurt and stops sharing. Your own doubt is unchanged.

options.text: Ask other friends which path is better
options.then: Three friends give three answers. None of them know your reasons.

steps.why: A friend's path is one example. Compare it with your own reasons.

steps.prompt: A month on, one thing has improved and one is still hard. What do you do?

options.text: Keep what works and adjust the hard part
options.then: The hard part takes a new approach. It's slow, but it moves.

options.text: Scrap everything because one part is hard
options.then: The plan is gone. The hard part comes with you.

options.text: Pretend the hard part isn't there
options.then: It lurks and shows up on test day.

options.text: Wait and hope the hard part fixes itself
options.then: A month later it's the same, and the deadline is closer.

steps.why: A good decision can survive a setback with small adjustments.

scenarios.debrief: A good decision can survive a setback; learn and adjust.
scenarios.relearn: A setback is data to adjust, not a reason to scrap a good plan.

scenarios.hook: Two coaching ads make opposite claims about the 'only' way to crack the exam.

steps.prompt: One ad says self-study is useless and the other says coaching is a waste. What do you do?

options.text: List what I need from a study plan
options.then: Your list has five items. Neither ad covers all of them.

options.text: Believe the louder, flashier ad
options.then: The flashy ad is hard to ignore. It says nothing you can check.

options.text: Pick the one with the toppers' photos
options.then: The faces are impressive. Nothing says what helped them.

options.text: Join the one that has a free trial
options.then: The trial is a sales pitch with a free chair.

steps.why: Marketing is loud. A list of what you need is quiet and useful.

steps.prompt: A friend who went to one of them says it changed her life. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what helped her and if it fits me
options.then: She explains that the small batch and weekly tests helped her.

options.text: Decide to join, since she's proof it works
options.then: You plan to sign up by evening. Your pace is different from hers.

options.text: Dismiss her because she has a bias
options.then: She goes quiet. A useful fact goes with her.

options.text: Ask the centre to confirm her story
options.then: They praise her warmly. That tells you nothing new.

steps.why: One person's result is a clue. Ask what exactly helped.

steps.prompt: You've tried a sample of each, and it's time to choose. What do you do?

options.text: Choose what fits how I study and my budget
options.then: The fit isn't glamorous. It's one you can keep up.

options.text: Choose the one with the nicer classroom
options.then: The chairs are comfy. The batches are huge.

options.text: Choose the one my friends joined
options.then: You'll have company. The pace is theirs, not yours.

options.text: Take both to be safe
options.then: The fees double, and your week gets very full.

steps.why: What fits your way of studying beats what looks impressive.

scenarios.debrief: Marketing claims aren't facts; decide by what fits you.
scenarios.relearn: Ignore ad hype; decide by what fits your own needs.

scenarios.hook: You keep putting off a decision and hope it will sort itself out.

steps.prompt: You open your calendar and the decision's deadline looks close. What do you do?

options.text: Admit delay is a choice and set a date
options.then: The date goes into your phone. A small knot loosens.

options.text: Put it off for one more week
options.then: The week passes and the knot returns.

options.text: Wait to see if the option closes by itself
options.then: Nobody closes it. Time is quietly doing it for you.

options.text: Start a long list of things to check first
options.then: The list keeps growing. The date never gets set.

steps.why: Putting a decision off is also a choice. Set a date to choose on purpose.

steps.prompt: A week later you sit down to deal with it and you feel nervous. What do you do?

options.text: Start with the smallest step I can take today
options.then: One phone call is done. The rest looks less heavy.

options.text: Wait until I feel braver
options.then: Braver doesn't arrive and the days continue.

options.text: Do other chores first and run out of time
options.then: The room is spotless. The question is untouched.

options.text: Ask a friend to just choose for me
options.then: She chooses quickly. You wonder if it suits you.

steps.why: A small first step is easier than waiting for courage.

steps.prompt: The option you wanted may close within days. What do you do?

options.text: Decide on purpose now, using what I know
options.then: It's a decision, not a drift. It feels like your own.

options.text: Keep delaying and see if it stays open
options.then: It stays open for two more days. Then it doesn't.

options.text: Choose in a panic on the last day
options.then: The choice comes fast. The reasons are missing.

options.text: Let it close and say it wasn't meant to be
options.then: The door shuts. 'Meant to be' covers the choice you avoided.

steps.why: Deciding on purpose beats drifting into a result.

scenarios.debrief: Avoiding a decision is still a choice: make it deliberately.
scenarios.relearn: Avoiding is a choice too; decide on purpose, not by drift.

scenarios.hook: Your family has firm views on how seriously a girl should plan her career.

steps.prompt: An uncle says girls shouldn't overthink careers and should pick a safe course early. What do you do?

options.text: Say my career deserves careful thought too
options.then: He laughs, then asks what you're considering.

options.text: Nod politely and stay quiet for the evening
options.then: He takes your nod as agreement and tells others.

options.text: Argue back until he finally says sorry
options.then: The room tenses. He holds his ground.

options.text: Tell him maybe he's right that girls overthink
options.then: He nods, pleased. The doubt sits with you for a while.

steps.why: Your career deserves the same careful thought as anyone's.

steps.prompt: Your cousin brother gets time and money to explore his options. What do you do?

options.text: Ask my parents for the same support
options.then: Your mother is surprised, then asks what you'd like to try.

options.text: Feel it's unfair and stay silent
options.then: The feeling grows. Nobody knows it exists.

options.text: Take it as proof I should settle early
options.then: The idea hardens. You haven't really tested it.

options.text: Demand more than he gets to even it out
options.then: They bristle. The talk becomes about fairness, not about you.

steps.why: Ask for the same room to explore. It starts a fairer conversation.

steps.prompt: A teacher asks what you want after school, and you aren't sure. What do you do?

options.text: Say I'm exploring and ask for help
options.then: She gives you three questions to think about and a contact.

options.text: Say whatever my family expects
options.then: She writes it down. The question closes.

options.text: Say I'll do what's easiest to arrange
options.then: The easy route sounds quick. It's missing what you want.

options.text: Say I haven't thought about it at all
options.then: She shrugs. You notice you've given nothing to work with.

steps.why: Exploring openly is a strong start. Careful thought is for everyone.

scenarios.debrief: Your career decision deserves the same care as anyone's.
scenarios.relearn: Reject the double standard; decide your career with full care.

scenarios.hook: A big choice is freezing you because you want a guarantee that it will work out.

steps.prompt: You've gathered the facts but still want proof it will work. What do you do?

options.text: Decide with what I know, uncertainty and all
options.then: The doubt doesn't vanish. Neither does your list of reasons.

options.text: Wait for one more piece of proof
options.then: A new piece of proof arrives and raises two new questions.

options.text: Wait for a gut feeling that it's right
options.then: The certainty doesn't come. The days go by.

options.text: Ask several people to promise it will go well
options.then: They promise kindly. None of them will be living your life.

steps.why: No choice is guaranteed. Deciding well with what you know is enough.

steps.prompt: A senior says there's no such thing as a risk-free choice. What do you do?

options.text: Ask how he made his own big choices
options.then: He tells you about one that went wrong and what he changed.

options.text: Take it as an excuse to choose at random
options.then: You pick with a coin. It feels flippant, then oddly scary.

options.text: Argue that he was simply lucky
options.then: He laughs and says luck helped, but so did a process.

options.text: Feel more scared and stall for time
options.then: The fear grows. The days keep passing.

steps.why: Hearing how others decide shows you the method behind a good choice.

steps.prompt: By the deadline you've made your choice, and a friend asks what happens if it doesn't work out. What do you do?

options.text: Say I'll adjust and learn if it doesn't
options.then: She nods. Saying it makes the fear a little smaller.

options.text: Panic and reopen the whole choice
options.then: The decision wobbles for a few days before you settle back on it.

options.text: Say it will definitely work out
options.then: She's reassured. You aren't, and you know it.

options.text: Change the topic fast
options.then: The subject changes. The question stays with you.

steps.why: A good decision includes a plan for adjusting if things go differently.

steps.prompt: A month in, things are going okay but not perfectly. What do you do?

options.text: Fix what I can and keep going
options.then: You adjust one thing. The next week goes better.

options.text: Decide the choice was a mistake
options.then: You start looking at other paths and lose a month.

options.text: Hide the problems so it looks perfect
options.then: Everyone thinks it's going smoothly. You feel alone with it.

options.text: Compare my path with a friend's smooth one
options.then: Her path looks easy from outside. Yours looks harder by comparison.

steps.why: A well-made choice can still have bumps. Adjusting is part of owning it.

scenarios.debrief: A good decision is made well, not guaranteed to turn out perfectly.
scenarios.relearn: Decide well with what you know; outcomes aren't fully yours to control.

scenarios.hook: A form asks you to commit to a course with fees you don't fully understand.

steps.prompt: The clerk says everyone signs here without reading. What do you do?

options.text: Ask him to explain each fee before I sign
options.then: He sighs and starts reading the lines out loud.

options.text: Sign quickly so I don't look unsure
options.then: The pen moves fast. A line in the middle looks odd.

options.text: Sign now and plan to ask questions later
options.then: Your signature is done. The questions pile up behind it.

options.text: Take the form home and sign without reading
options.then: You sign at home that night. A few days later you finally open the fee page.

steps.why: Understand the form before you sign. Asking is not weakness.

steps.prompt: Looking over the fee lines, you notice extra charges you hadn't planned for. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what each extra covers and what's optional
options.then: One charge turns out to be optional. Two aren't.

options.text: Ignore them since they look small
options.then: The small ones add up on a page you only skimmed.

options.text: Assume they're normal and not ask
options.then: They might be. You've no way to know.

options.text: Decide the centre is cheating and walk out
options.then: You leave angry and never find out what was fair. Your mother asks to see the final amount.

steps.why: Ask what each cost covers, which ones are optional, and why.

steps.prompt: You and your mother look at the final amount together. What do you do?

options.text: Check it against our budget first
options.then: The total is heavy but possible with a payment plan.

options.text: Pay it all so we're done
options.then: The payment goes through. Next month is tight.

options.text: Agree to it and hope we'll manage
options.then: Hope is warm. The shortfall is waiting on the 5th.

options.text: Ask my cousin to pay the difference
options.then: He agrees quickly. Now money sits between you.

steps.why: Match the real total to your budget before committing money.

scenarios.debrief: Gather the facts and ask questions before committing.
scenarios.relearn: Understand the facts before you sign or commit money.

scenarios.hook: Friends dare you to do something risky to prove you aren't scared.

steps.prompt: Everyone is watching as a friend dares you. What do you do?

options.text: Say I don't need to prove anything
options.then: A few friends groan. One looks away.

options.text: Tell myself it's quick, so it won't matter
options.then: You hover at the edge while they watch. Your heart is racing.

options.text: Think I have to prove them wrong
options.then: They keep watching. Your pride and your unease pull in opposite directions.

options.text: Tell myself a real friend would just do it
options.then: You stall while they watch. The dare is still hanging over you.

steps.why: A dare isn't a value. You can say no without making a speech.

steps.prompt: A day later, the group dares you again. A friend calls anyone who hesitates a coward, and the others laugh. What do you do?

options.text: Stay calm and say I decide for myself
options.then: The laughter fades. Someone changes the subject.

options.text: Hit back with a joke about him
options.then: The joke lands hard. He goes quiet and angry.

options.text: Wonder if they're right and I am a coward
options.then: The laughing goes on. The word follows you home.

options.text: Decide none of them were ever real friends
options.then: You pull back and sit alone. The weeks are lonely.

steps.why: Staying calm shows the dare has no power over your decision.

steps.prompt: Later, one friend privately admits he didn't want to do it either. What do you do?

options.text: Say I felt the same and suggest telling a trusted adult
options.then: He grins, relieved. You both feel lighter and plan who to tell.

options.text: Tell him he should have said so
options.then: He frowns. The talk ends there.

options.text: Say nothing and keep it to myself
options.then: You both go home with the same feeling, alone.

options.text: Tease him about it in front of others
options.then: The others laugh. He never trusts you the same way.

steps.why: A dare is pressure, never your fault. A trusted adult can back you both up.

scenarios.debrief: A dare is pressure, never your fault. Decide by your own values, and tell a trusted adult if it feels unsafe.
scenarios.relearn: Don't let a dare decide for you; choose by your values.

scenarios.hook: A choice you made didn't work, and you feel like a failure at deciding.

steps.prompt: A result comes back showing the choice didn't work. What do you do?

options.text: See it as one event and look at what happened
options.then: You make a short list of what you'd change.

options.text: Tell myself I'll always choose badly
options.then: The thought sits heavy. It fits too neatly.

options.text: Decide never to choose big things again
options.then: The pressure lifts. Your options shrink with it.

options.text: Hide it from everyone
options.then: Nobody knows. You carry it alone, and it gets heavier.

steps.why: One result is data, not a verdict on who you are.

steps.prompt: A friend asks if you're okay since you've gone quiet. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her honestly what happened
options.then: She listens and says she's had a plan flop too.

options.text: Say I'm fine and change the subject
options.then: She frowns, unsure. The quiet continues.

options.text: Say it's all my fault and leave it there
options.then: She tries to cheer you up. It doesn't help much.

options.text: Make a joke so she won't ask
options.then: She laughs. The joke covers the thing you needed to say.

steps.why: Sharing a miss shrinks it and lets people support you.

steps.prompt: A smaller, similar decision comes up. What do you do?

options.text: Decide using what I learned
options.then: You catch the old warning sign early and adjust.

options.text: Refuse to decide to stay safe
options.then: The choice gets made by default.

options.text: Ask her to decide for me
options.then: She gives a quick answer. It isn't about your life.

options.text: Do the exact opposite of last time
options.then: You swing to the other extreme. It fits no better, because you never checked why it failed.

steps.why: Using what a miss taught you is how judgement grows.

scenarios.debrief: A choice that didn't work is data, not a verdict on you.
scenarios.relearn: Learn from a decision that flopped; that's deciding well over time.

scenarios.hook: A big decision keeps you up at night, and your school counsellor, Mr. Reddy, notices you look tired.

steps.prompt: Mr. Reddy asks how you're doing. You haven't slept well in days. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him what's weighing on me
options.then: He listens first. He doesn't tell you what to choose.

options.text: Say I'm fine and it's honestly nothing
options.then: He nods, but his eyes stay on you for a moment.

options.text: Say I should handle it on my own like an adult
options.then: He says that's an understandable wish. The door stays open.

options.text: Say I'm just tired from all the studying
options.then: He notes the studying and asks no more.

steps.why: Saying the heavy thing out loud is the first step of sharing it.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Mr. Reddy sees you still look tired. He suggests talking with your parents about what's weighing on you. What do you do?

options.text: Agree and ask him to help me start
options.then: He offers to help you find the words to start.

options.text: Say they'd only add pressure, so I won't
options.then: He nods, and says pressure is real. Then he asks what might help.

options.text: Say I'll tell them if it gets any worse
options.then: The decision stays unshared until the next bad night.

options.text: Say I'd rather talk to my friends only
options.then: Friends help. They don't know the facts as you do.

steps.why: A trusted adult, at home or at school, can help carry the decision and the facts.

steps.prompt: At home your mother senses something and asks. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her it's heavy and I need help
options.then: Her shoulders drop. She says she's glad you said it.

options.text: Say it's nothing for her to worry about
options.then: She doesn't believe you. She lets it rest for tonight.

options.text: Say I can handle it so she needn't ask
options.then: She nods, wounded. The night is long.

options.text: Tell her only the half that's easy
options.then: She helps with the half. The rest sits unsaid.

steps.why: Telling a trusted adult the whole picture lets them actually help.

steps.prompt: In the weeks after, some sleepless nights still come back. What do you do?

options.text: Go back to Mr. Reddy and keep a rest routine
options.then: Mr. Reddy listens, then says Tele-MANAS 14416 is there too if the nights stay heavy.

options.text: Go back to carrying it alone
options.then: The weight returns by midnight. You tell nobody.

options.text: Stay up working it out in secret
options.then: The nights get longer. The decision doesn't move.

options.text: Take it as a sign I'm failing at this
options.then: The thought is loud at 2 a.m. It isn't true.

steps.why: Sharing with people and resting is strength. Heavy nights deserve real support.

scenarios.debrief: Big decisions are easier shared; leaning on people is a strength.
scenarios.relearn: Lean on a trusted adult or mentor for a heavy decision.

scenarios.hook: "A mature person decides instantly and never wavers."

myth.un: A mature person decides instantly and never wavers.
myth.re: Mature deciding takes the time it needs; pausing to think isn't weakness.
myth.why: Big choices deserve real thought, not a snap answer.

scenarios.relearn: Taking time on a big decision is mature, not indecisive.

scenarios.hook: "If you decide right, nothing will ever go wrong."

myth.un: Decide right and nothing will ever go wrong.
myth.re: Even a well-made decision can hit bumps; the skill is deciding well, not controlling outcomes.
myth.why: Outcomes depend on things outside your control; good process is what's yours.

scenarios.relearn: Deciding well doesn't guarantee a smooth outcome.

scenarios.hook: "Asking advice on a decision means you're not capable."

myth.un: Asking advice means you're not capable.
myth.re: Gathering input is part of deciding well; capable people seek perspective.
myth.why: More information and viewpoints make for a wiser choice.

scenarios.relearn: Seeking advice is part of a good decision, not a weakness.

scenarios.hook: "Once you decide, changing your mind is failure."

myth.un: Changing your mind once you've decided is failure.
myth.re: Updating a choice as you learn more is wisdom, not failure.
myth.why: New facts can fairly change a good decision.

scenarios.relearn: Updating a decision with new facts is wise, not failure.

scenarios.hook: "There's a single perfect career and you must find it now."

myth.un: There's one perfect career you must find right now.
myth.re: Many paths can fit you; you decide well by your values, and paths can evolve.
myth.why: Careers shift over a lifetime; no one choice locks your whole future.

scenarios.relearn: No single perfect path; decide by your values and stay open.

scenarios.hook: "Following your own values over family wishes is selfish."

myth.un: Choosing by your own values over family wishes is selfish.
myth.re: Within safety and law, deciding your own life by your values is healthy agency, heard respectfully.
myth.why: You can listen to family and still own choices about your own life.

scenarios.relearn: Deciding your own life by your values is agency, not selfishness.

scenarios.hook: "A girl shouldn't decide her own future. Others know better."

myth.un: A girl shouldn't decide her own future; others know better.
myth.re: Everyone gets to decide their own future by their own values, within safety and the law.
myth.why: The right to decide your life isn't smaller for anyone because of gender.

scenarios.relearn: Your future is yours to decide; a double standard isn't a fact.
