scenarios.hook: Lensy: a good decision is one made well, not one guaranteed to turn out perfectly.
scenarios.affirm: Letting go of 'it must turn out perfectly' frees you to decide as well as you can.
scenarios.relearn: Aim to decide well; outcomes aren't fully in your control.

scenarios.hook: Arjun: when family input is loud, what helps you still hear your own values?
scenarios.affirm: Each of these makes room for your own voice alongside everyone else's.
scenarios.relearn: Make room for your own values even when others' input is loud.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: think about a money choice coming up. What matters most to you in it?
scenarios.affirm: Whatever you chose, weighing it on purpose is what a smart money choice looks like.
scenarios.relearn: Weigh needs, long-term cost and not being rushed in money choices.

scenarios.hook: Sneha: when others push their timeline on you, what reminds you it's your life?
scenarios.affirm: Holding onto your goals and your picture of the future keeps the timeline yours.
scenarios.relearn: Your goals and your vision keep your timeline your own.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which part of deciding like an adult do you most want to grow?
scenarios.affirm: Growing any one of these makes your future choices wiser and more truly yours.
scenarios.relearn: Facts, values, resisting pressure and owning it are all growable skills.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines using pressure, not a real reason, to push your choice.

scene.text: "Decide right now or lose the seat forever"
"Here are the actual fees in writing"
"Everyone in your batch already signed up"
"Take a day to think it over"
"Ask whatever questions you have"

scenarios.why: False urgency and 'everyone's doing it' are pressure tactics. The rest respect your choice.
scenarios.relearn: Spot false urgency and 'everyone's doing it' as pressure, not reasons.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two money red flags in this pitch.

scene.text: "Returns are guaranteed, zero risk"
"Here's the written rate and terms"
"Put in all your savings today only"
"You can ask for the full document"
"Take time to compare options"

scenarios.why: 'Guaranteed, zero risk' and 'all your savings today' are classic money red flags.
scenarios.relearn: Spot 'guaranteed returns' and 'all-in now' as money red flags.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that pressure you instead of helping you decide.

scene.text: "Don't overthink, just trust me"
"Let's look at the facts together"
"Sort it out alone, that's the grown-up way"
"What matters to you here?"
"We can ask someone who knows"

scenarios.why: 'Don't overthink' and 'sort it alone' shut down good deciding. The rest support it.
scenarios.relearn: Spot 'don't overthink' and 'do it alone' as pressure, not help.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two manipulative lines a pushy 'mentor' might use.

scene.text: "Pay now, the offer vanishes at midnight"
"You can verify my credentials"
"I guarantee you a top rank"
"Compare me with other options"
"Take your time to decide"

scenarios.why: A vanishing offer and a guaranteed rank are manipulation. Honesty invites checking and time.
scenarios.relearn: Spot vanishing offers and guaranteed results as manipulation.

scenarios.hook: Sneha: spot the two lines that pressure a girl out of deciding for herself.

scene.text: "Don't think too much, just settle"
"What future do you actually want?"
"Girls shouldn't be this picky"
"Take the time you need"
"Your goals matter here"

scenarios.why: 'Just settle' and 'girls shouldn't be picky' are pressure; the rest back her own choice.
scenarios.relearn: Spot 'just settle' and gendered guilt as pressure, not reasons.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that skip the facts a real decision needs.

scene.text: "Just go with your gut, who needs details"
"Let's read the actual terms"
"Asking questions makes you look weak"
"We can double-check the numbers"
"What does the document say?"

scenarios.why: Skipping details and shaming questions block good deciding. Facts and questions help.
scenarios.relearn: Spot 'skip the details' and 'questions look weak' as anti-fact pressure.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines pushing you to follow the crowd over your own values.

scene.text: "Everyone picked this, so should you"
"What fits your own goals?"
"You'll be left out if you don't"
"Let's weigh this for you"
"Your reasons matter most"

scenarios.why: 'Everyone picked this' and 'you'll be left out' are crowd pressure, not your values.
scenarios.relearn: Spot crowd pressure and fear-of-missing-out as not-your-values lines.

scenarios.hook: An uncle insists you choose your stream his way, and he wants your answer today.
scenarios.setup: He taps the table at a family lunch.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "Smart kids pick commerce. Decide now."

options.text: "I hear you. I'll weigh it myself first."
options.then: He leans back. "Hmm. Don't take forever."

options.text: "Okay. Whatever you say, Uncle."
options.then: He beams. "Good, that's one less thing." Your father frowns. "Let's hear what you really think, beta."

options.text: "Commerce is boring. I won't do it."
options.then: His face hardens. "Boring? You're being childish."

options.text: "I'll ask my father to answer you."
options.then: He waves a hand. "Your father will say what I say."

steps.why: Respecting his view while keeping the final call yours keeps the talk open.

steps.prompt: Your uncle adds: "My own son did well in commerce. That is the safe path, you know."

options.text: "I'm checking costs and jobs for both."
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "At least you're thinking. Fine."

options.text: "You're right. I shouldn't take any risk."
options.then: He pats your shoulder. "Sensible." Your stomach drops.

options.text: "Your son isn't me. Stop comparing us."
options.then: He frowns. "Watch your tone."

options.text: "Can we not talk about this at lunch?"
options.then: He shrugs. "We'll talk about it later, then."

steps.why: Doing your own homework shows you're deciding seriously, not just disagreeing.

steps.prompt: As lunch ends, your uncle asks: "So when will you tell us your answer?"

options.text: "By Sunday. I'll share my reasons too."
options.then: He nods slowly. "Sunday, then. I'll listen."

options.text: "Whenever. It doesn't matter what I pick."
options.then: He laughs. "Of course it matters. Don't be silly."

options.text: "Never. It's none of your business."
options.then: The table goes quiet. Your father looks at his plate.

options.text: "Maybe tomorrow. I'll go with commerce."
options.then: He smiles. "Good." You feel a stone in your chest.

steps.why: Naming a day and your reasons keeps the decision yours and respectful.

scenarios.relearn: Respect others' input, but keep the final choice your own.

scenarios.hook: A salesperson is rushing you to sign up for a costly course.
scenarios.setup: She slides the form toward you with a pen.

steps.prompt: She says: "This price is only for the next ten minutes!"

options.text: "If it's fair, it'll stay fair tomorrow."
options.then: Her smile stays. "Hmm. It might not be here."

options.text: "Alright. Where do I put my name?"
options.then: She smiles. "Just your name for now. The fee can be sorted later."

options.text: "Then I'll pay half right now."
options.then: She nods fast. "That also works. Let me print the form."

options.text: "Why are you pressuring me? Forget it."
options.then: Her smile drops. "Your loss. Sign the booking at least."

steps.why: A fair deal can wait a day. Pressure to hurry is the warning sign.

steps.prompt: She says: "Just sign here now. It's only a booking."

options.text: "I'll sign once I've read the fee terms."
options.then: She slides over a leaflet. "It's all in there." The refund line is tiny.

options.text: "Okay. A booking can't hurt."
options.then: She smiles. "Exactly." The form says the fee is not refundable.

options.text: "Can you drop the fee if I sign now?"
options.then: She leans in. "Maybe. Sign first."

options.text: "I'll sign if my friend gets a discount too."
options.then: She laughs. "Bring your friend. We'll see."

steps.why: Reading the terms before you sign shows what you're agreeing to.

steps.prompt: She says: "The price goes up tomorrow, so decide today."

options.text: "Then I'll pay more later, once I've checked."
options.then: She pauses. "Fair enough. Here's my card."

options.text: "Fine. I'll sign today then."
options.then: She holds out the pen quickly. "Smart."

options.text: "I'll come back tomorrow with money."
options.then: She nods. "I'll note your name."

options.text: "Forget it. I'm done with courses."
options.then: She shrugs. "Suit yourself."

steps.why: A good price for the right course will still be a good price after a pause.

scenarios.relearn: Call out false urgency; a fair deal survives a pause.

scenarios.hook: A relative at a wedding pushes you to settle the marriage question right away.
scenarios.setup: She finds you near the buffet.

steps.prompt: She says: "Why delay? Decide today. It shows maturity."

options.text: "I need time. I'll talk to my parents first."
options.then: She raises her eyebrows. "Hmm. Well."

options.text: "Maybe I'm being childish. Never mind."
options.then: She pats your arm. "A mature person wouldn't say never mind."

options.text: "You're being rude. Stop asking."
options.then: Her face hardens. "Is that how you talk to elders?"

options.text: "Maybe a mature person should decide fast."
options.then: She nods. "Good. Don't make me wait long."

steps.why: Your timeline is yours. Maturity is deciding well, not fast.

steps.prompt: She says: "At your age I was already married. What are you waiting for?"

options.text: "Times have changed. I'm taking my own time."
options.then: She pauses. "Hmm. Maybe so."

options.text: "You're right. I'm wasting time."
options.then: She nods happily. "Now you see."

options.text: "That's an old-fashioned way to think."
options.then: She frowns. "Old-fashioned? That's disrespectful."

options.text: "Maybe I'm just being stubborn."
options.then: She nods. "Stubborn people miss their chances." The words stay with you.

steps.why: Marriage under 18 isn't allowed, and none of this is your fault. Your own timeline is yours to keep.

steps.prompt: She says: "Then tell me when you've decided."

options.text: "Thanks. Marriage isn't on the table now."
options.then: She softens. "Alright. But the family will keep asking."

options.text: "I'll tell you by the end of next month."
options.then: She smiles. "Good. I'll ask on the first."

options.text: "Why do you need to know?"
options.then: She stiffens. "Because I'm family."

options.text: "Maybe I'm keeping everyone waiting for nothing."
options.then: She sighs. "Then don't wait for nothing. We all want an answer soon."

steps.why: A warm, firm answer keeps your timeline and the relationship.

scenarios.relearn: You get to set your own timeline on a life decision.

scenarios.hook: Friends dare you into a risky choice to prove you're brave.
scenarios.setup: They crowd around you after class.

steps.prompt: A friend says: "Scared? Just do it. Don't think."

options.text: "I decide by what's right for me."
options.then: He groans. "You and your speeches." The others exchange glances.

options.text: "If I say no, nobody will want me around."
options.then: A few of them laugh. "Nobody said that. Stop overthinking." You feel a knot in your stomach.

options.text: "I'll do it if you all do it first."
options.then: They exchange looks. "You first."

options.text: "Maybe they're right. Maybe I am scared."
options.then: He shrugs. "Then prove it."

steps.why: A dare is pressure. Your own values decide.

steps.prompt: Another friend says: "Come on, don't be boring. Everyone's in."

options.text: "Everyone being in isn't my reason."
options.then: She shrugs. "Okay, your call."

options.text: "Maybe everyone's in because it's fine."
options.then: She grins. "Exactly. Stop overthinking." You aren't sure you believe her.

options.text: "Then you all go. I don't care."
options.then: She frowns. "Why are you so touchy?"

options.text: "Fine. I'll think about it, maybe."
options.then: She grins. "Maybe means yes."

steps.why: 'Everyone's doing it' isn't a reason. Check it against your own goals.

steps.prompt: A friend takes you aside the day before: "Whatever you said earlier, it's time to decide for real. Pull out and it's your loss."

options.text: "I'm out. If it's risky, I'll tell a teacher."
options.then: He pauses. "Hmm. Okay, your call."

options.text: "Everyone's counting on me, so I can't back out."
options.then: He nods. "Exactly. Don't let them down." The knot in your stomach tightens.

options.text: "Fine. I didn't want to be in on this anyway."
options.then: He scowls. "Whatever."

options.text: "Maybe I should have just done it."
options.then: He shrugs. "Maybe." The doubt stays with you.

steps.why: You can say no, and pressure is never your fault. If it's risky, a trusted adult can help.

scenarios.relearn: Decide by your values, not to win a dare.

scenarios.hook: At a family gathering, a relative dismisses your career plan in front of everyone.
scenarios.setup: The room goes quiet as you look up.

steps.prompt: Your relative says: "Design? That's no career. Pick engineering."

options.text: "I chose this after real thought."
options.then: He sniffs. "Hmm. We'll see about that."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. Maybe I'm being unrealistic."
options.then: He nods, pleased. "Perhaps. Though I doubt you ever thought it through."

options.text: "You know nothing about design."
options.then: He stiffens. "Is that how you speak to me?"

options.text: "Maybe I'll do both, so nobody is upset."
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "Both? Sounds like you haven't decided."

steps.why: Standing by a considered choice, calmly, is respect for yourself.

steps.prompt: He says: "Show me one designer who earns well, if you've thought it through."

options.text: "I can share courses and jobs I found."
options.then: He folds his arms. "Do that, then."

options.text: "I can't think of one right now."
options.then: He smirks. "Exactly."

options.text: "Plenty do. You just don't know."
options.then: He scoffs. "Name one." You name none, and he waves it away.

options.text: "I'll ask my father to answer you."
options.then: He turns to your father. "Well?"

steps.why: Facts beat arguments. Bring what you've found.

steps.prompt: He turns to you: "And what if it fails?"

options.text: "Then I'll learn and adjust. I have a backup."
options.then: He nods slowly. "At least you've thought about it."

options.text: "Then I'll do engineering, like you said."
options.then: He smiles. "Now you're being sensible."

options.text: "It won't fail. I'm sure of it."
options.then: He laughs. "Nobody is sure."

options.text: "Why are you being so negative?"
options.then: He bristles. "I'm being realistic."

steps.why: A good decision includes a plan for adjusting if it doesn't go as hoped.

scenarios.relearn: Stand by a values-based choice calmly, even when it's dismissed.

scenarios.hook: A classmate pressures you to put money into a 'sure-shot' investment tip.
scenarios.setup: She waves her phone at you in the canteen.

steps.prompt: She says: "Everyone's putting money in. Hurry up!"

options.text: "I'll check the facts and the risk first."
options.then: She sighs. "You and your checking."

options.text: "Okay. I'll just follow everyone."
options.then: She grins. "Smart. Here's the link."

options.text: "Give me the link. I'll send some now."
options.then: She types fast. "Sent the link. Do it now, before it closes."

options.text: "I'll put in half and keep half."
options.then: She shrugs. "Half is better than nothing."

steps.why: A crowd's excitement is not evidence. Check the facts and the risk.

steps.prompt: She says: "The tip is a secret, so don't go asking around about it."

options.text: "I won't trust a secret. I'll ask my parents."
options.then: She frowns. "Then you'll miss out."

options.text: "Okay. I trust you."
options.then: She smiles. "Good. You won't regret it."

options.text: "Then tell me who gave you the tip."
options.then: She hesitates. "I can't say. That's the point."

options.text: "I'll ask my friends if they trust it."
options.then: She scoffs. "They're all in already."

steps.why: A secret you can't check is a reason for more care. Ask a parent or teacher.

steps.prompt: She says: "Last call. I'll be rich, and anyone who skips this will be sorry."

options.text: "Maybe. I'd rather check than rush."
options.then: She rolls her eyes. "Whatever."

options.text: "Wait. Take my pocket money."
options.then: She takes it quickly. "See? Easy."

options.text: "You'll regret this when it fails."
options.then: She glares. "It won't."

options.text: "Fine. I'll follow, so you stop teasing."
options.then: She smirks. "About time."

steps.why: Staying calm when teased keeps the decision yours.

scenarios.relearn: Verify facts and risk before following a money tip.

scenarios.hook: You've been carrying a heavy decision alone, and your school counsellor, Mr. Reddy, offers to help.
scenarios.setup: He catches you in the corridor after class.

steps.prompt: Mr. Reddy says: "You don't have to figure this out by yourself."

options.text: "Thank you. I'd really value talking it through."
options.then: He smiles. "Good. Come in. We'll take it step by step."

options.text: "No. I should handle it on my own."
options.then: He nods. "The offer stays open. Any time."

options.text: "It's nothing. I don't want to waste your time."
options.then: He shakes his head. "You aren't wasting it."

options.text: "Maybe later. Not today."
options.then: He nods. "All right. My door is open."

steps.why: Accepting help on a heavy decision is a strength.

steps.prompt: Mr. Reddy says: "Whenever you're ready, we can start with what makes it feel so heavy."

options.text: "I'm afraid of choosing wrong."
options.then: He nods. "That's a real worry. Thank you for naming it."

options.text: "Maybe I'm just being dramatic."
options.then: He shakes his head. "Heavy is heavy. Try me."

options.text: "Please just tell me what to do."
options.then: He smiles. "I can't choose for you. I can help you think."

options.text: "Nothing really. Can we stop?"
options.then: He leans back. "We can pause. I'm here when you're ready."

steps.why: Naming the real worry is where a heavy choice starts to feel lighter.

steps.prompt: The next time you meet, he asks: "Who else could help you with this?"

options.text: "My parents, and maybe a friend."
options.then: He nods. "Good. And Tele-MANAS 14416 is there if it gets heavier."

options.text: "No one. I'd just be a burden."
options.then: He frowns gently. "Asking for support isn't a burden."

options.text: "Only you. I don't want anyone else to know."
options.then: He nods. "I'll listen. Over time, think about who else you trust."

options.text: "Someone online will know better."
options.then: He tilts his head. "Maybe. A person who knows you matters more."

steps.why: You don't have to do it alone. Reaching out is part of deciding well.

scenarios.relearn: Accepting help on a heavy decision is a strength.

scenarios.hook: Someone shames you for asking questions before a big decision.
scenarios.setup: She sighs loudly at the course counter.

steps.prompt: She says: "Why so many questions? Just decide already."

options.text: "Good questions make a good decision."
options.then: She sighs. "Fine. Ask away."

options.text: "Sorry. I'll stop asking and just pick."
options.then: She nods briskly. "Good. Sign here."

options.text: "Fine. Which one's cheapest? I'll take it."
options.then: She taps the form. "This one. Sign."

options.text: "I'm not asking much. Why are you angry?"
options.then: She bristles. "I'm not angry. I'm busy."

steps.why: Asking questions is part of deciding well.

steps.prompt: She adds: "Other students just sign and go. That's how it works here."

options.text: "Maybe. I want to understand first."
options.then: She shrugs. "As you like."

options.text: "Then I'll be like them and stop."
options.then: She smiles. "Easy, isn't it?"

options.text: "Other students probably regret it."
options.then: She glares. "That's rude."

options.text: "I'll ask a friend instead."
options.then: She waves. "Go ahead. I'm not stopping you."

steps.why: Other people's pace isn't yours. Understanding comes before signing.

steps.prompt: She holds out the pen and says: "Anything you want to know before you sign?"

options.text: "What's the full fee, and the refund rule?"
options.then: She slides over a printed sheet. "It's all here."

options.text: "Which course is the most popular one here?"
options.then: She smiles. "This one. Everybody joins it."

options.text: "Whatever you recommend."
options.then: She taps the most expensive one. "This one."

options.text: "Nothing. I'll just sign."
options.then: She hands you the pen. "Great."

steps.why: Specific questions about cost and refunds get you real facts.

scenarios.relearn: Asking questions is part of deciding well, not a weakness.

scenarios.hook: "If boards stress you out, you're just not built for studying."

myth.un: Feeling stressed by boards means you're not built for studying.
myth.re: Exam stress is a normal response to a big moment, not a verdict on your ability.
myth.why: Stress is your body taking the exam seriously, and tools can settle it.

scenarios.relearn: Exam stress is normal, not proof you can't do it.

scenarios.hook: "A bad board result means your whole future is finished."

myth.un: A bad board result means your future is finished.
myth.re: Results matter, but many routes stay open: repeats, other streams, other colleges.
myth.why: Plenty of people reach good lives by paths that didn't start with top marks.

scenarios.relearn: One result doesn't close your future; many paths stay open.

scenarios.hook: "Real adults handle stress without ever feeling overwhelmed."

myth.un: Capable adults never feel overwhelmed by stress.
myth.re: Even capable adults feel overwhelmed; what they do is use tools and lean on people.
myth.why: Coping isn't the absence of stress, it's how you meet it.

scenarios.relearn: Feeling overwhelmed isn't failing; how you meet it is what counts.

scenarios.hook: "Leaving home for college should feel exciting, not scary."

myth.un: Leaving home should feel only exciting, never scary.
myth.re: Big moves usually feel both excited and scared at once, and that mix is normal.
myth.why: Two feelings can be true together; the fear doesn't cancel the readiness.

scenarios.relearn: Feeling scared and excited about a big move is normal, not a warning.

scenarios.hook: "Taking a study break is just being lazy."

myth.un: Taking breaks while studying is being lazy.
myth.re: Short rests, sleep and movement are part of studying well, not the opposite of it.
myth.why: A rested brain remembers and focuses better than an exhausted one.

scenarios.relearn: Rest and breaks are part of studying well, not laziness.

scenarios.hook: "You should be over a setback by now; still hurting means something's wrong with you."

myth.un: Still hurting from a setback means something's wrong with you.
myth.re: Hard things take time to settle; there's no fixed deadline for feeling okay again.
myth.why: Healing has its own pace, and being gentle with yourself speeds it more than rushing.

scenarios.relearn: There's no deadline for a setback to stop hurting; healing takes its own time.

scenarios.hook: "Telling a parent you're struggling will just disappoint them."

myth.un: Telling your family you're struggling only disappoints them.
myth.re: Most people who care would rather know early so they can stand with you.
myth.why: Carrying it alone is heavier than the honest conversation usually is.

scenarios.relearn: Letting people who care in early is strength, not a disappointment.

scenarios.hook: "A topper should never feel anxious; the anxiety means you'll slip."

myth.un: A topper feeling anxious means they're about to slip.
myth.re: High performers feel pressure too; naming it and using tools keeps it from running you.
myth.why: Anxiety is about how much you care, not a prediction of failure.

scenarios.relearn: Doing well and still feeling anxious is normal; tools keep it in check.

scenarios.hook: "Pulling an all-nighter before the paper shows real dedication."

myth.un: An all-nighter before the exam proves your dedication.
myth.re: Sleep before a paper helps recall far more than a sleepless cram does.
myth.why: A tired brain forgets and panics; rest is the smarter exam strategy.

scenarios.relearn: Sleep before a paper beats an all-nighter for recall and calm.

scenarios.hook: "If you don't know what comes after Class 12, you've already fallen behind."

myth.un: Not knowing your path after Class 12 means you've fallen behind.
myth.re: Plenty of people figure their direction over time; the next step is enough to start.
myth.why: You don't need the whole map to take a good first step.

scenarios.relearn: Not having it all mapped after school isn't behind; the next step is enough.

scenarios.hook: "Heavy stress that won't lift is just something to push through quietly."

myth.un: Heavy stress that won't lift is something to push through quietly.
myth.re: Stress that stays heavy for weeks deserves real support, like Tele-MANAS 14416 or a trusted adult.
myth.why: Reaching out early stops it from growing, and help-seeking is strength.

scenarios.relearn: Persistent heavy stress deserves support like Tele-MANAS 14416, not silent pushing.

scenarios.hook: "Coming out and sitting boards at once means you should just toughen up."

myth.un: Facing two big things at once means you should just toughen up.
myth.re: Carrying a lot at once is genuinely hard; pacing it and leaning on people is the strong move.
myth.why: Strength is using support and going step by step, not white-knuckling alone.

scenarios.relearn: Carrying a lot at once is hard; pacing and support is the strong move.

scenarios.hook: Two months to boards, and you freeze every time you open a book.

steps.prompt: You sit down with a book and your mind goes blank. What do you do?

options.text: Pick one easy topic and read for ten minutes
options.then: The topic goes in. The page feels less like a wall.

options.text: Wait until I feel motivated to start
options.then: The motivation doesn't arrive. The evening disappears.

options.text: Open the hardest chapter to be done with it
options.then: The hard chapter makes the freeze worse.

options.text: Put the book away and check my phone
options.then: The phone gives you comfort for an hour. The book is still shut.

steps.why: A tiny first step melts a freeze better than waiting.

steps.prompt: A friend says she's already finished half the syllabus. What do you do?

options.text: Keep going at my own pace and ask her for tips
options.then: She shares two tips. Neither of you has it all figured out.

options.text: Panic and try to match her pace
options.then: You study hard for two days. Then you feel worse.

options.text: Decide there's no point now
options.then: The idea feels like relief. It isn't true.

options.text: Ask for her notes and skip making mine
options.then: Her notes are neat. They're hers, not yours.

steps.why: Comparing yourself to someone else's pace doesn't help your own.

steps.prompt: A week later, you've done some work but still feel stuck. What do you do?

options.text: Tell a teacher or parent I'm stuck
options.then: Your teacher suggests a plan and a short check-in each week.

options.text: Push harder with less sleep
options.then: The nights get short. The freeze comes back.

options.text: Decide I'm bad at exams
options.then: The thought repeats and weighs more each day.

options.text: Keep it to myself and hope it passes
options.then: Nobody knows. The weeks keep passing.

steps.why: Asking for help early is a strength, and boards are not a measure of your worth.

scenarios.debrief: A freeze melts when you shrink the task to one small step you can start today.
scenarios.relearn: Beat exam freeze by starting one small topic, not waiting for motivation.

scenarios.hook: You bombed a practice paper and your thoughts are spiralling.

steps.prompt: The marked paper is in your bag at home. What do you do first?

options.text: Note which topics lost marks, then take a short walk
options.then: The marks cluster in two chapters. The walk slows your thoughts a little.

options.text: Decide you're hopeless and stop studying today
options.then: The evening passes quietly and the paper stays unopened. The dread is still there at night.

options.text: Ask a friend for her score before looking at yours
options.then: Her score is higher. You feel worse, and you still haven't read your own mistakes.

options.text: Redo the whole paper tonight to prove yourself
options.then: You're up past midnight and the second attempt is rushed. You feel more tired than sure.

steps.why: Marks show what to revise, and a walk steadies the spiral.

steps.prompt: A few days later, another test comes back lower than you hoped. What do you do?

options.text: Read your mistakes and plan one chapter to fix
options.then: You can see a small gain since the last paper. The plan fits on one page.

options.text: Look only at the total and put the paper away
options.then: The number stays in your head and the mistakes stay unread.

options.text: Tell yourself this proves you can't do it
options.then: The thought gets louder by evening, and you open no book.

options.text: Study six hours straight to make up for it
options.then: By the fourth hour you're rereading one page, and your head aches.

steps.why: Reading your own mistakes turns a score into a plan.

steps.prompt: The real exam is two weeks away and you wake up anxious. What do you do?

options.text: Tell a teacher which topics worry you and ask for help
options.then: She suggests two extra sessions and a timetable. The list feels shorter.

options.text: Keep it to yourself so nobody worries
options.then: You hold the worry alone and it follows you into every study hour.

options.text: Revise only your strongest subjects to feel calm
options.then: Revising what you know feels easy. The weak chapters stay untouched.

options.text: Study through the night with no breaks
options.then: Your notes blur by morning, and the anxiety is still sitting there.

steps.why: Asking early gets you a plan and support before the pressure peaks.

scenarios.debrief: A bad mock is feedback to act on, not your worth.
scenarios.relearn: Treat a bad practice score as data to revise from, not proof you're hopeless.

scenarios.hook: You move to a hostel in a new city next month, and the dread feels heavy.

steps.prompt: Packing hasn't started and your stomach drops whenever you think of it. What do you do?

options.text: Write a short to-do list and start with one item
options.then: The list has eight items. Ticking off the first makes the month feel less shapeless.

options.text: Refuse to think about it until the day you leave
options.then: The weeks pass quietly. The dread grows a little each time you glance at the boxes.

options.text: Tell yourself you should be excited, not scared
options.then: You smile when relatives ask. Underneath, the heavy feeling hasn't moved.

options.text: Ask your parents to sort out everything for you
options.then: They pack and book tickets happily. You feel looked after, and still unready.

steps.why: A small list turns a vague dread into steps you can do.

steps.prompt: A week before you leave, a cousin who lived in a hostel offers advice. What do you ask her?

options.text: What the first week is like, and can I save your number
options.then: She describes the mess timings and the warden's rules. You save her number.

options.text: Only about the food and the room size
options.then: You hear about food and rooms. Nothing about how the first nights feel.

options.text: Nothing. You say you're fine
options.then: She shrugs and moves on. You have the same questions at midnight.

options.text: Whether she can come along and settle you in
options.then: She can't take the days off. The thought of going alone gets louder.

steps.why: Someone who has done it can tell you what to expect and stay a call away.

steps.prompt: On the day you leave, the goodbye at the station turns tearful. What do you do?

options.text: Agree on a weekly call time with your family
options.then: Your mother says Sundays at seven. She writes it on her hand and smiles through tears.

options.text: Say a quick goodbye so nobody cries
options.then: You hug fast and board. The tears come later, in the train.

options.text: Promise to call every single day
options.then: Everyone nods and relaxes. You wonder how you'll keep that up once classes start.

options.text: Tell them not to worry because you won't miss home
options.then: Your father looks quietly hurt. The words feel odd in your throat.

steps.why: A fixed weekly call keeps home close without a promise you can't keep.

steps.prompt: Two weeks into hostel life, the evenings feel lonely. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with a floormate at dinner and stay in touch with home
options.then: A floormate waves you over and introduces you to two others. Dinner is the first loud, easy hour of your week.

options.text: Stay in your room until the feeling passes
options.then: The evenings stay quiet. The feeling is still there on the third night.

options.text: Decide the move was a mistake and ask to go home
options.then: Your parents say they'll talk it over on Sunday. Your room feels very far from them.

options.text: Scroll through friends' photos from home every evening
options.then: Their photos make home look closer and the hostel look emptier.

steps.why: Small contact with people nearby builds a new circle while home stays close.

scenarios.debrief: A big move gets lighter when you prepare and keep your people close.
scenarios.relearn: For a move: prepare a little and plan to stay connected to your people.

scenarios.hook: You didn't get the college you wanted, and the disappointment is crushing.

steps.prompt: The news is still sinking in and the house is quiet. What do you do first?

options.text: Let yourself feel it and tell one person you trust
options.then: Your sister sits beside you without fixing anything. The crying comes, then eases.

options.text: Declare that your life is ruined and shut your door
options.then: The room is dark and quiet. Nobody knows how bad it feels.

options.text: Open the next list and apply everywhere tonight
options.then: You send six forms by midnight. The loss hasn't been felt yet, only covered.

options.text: Tell everyone you never really wanted that college
options.then: People nod politely. You can tell you don't believe it yourself.

steps.why: Feeling the loss with someone beside you lets you move on.

steps.prompt: A few days later, your parents ask what you plan to do. What do you say?

options.text: That you want to look at options together this weekend
options.then: Your father pulls out a notebook. Three options come up that you hadn't considered.

options.text: That you don't want to talk about it at all
options.then: They nod and leave it. The question will come back at the next meal.

options.text: That you'll do whatever they decide
options.then: They look relieved and a little worried. The decision is now in their hands.

options.text: That you'll retake the exam next year, no matter what
options.then: They agree for now. Nobody asks what you'd do if you changed your mind.

steps.why: Looking at real options together keeps the decision shared and yours.

steps.prompt: A cousin says, 'With your marks, it was your own fault.' What do you do?

options.text: Say you're doing your best and ask for his ideas
options.then: He shrugs, then mentions a course he knows. The sting stays, but it's a lead.

options.text: Agree that it was your fault
options.then: Your chest tightens. The thought follows you through the evening.

options.text: Snap at him and leave the room
options.then: He looks startled. Your parents ask later what happened.

options.text: Laugh it off and change the topic
options.then: The conversation moves on. The comment keeps replaying that night.

steps.why: You can take useful ideas without taking on blame.

steps.prompt: Admissions for the next option close in a week and you feel stuck. What do you do?

options.text: Make a list of deadlines and book a counsellor's visit
options.then: The counsellor helps compare two courses. The week suddenly has a shape.

options.text: Wait until you feel ready to decide
options.then: The days pass. The deadline is closer, and the feeling is the same.

options.text: Pick the option your friends are choosing
options.then: Your friends are glad. Their reasons don't quite match yours.

options.text: Grab the first seat on offer without comparing it to anything
options.then: A seat is yours by evening. Whether it fits you, you haven't asked yet.

steps.why: A deadline list and a guide make choosing possible when you feel stuck.

scenarios.debrief: A door closing hurts and isn't the end.
scenarios.relearn: For a disappointment: feel it, then explore real options with support.

scenarios.hook: Family money is tight, and you're the first at home to chase higher studies.

steps.prompt: The college forms are open and you don't know where to begin. What do you do?

options.text: Write down every deadline and ask a teacher about scholarships
options.then: The page shows five dates. Your teacher says two scholarships fit your marks.

options.text: Assume it's out of reach and don't open the forms
options.then: The forms stay closed for days. Then your teacher asks why you haven't started.

options.text: Ask a friend whose family pays full fees to explain it all
options.then: He explains how his family handled it. Nothing applies to your situation.

options.text: Wait for a relative who has studied to call you
options.then: Nobody calls. A week of the window slips away.

steps.why: A list of deadlines plus one person who knows makes the system workable.

steps.prompt: A few days on, your teacher mentions a fee waiver form that needs documents. What do you do?

options.text: Ask exactly which papers are needed and collect one a day
options.then: The list has four papers. One a day fits around school and home.

options.text: Say you'll look into it later, once things are calmer
options.then: Calmer days don't come. The form sits in your bag.

options.text: Ask your parents to deal with the offices for you
options.then: They go once and return confused. The clerk wanted you there to sign.

options.text: Download a form from an unofficial site instead of the office
options.then: The site's form isn't the one the office uses. Two days are gone.

steps.why: Asking exactly what's needed and doing one piece at a time keeps it moving.

steps.prompt: Your parents worry about the cost and say maybe you should work instead. What do you say?

options.text: Tell them about the fee waiver and ask to decide together
options.then: Your mother reads it slowly. Her face softens, and she asks how it works.

options.text: Say they shouldn't worry and you'll manage alone
options.then: They look relieved and uneasy. You have no plan for the gap.

options.text: Say you'll drop the idea, so you don't burden them
options.then: The room goes quiet. Nobody feels better.

options.text: Argue that studying is the only way to a good life
options.then: Your father stiffens. The talk ends with raised voices.

steps.why: Showing real options helps your family weigh cost and hope together.

steps.prompt: A friend says the whole process is a scam for people like you. What do you do?

options.text: Check the college's official list and ask your teacher
options.then: The official page matches what your teacher told you. The process looks real.

options.text: Believe your friend and skip the forms
options.then: You close the tab. The doubt stays with you for days.

options.text: Ask a stranger online to handle the application for a fee
options.then: The stranger replies fast and asks for money. Your teacher looks worried when you mention it.

options.text: Hide the whole thing from everyone
options.then: You carry it alone. The forms feel heavier at night.

steps.why: Checking with official sources and a trusted adult protects you from rumours and scams.

scenarios.debrief: A checklist and one good guide make adult systems doable.
scenarios.relearn: For unfamiliar systems: break it into deadlines and ask someone who knows.

scenarios.hook: Your sleep, food and study have all slipped during exam season.

steps.prompt: It's 1 am and you're still at your desk with a cold dinner. What do you do?

options.text: Set a fixed sleep time, starting tonight
options.then: You close the books at half past one. Falling asleep takes a while, but you do.

options.text: Drink more tea and keep studying
options.then: The tea keeps you awake, but the pages blur and you reread the same line.

options.text: Plan to catch up on sleep after the exams
options.then: The plan sounds sensible at 1 am. Tomorrow starts exactly the same way.

options.text: Tell yourself every topper sleeps this little
options.then: It feels like joining a club. Your eyes sting and your head is foggy.

steps.why: A fixed sleep time is the base that your studying stands on.

steps.prompt: The next day your mother notices you've skipped lunch again. What do you do?

options.text: Add one simple meal at a fixed time, even a quick one
options.then: You eat dal and rice at two. Your head feels clearer for the afternoon paper.

options.text: Say you'll eat after the next chapter
options.then: The chapter takes three hours. You eat cold food at five and feel flat.

options.text: Say you're not hungry and it's fine
options.then: She frowns and lets it go. By evening you can't focus.

options.text: Eat only chips and sweets for quick energy
options.then: The sugar gives a short lift. An hour later you're sleepy again.

steps.why: One steady meal gives your brain fuel for the whole afternoon.

steps.prompt: Two days before the paper, a friend invites you to an all-night study session. What do you do?

options.text: Join for two hours, then head home to sleep
options.then: The group groans a little. You get a lot done and sleep by midnight.

options.text: Stay the whole night so you don't miss out
options.then: The group is lively, and at 4 am no one is learning much.

options.text: Say no and study alone until 3 instead
options.then: Alone, you reread the same pages. You wake up with a sore head.

options.text: Skip studying entirely and rest for two days
options.then: You sleep well. The syllabus still sits there, and you worry about it.

steps.why: Studying with friends while guarding your sleep keeps you sharp for the paper.

scenarios.debrief: You can't cope on empty. Steady one basic at a time.
scenarios.relearn: In exam season, rebuild sleep and food first; you can't study well on empty.

scenarios.hook: A close friend says they feel hopeless and can't see the point of anything.

steps.prompt: Your friend says it quietly after class. What do you do?

options.text: Listen, say you're glad they told you, and find help today
options.then: Their shoulders drop. They say it has been like this for weeks, and they don't say no.

options.text: Tell them to cheer up and think of something happier
options.then: Your friend nods and goes quiet. The subject is closed.

options.text: Promise to keep it a secret and tell absolutely no one
options.then: They thank you. You now carry something heavy on your own.

options.text: Say every teenager feels like this sometimes
options.then: They shrug. You can tell they don't feel understood.

steps.why: Listening and getting help started today shows they aren't alone. It is never their fault.

steps.prompt: At lunch, your friend still looks flat and quiet. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with them and say a trusted adult should know
options.then: They hesitate and say they fear being judged. They don't say no.

options.text: Sit with them and chat about ordinary things all lunch
options.then: They half smile. Nothing about the heavy feeling is said.

options.text: Give them some space and wait for them to bring it up
options.then: They eat alone. You wonder whether you should have spoken.

options.text: Tell your friend group so everyone can cheer them up
options.then: Messages pile up in the group. Your friend feels watched and stops replying.

steps.why: A trusted adult can help in ways a friend can't.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks what a counsellor would even say. What do you tell them?

options.text: That counsellors listen without judging, and offer to go along
options.then: They ask if you'd really come. You say yes.

options.text: That they should try working it out on their own first, as it may pass
options.then: They nod and try. By the last period nothing has changed.

options.text: That counsellors are only for very serious cases
options.then: They go quiet and look unsure. You tell them you're still here if they change their mind.

options.text: What you read online about how they must be feeling
options.then: They stiffen. You sound sure, and they feel labelled.

steps.why: Counsellors listen without judgment, and going along makes the first step easier.

steps.prompt: Later that day, your friend says they're ready to talk to someone. What do you do?

options.text: Stay beside them as they speak to an adult or call Tele-MANAS 14416
options.then: Your class teacher listens carefully and says she's glad they came.

options.text: Send them the Tele-MANAS 14416 number and leave them to call
options.then: They stare at the number for a long time. The call isn't made that day.

options.text: Message their parents today without telling your friend first
options.then: Their parents get a hurried message. Your friend finds out afterwards and wishes you had asked them first.

options.text: Say they should wait a few days to see if it passes
options.then: The days pass. The heavy feeling is still there when you meet again.

steps.why: Staying beside them while an adult or Tele-MANAS 14416 helps makes the first step safer.

steps.prompt: Weeks on, your friend is a little lighter, but you feel drained. What do you do?

options.text: Tell a trusted adult you need support too, and keep checking in
options.then: Your aunt listens. You still check in with your friend, but not every hour.

options.text: Pretend you're fine so you can stay the strong one
options.then: Your friend leans on you more. You feel tired in a way sleep doesn't fix.

options.text: Pull away from your friend to protect yourself for now
options.then: Your friend notices the silence and wonders what they did.

options.text: Check on them every hour and drop everything else you are doing
options.then: Your schoolwork slips. They feel the pressure of being watched.

steps.why: Supporting others lasts longer when you have support too.

scenarios.debrief: A friend's hopeless feeling is no one's fault. Stay with them and help them reach support.
scenarios.relearn: If a friend feels hopeless: listen and help them reach Tele-MANAS 14416.

scenarios.hook: Your stress has felt heavy for weeks, and it won't lift.

steps.prompt: It's Sunday evening and your chest feels tight again. What do you do?

options.text: Tell a trusted adult how heavy it has felt for weeks
options.then: Your aunt puts her tea down and listens. She asks you to say more.

options.text: Tell yourself to be strong and push on through the evening
options.then: You study on. The tightness comes back as soon as you stop.

options.text: Wait until the exams are over to feel better
options.then: The exams are weeks away. The weight stays with you in the meantime.

options.text: Scroll your phone all night to switch off
options.then: The screen takes your mind away for an hour. The tight chest returns at midnight.

steps.why: Heavy stress for weeks is worth sharing with someone you trust.

steps.prompt: A relative says it's normal in exam season and you'll be fine. What do you do?

options.text: Say it feels heavier than usual and you'd like to talk to someone
options.then: She is quiet for a moment. "Okay. Let's find someone who can help," she says.

options.text: Agree with her and drop the subject
options.then: The chat moves on to snacks. The weight is still there when you go to bed.

options.text: Try only exercise and early nights for a few more weeks
options.then: You feel a little better some days. The heavy feeling keeps returning.

options.text: Say that nobody understands, then leave the room
options.then: The door closes loudly. The room feels very quiet afterwards.

steps.why: Saying it plainly helps people take your stress seriously.

steps.prompt: Your teacher mentions Tele-MANAS 14416 and the school counsellor. What do you do?

options.text: Note the number and ask the counsellor for a time
options.then: The counsellor has a slot on Thursday. She writes it on a slip.

options.text: Say that's only for people who are really struggling
options.then: Your teacher nods slowly and says the offer stays open. You find yourself thinking about it that night.

options.text: Save the number and never call
options.then: The number sits in your phone. The stress is still there, and so is the counsellor's offer.

options.text: Ask a friend to call on your behalf
options.then: Your friend calls and learns what to say. Support for you is still waiting.

steps.why: Tele-MANAS 14416 and a school counsellor are there for stress like yours.

steps.prompt: A few days later, the thought of talking to the counsellor makes your nerves jump. What do you do?

options.text: Jot down a few things to say and tell a parent you'd like to go
options.then: Your parent reads your notes quietly and squeezes your hand.

options.text: Put it off again because it feels embarrassing to talk about
options.then: The nerves ease for a day, then return. You book a slot the following week.

options.text: Ask your parent to tell the counsellor everything for you
options.then: Your parent offers to explain it. The counsellor's office says they will want to hear from you too.

options.text: Go to the counsellor with no plan and hope the words come
options.then: In the room the words tangle. You leave unsure whether you said it.

steps.why: Writing a few words down and telling a parent makes the first visit easier.

steps.prompt: After a few visits you feel lighter, and the exams are close. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the support going, along with rest and routines
options.then: The counsellor and a trusted adult at home both know your plan. The exams feel less lonely.

options.text: Stop everything now that you feel better
options.then: You skip the next visit. A week later the weight creeps back.

options.text: Go back to pushing hard on your own
options.then: Your hours go up and your sleep goes down. The tight chest returns.

options.text: Wonder if you needed help, since classmates seem to cope alone
options.then: They seem fine from the outside. You start doubting whether you ever needed help.

steps.why: Staying connected to support helps the lighter days last.

scenarios.debrief: Heavy stress for weeks is never a weakness or your fault. Reaching support like Tele-MANAS 14416 is strength.
scenarios.relearn: For weeks of heavy stress, reach a trusted adult or Tele-MANAS 14416.

scenarios.hook: Your result comes out tomorrow, and the waiting has your stomach in knots.

steps.prompt: It's 9 pm and you can't sit still. What do you do?

options.text: Do one calming thing, like a walk or some music
options.then: Twenty minutes in, your breathing is slower. The knot loosens a little.

options.text: Refresh the result site every few minutes
options.then: The page stays the same. Each refresh winds you tighter.

options.text: Call friends to guess your marks together
options.then: Everyone guesses differently. You feel less sure than before.

options.text: Tell yourself you'll surely fail so it can't hurt
options.then: The thought feels like armour for a minute. Then it feels heavy.

steps.why: A calming routine steadies the wait when the result is out of your hands.

steps.prompt: A cousin texts asking what happens if you score low. What do you do?

options.text: Reply that one result won't define you, then chat about something else
options.then: She sends a laughing emoji and a funny story. The knot stays quiet for a while.

options.text: Ignore it and mute her
options.then: The message sits unanswered. The question keeps running in your head.

options.text: Reply with a list of every bad outcome you can think of
options.then: The list gets longer the more you type. Your heart starts racing.

options.text: Reply that it will definitely be fine
options.then: She replies with a thumbs up. You don't quite believe it yourself.

steps.why: Facing the 'what if' calmly keeps one number from defining you.

steps.prompt: The next morning the result link goes live. What do you do?

options.text: Take a breath, then open it, with company if you like
options.then: Your brother sits beside you. Whatever the page says, you're not on your own.

options.text: Rush to open it before you've taken even one breath
options.then: Your heart pounds as the page loads. You read the number too fast to take it in.

options.text: Ask a friend to check it first and tell you
options.then: Your friend's message takes a long time to arrive. Your phone buzzes before you're ready.

options.text: Put it off until the evening and keep yourself busy all day
options.then: The hours drag. The knot grows with each one.

steps.why: A steady breath, and company if you want it, helps whatever the number is.

scenarios.debrief: You can't speed up a result. Steady the wait instead.
scenarios.relearn: Steady the wait before a result; one number won't define your worth.

scenarios.hook: You've taken a year to reattempt your entrance exam, and shame has you hiding.

steps.prompt: A school friend invites you to a get-together where everyone will ask about plans. What do you do?

options.text: Go, and say you're taking a second shot
options.then: A few faces soften. One friend says she's rooting for you.

options.text: Skip it so nobody sees you as having failed
options.then: You stay home. The group chat carries on without you.

options.text: Go, but dodge every question about your year
options.then: You talk about cricket all evening. Nobody learns anything about you.

options.text: Go, and say you chose this year to relax, nothing more
options.then: People nod. The small lie sits in your chest on the way home.

steps.why: Saying it plainly shows the year as a plan, not a secret.

steps.prompt: Your study plan for the year is still a blank page. What do you do?

options.text: Draw up a weekly plan and ask a mentor to review it
options.then: The mentor trims the plan to a pace you can keep. You feel it's yours.

options.text: Start with twelve-hour days to make up for lost time
options.then: The first week is intense. By the third, you're worn out and behind again.

options.text: Wait until you feel motivated to begin
options.then: Days drift past. The motivation doesn't arrive on its own.

options.text: Copy a topper's plan from the internet, line by line
options.then: The plan has hours that don't suit you. You fall off it in ten days.

steps.why: A plan that fits you, with someone to review it, is easier to keep.

steps.prompt: Midway through the year, a mock result lands below the cut-off. What do you do?

options.text: Look at what it shows, adjust the plan and tell someone you trust
options.then: The mock shows two weak areas. The plan changes, and you feel steadier.

options.text: Decide this whole year was a waste
options.then: The thought darkens your evening. You study less the next day.

options.text: Hide the result from your family
options.then: Nobody asks. The result sits at the bottom of your bag.

options.text: Switch to a new coaching centre without finding out why
options.then: The new centre has a different plan. The weak areas follow you there.

steps.why: A mock is information. Use it to adjust, with people who back you.

steps.prompt: A friend who got in posts college photos, and it stings. What do you do?

options.text: Let yourself feel it, then call a friend who backs you
options.then: Your friend listens and says the year takes guts. The sting eases a little.

options.text: Scroll through all their pictures for hours
options.then: Each picture adds to the ache. The night slips away.

options.text: Cut off every friend who got in
options.then: Your phone is quieter. The year feels lonelier.

options.text: Message them that it's unfair that they got in
options.then: Your friend replies with a puzzled emoji. The chat goes cold.

steps.why: Feeling it and leaning on friends who back you keeps a hard year from being a lonely one.

scenarios.debrief: A reattempt is a second shot, not a verdict.
scenarios.relearn: A drop year is a second shot, not failure; stay connected to your people.

scenarios.hook: Mid-exam, your mind goes blank and panic rises in the hall.

steps.prompt: The first question looks unfamiliar and your hands feel cold. What do you do?

options.text: Put the pen down and take a few slow breaths
options.then: After a minute your hands warm up and the words on the page make sense.

options.text: Keep staring at the question until it makes sense
options.then: The clock seems louder. The page looks even less familiar.

options.text: Glance around the hall to see how others are doing
options.then: Everyone seems to be writing. Your panic goes up a notch.

options.text: Start writing anything so that you look busy
options.then: You fill half a page with loose lines. You can't connect them.

steps.why: A pause and slow breaths settle panic enough for your memory to return.

steps.prompt: The next question looks hard too. What do you do?

options.text: Skip to the easiest question and begin there
options.then: The easy answer flows. You feel your confidence returning.

options.text: Stay on the hard one until you crack it
options.then: Ten minutes go by and the answer still hasn't come.

options.text: Tell yourself you've already failed
options.then: The thought is loud. Your pen slows down.

options.text: Ask the invigilator to hint at the answer
options.then: She says she can only explain the rules. You've lost another minute.

steps.why: Starting with the easiest question builds momentum and calms you down.

steps.prompt: Ten minutes before the end, two questions are still unanswered. What do you do?

options.text: Write what you do know for each, then check the time
options.then: Two short, clear answers go down. You finish with a minute to spare.

options.text: Leave them blank because it's too late
options.then: The paper has two empty spaces. You hand it in unsure.

options.text: Re-read your earlier answers one more time instead
options.then: The first answers look fine. The last ten minutes are gone.

options.text: Scribble random guesses everywhere and hope
options.then: The lines are messy, and you can't tell which ones make sense.

steps.why: Writing what you know earns what you can, and a steady pace keeps your mind clear.

scenarios.debrief: A blank mid-exam usually passes. Breathe, then begin with the easy one.
scenarios.relearn: If your mind blanks in an exam: breathe, then start with the easiest question.

scenarios.hook: Boards, chores and a part-time job have you stretched to breaking.

steps.prompt: On Tuesday night your list has seven things and you have time for three. What do you do?

options.text: Pick the three that matter most and let the rest wait
options.then: The three get done properly. The other four wait without any harm.

options.text: Stay up and finish all seven, and tell nobody you're tired
options.then: You finish at 2 am. You feel hollow and the next day is worse.

options.text: Do the quickest tasks first and feel productive
options.then: You tick off five small items. The two big ones are still waiting.

options.text: Try to finish all seven perfectly
options.then: Each task takes twice as long. By midnight, four are half done.

steps.why: Choosing what matters most keeps your effort where it counts.

steps.prompt: The weekend chores keep landing on you. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with your family and ask them to share the chores
options.then: Your mother thinks, then splits them into a list. Your sister takes two.

options.text: Take it all on quietly so there's no fight
options.then: The house is peaceful. You are quietly exhausted.

options.text: Complain loudly that you're the only one who works
options.then: Voices rise at dinner. The chores stay with you.

options.text: Do the chores late at night and sleep less
options.then: The kitchen is tidy at midnight. The alarm at six feels brutal.

steps.why: A calm ask with a clear list helps your family share the load.

steps.prompt: Your shop owner asks if you can work extra hours this month. What do you say?

options.text: That you'll keep your usual hours until the boards are over
options.then: He frowns, then agrees and says he'll revisit the roster after your exams.

options.text: Yes to all the extra hours, and study on the bus
options.then: You say yes. The bus is noisy and your notes stay in your bag.

options.text: A flat no, with no explanation
options.then: He looks surprised. The mood at the shop turns cold.

options.text: Nothing, and then just not turn up
options.then: He phones twice. You are in trouble and worried about the job.

steps.why: Honest limits with your employer protect both the job and your exams.

steps.prompt: Boards start in two weeks and you realise you haven't rested in days. What do you do?

options.text: Block one rest hour each day and treat it like a class
options.then: The hour is quiet. Your studying afterwards is sharper than before.

options.text: Rest after boards, not before
options.then: The days run together. Your energy drops with every hour.

options.text: Rest only when you can't stay awake
options.then: You nod off over your notes at odd hours. The pages blur.

options.text: Study through Sunday too, to make up the time
options.then: You gain a few hours. The next week starts already tired.

steps.why: Rest is part of the plan, not a reward you earn after it.

scenarios.debrief: Stretched thin? Prioritise, share the load and guard your rest.
scenarios.relearn: When stretched thin, prioritise, share tasks, and protect rest.

scenarios.hook: A classmate seems to have everything sorted, and you keep comparing your prep to theirs.

steps.prompt: You see their late-night study post and feel behind. What do you do?

options.text: Close the app and note what you finished today
options.then: Your list shows three topics done. You feel a little steadier.

options.text: Scroll through all their other posts for an hour
options.then: Each post makes your own work look smaller. The hour is gone.

options.text: Message to ask how many hours they study
options.then: They reply nine hours. You can't tell whether it's true or what it means.

options.text: Study until 2 am to catch up with them
options.then: Your eyes burn. You can't recall the last chapter the next morning.

steps.why: Your own finished list tells you more than their feed does.

steps.prompt: In the corridor, classmates start comparing marks. What do you do?

options.text: Say you're working on your own progress and ask how others revise
options.then: A girl names a revision trick. You pick up one useful idea.

options.text: Join in and rank everyone from top to bottom
options.then: The talk gets competitive. Your chest tightens.

options.text: Say your marks are higher than they really are
options.then: They look impressed. You feel nervous that it'll come out.

options.text: Walk off and skip lunch to avoid the chat
options.then: You sit alone with your thoughts. Lunch hour passes slowly.

steps.why: Talking about your own progress and learning from others is more useful than ranking.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks what your goal is for the next month. What do you say?

options.text: One topic to improve, and how you'll check it
options.then: She writes it down and suggests a weekly test. You leave with a clear aim.

options.text: To beat the topper
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. The goal depends on someone else's marks.

options.text: To study more hours than everyone else in class
options.then: She smiles. Hours alone don't show whether you're learning.

options.text: That you don't know, and shrug
options.then: She nods and moves on. You walk out with no aim.

steps.why: A goal measured against your own progress is yours to control.

scenarios.debrief: Comparison steals focus. Measure against your own progress.
scenarios.relearn: Beat exam comparison by tracking your own progress, not a classmate's feed.

scenarios.hook: The result you feared is out, and it's lower than you hoped.

steps.prompt: You see the number on the screen and your face goes hot. What do you do?

options.text: Let yourself be upset, then find someone you trust
options.then: Your mother sits beside you. You cry, and she doesn't rush to fix it.

options.text: Decide the number proves you're worthless
options.then: The thought repeats all evening. Dinner goes cold on your plate.

options.text: Tell everyone it's fine and keep on smiling
options.then: Relatives say you look calm. Your smile starts to ache by evening.

options.text: Lock yourself in and refuse to speak to anyone
options.then: The door stays closed. Hours later you still haven't eaten.

steps.why: Feeling it with someone beside you lets the hurt move through.

steps.prompt: That evening, relatives call to ask about your marks. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll make a plan soon, and thank them for asking
options.then: Your uncle sighs, then says he'll send a contact. The call is shorter than you feared.

options.text: Let a parent answer while you hide in your room
options.then: Your parent mumbles an excuse. The calls keep coming.

options.text: Say the paper was unfair and blame the teachers
options.then: Your aunt tuts in agreement. The question of what next stays untouched.

options.text: Say you never cared about marks anyway
options.then: The line goes quiet. You feel it isn't quite true.

steps.why: Saying a plan is coming, without owing anyone a number, keeps it from deciding your worth.

steps.prompt: A few days on, your parents want to discuss next steps. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with them and map real options, including retakes
options.then: Your father makes a list. There are four options you hadn't considered.

options.text: Say you'll do whatever they decide
options.then: They look relieved and a little uneasy. The decision is now in their hands.

options.text: Say you don't want to talk about it yet
options.then: They agree. The unspoken question sits at the dinner table.

options.text: Insist on a retake right away without looking at anything else
options.then: Your mother nods slowly. Nobody has checked what else could work.

steps.why: Mapping real options with the people who back you turns hurt into a plan.

scenarios.debrief: A low result can hurt and still not define you.
scenarios.relearn: A low result is a score, not your worth; feel it, then plan next steps with support.

scenarios.hook: A close friendship is fading as you and your friend move to different cities.

steps.prompt: You haven't heard from your friend in three weeks. What do you do?

options.text: Message to say you miss them and suggest a regular call
options.then: They reply in minutes. "I miss you too! Sundays work for me," they write.

options.text: Wait for them to message you first
options.then: The phone stays quiet. A fourth week begins.

options.text: Act like it doesn't matter and stop checking
options.then: You feel a bit lighter on some days. The ache returns when you see their name.

options.text: Send a long message blaming them for drifting away
options.then: They reply a day later, hurt. The chat ends on a sour note.

steps.why: Reaching out first, with a simple plan, keeps the friendship going.

steps.prompt: A week later, you and your friend end up on a call, and it feels awkward. What do you do?

options.text: Say it feels different now and ask what works for both
options.then: They laugh with relief. "I thought it was just me," they say.

options.text: Fill the silence with jokes and avoid the topic
options.then: You laugh a lot. Afterwards you realise nothing was said.

options.text: End the call early, saying you're busy
options.then: They say okay. You feel the gap widen.

options.text: Agree to call every single day, though your timetables clash
options.then: Both of you say yes. By the second week, the calls start slipping.

steps.why: Naming the change openly lets you both shape what the friendship becomes.

steps.prompt: Your friend posts photos with new friends in their city. What do you do?

options.text: Feel the pang, be glad for them, and reach out for a call
options.then: The pang fades by evening. The next call is warm and easy.

options.text: Take it as proof you've been replaced
options.then: The thought grows. You stop answering their messages for days.

options.text: Unfollow them so it hurts less
options.then: Your feed is calmer. The friendship feels farther away.

options.text: Comment cheerfully and hide how you feel
options.then: They send hearts. You feel more alone than before.

steps.why: Friendships change shape, and being kind to yourself helps you adjust.

scenarios.debrief: Friendships change when people move. Name it and stay in touch.
scenarios.relearn: For a fading friendship: name the change and stay in touch.

scenarios.hook: You're the eldest, everyone leans on you, and you're quietly drowning too.

steps.prompt: Your parents ask you to handle three more things this week. What do you do?

options.text: Tell an aunt you trust that it's been heavy lately
options.then: Your aunt puts down her cup. She says she's noticed, and she's glad you said it.

options.text: Say yes to all three and smile, as you always do
options.then: They thank you warmly. You go to your room and sit very still.

options.text: Say yes, then do them badly and feel guilty about it
options.then: Two get done late. The guilt sits on top of the tiredness.

options.text: Say nobody else in the house does anything
options.then: Voices rise. The three things are still yours.

steps.why: Telling someone you trust lets you stop carrying it all alone.

steps.prompt: A few days later, your younger brother asks for help with a project. You're tired. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him you can help for twenty minutes, then rest
options.then: He nods and gets to work. When time's up, he says he'll try the rest himself.

options.text: Do the whole project for him so that it's all finished
options.then: He is delighted. You are awake until midnight.

options.text: Snap that he should work it out alone
options.then: He goes quiet and shuts the door. You feel awful.

options.text: Say yes and stay up late as usual
options.then: The project gets done. The next day you're foggy at school.

steps.why: Giving what you can and protecting some rest is care for you and him.

steps.prompt: A friend asks you out for an hour on Saturday. What do you do?

options.text: Go, and let yourself switch off for the hour
options.then: You laugh for the first time in days. Home still stands when you return.

options.text: Say no because home needs you
options.then: Your friend says maybe next time. The weekend stays heavy.

options.text: Go, but check your phone for home every five minutes
options.then: You are there in body. Every buzz pulls you back.

options.text: Say you're fine and have no time
options.then: Your friend says okay. You watch the clock tick through Saturday.

steps.why: A little time for yourself keeps you able to give to others.

steps.prompt: At a family gathering, an uncle says you're the strong one and nobody worries about you. What do you do?

options.text: Say you're strong, and that you need support sometimes too
options.then: A hush. Then your aunt says, "Then we should ask more often."

options.text: Smile and say nothing
options.then: Your uncle pats your shoulder. The comment follows you home.

options.text: Joke that you're just tired of being the strong one here
options.then: Laughter. Nobody asks what you meant.

options.text: Snap that nobody in the family ever cares about you at all
options.then: The room freezes. Your mother looks hurt.

steps.why: Even the strong one needs support, and saying so plainly lets people give it.

scenarios.debrief: Being the strong one doesn't mean coping alone.
scenarios.relearn: Even the dependable one needs support; tell a trusted person.

scenarios.hook: Under exam stress, you snapped at your sibling, and you feel awful about it.

steps.prompt: Your sibling is sitting quietly in the next room. What do you do?

options.text: Go in and apologise, saying that stress got to you
options.then: Your sibling looks up, surprised. "Okay. Thanks for saying that," they say.

options.text: Wait for them to speak to you first
options.then: Neither of you talks. Dinner is tense and quiet.

options.text: Say they started it, so it's partly their fault
options.then: They pull a face. The quarrel restarts at a lower volume.

options.text: Leave a snack by their desk and say nothing about it
options.then: They take the snack. Neither of you mentions what happened.

steps.why: Owning what you did, plainly, begins the repair.

steps.prompt: Your sibling says, 'You always do this when you're stressed.' What do you do?

options.text: Listen and say you hear it, then ask what would help
options.then: They think a moment. "Just tell me when you need space," they say.

options.text: List every pressure you're under to explain yourself
options.then: Your sibling folds their arms. It sounds like an excuse.

options.text: Say you'll try, then change the subject
options.then: They nod. The question hangs in the room.

options.text: Promise you'll never snap at them again, ever
options.then: They want to believe you. Both of you know it's too big a promise.

steps.why: Listening to the pattern and asking what helps makes the repair real.

steps.prompt: Two weeks later, stress is high again and your temper is rising. What do you do?

options.text: Step away and tell your sibling you need ten minutes
options.then: They nod and give you space. You return calmer and say sorry for rushing off.

options.text: Push through and hope you stay calm
options.then: The effort shows. Your voice rises as the questions keep coming.

options.text: Let it build, then apologise afterwards
options.then: The outburst comes. You apologise again, and they look tired.

options.text: Walk out of the house without a word
options.then: Your family worries for an hour. Nobody knows where you went.

steps.why: Spotting your stress signal early and saying so spares the people you love from it.

scenarios.debrief: Stress can make us snap. Owning it is the repair.
scenarios.relearn: If stress made you snap, apologise honestly and make it right rather than just excusing it.

scenarios.hook: After boards end, you feel oddly flat and lost instead of relieved.

steps.prompt: A week after the last paper, the days feel empty. What do you do?

options.text: Treat it as a normal comedown and build a gentle routine
options.then: You fix a wake-up time and a walk. The days start to have a shape again.

options.text: Assume something is deeply wrong with you
options.then: The thought grows through the day. You feel more alone than before.

options.text: Stay in bed most days and wait until the feeling passes
options.then: The days blur together. The flat feeling is still there on Sunday.

options.text: Jump straight into prep for the next entrance exam this week
options.then: You open a new book. The tiredness shows up by the third day.

steps.why: A flat patch after a big push is common, and a gentle routine helps.

steps.prompt: A friend says everyone is partying and you should come. What do you do?

options.text: Say you feel flat and meet one friend for a walk
options.then: Your friend listens as you walk. "Same here," she says. "I thought it was just me."

options.text: Go to every party to feel something
options.then: The music is loud. You feel the flatness more in the crowd.

options.text: Say you're fine and say no to everything
options.then: Your phone goes quiet. The days feel longer.

options.text: Tell her you've turned boring and she's better off
options.then: She laughs it off. You aren't sure she heard how you meant it.

steps.why: A quiet catch-up with one friend helps more than a crowd does.

steps.prompt: Your mother asks why you seem low. What do you say?

options.text: That it's a flat patch after the push and you want company
options.then: She makes tea and sits beside you. Neither of you hurries the talk.

options.text: That it's nothing and you're just tired
options.then: She nods slowly. The tea goes cold on the table.

options.text: That you hate how you feel and that it's all your own fault
options.then: Her face falls. She says it isn't, and you can't quite believe her yet.

options.text: That you want to be left alone for a month
options.then: She says okay. The month looks long from where you sit.

steps.why: Telling someone close how you feel lets them stay near you.

steps.prompt: A month on, you still feel flat on most days and your sleep is off. What do you do?

options.text: Tell a trusted adult and ask about Tele-MANAS 14416
options.then: Your father listens and says he'll arrange a visit. It feels like a weight shared.

options.text: Wait it out, since it will pass eventually
options.then: Another month goes by. The flat days keep their grip.

options.text: Fill every hour with new tasks so you don't feel it
options.then: You stay busy. At night the feeling is waiting for you.

options.text: Decide that this is just who you are now
options.then: The idea settles in. You stop looking forward to anything.

steps.why: A flat patch that lingers is a good reason to reach support. It is not your fault.

scenarios.debrief: A flat patch after a big push is normal. Reach support if it lingers.
scenarios.relearn: Post-exam flatness is normal: rebuild a gentle routine, reconnect, and tell someone if it lingers.
