scenarios.relearn: "Don't show weakness" and "adults never need support" are the red flags; leaning on people is strength.

scenarios.hook: Your results are weeks away, and a relative's talk about money has been getting to you.
scenarios.setup: At a family lunch, she brings it up again.

steps.prompt: Your aunt says: "Score below 90 and you've wasted everyone's money."

options.text: "I'm doing my best. My worth isn't one number."
options.then: Her fork pauses. "I only want you to take it seriously," she says.

options.text: "You're right, Aunty. I'll try much harder from now on."
options.then: She nods, satisfied. The food on your plate goes untouched.

options.text: "You've never paid a single rupee towards my fees!"
options.then: The table goes silent. Your mother gives you a sharp look.

options.text: "Then I won't tell anyone if I do badly."
options.then: She says nothing. The thought of hiding it settles in your stomach.

steps.why: Answering honestly keeps your worth separate from a single number.

steps.prompt: Your aunt says: "I'm only saying this because we all sacrificed for you."

options.text: "I'm grateful. I'm still giving it my best."
options.then: She softens a little. "That's all we ask," she says.

options.text: "I never asked you to sacrifice anything."
options.then: She puts her glass down hard. "Is that what you think?"

options.text: "Then I'm sorry I'm such a burden."
options.then: A pause. She seems unsure what to say, and you stare at your plate.

options.text: "I'll make it up to everyone with a top score."
options.then: She smiles. You feel a heavy promise settle on your shoulders.

steps.why: Gratitude and effort can sit alongside your worth, without owing anyone a score.

steps.prompt: Your mother asks: "And if the result comes lower than you hope? What then?"

options.text: "I'll be upset, and we'll look at options together."
options.then: Her face relaxes. "Yes. We'll do that," she says.

options.text: "It won't. I'll make sure of that, whatever it takes."
options.then: She nods, but her eyes stay worried. Nobody knows what you've promised.

options.text: "Then I'll have ruined everything."
options.then: She frowns. "Beta, no one said that." The idea stays with you.

options.text: "I don't want to talk about it."
options.then: She lets it go. The question stays on the table.

steps.why: Planning with your family for a lower result keeps one number from ruling you.

scenarios.relearn: You can answer pressure honestly and keep your worth out of a single number.

scenarios.hook: Stress has felt heavy for weeks, and you want to tell a parent.
scenarios.setup: Tonight your father notices your face.

steps.prompt: Your father asks: "You've been quiet lately. Is something on your mind?"

options.text: "I've been struggling for weeks. I think I need support."
options.then: He mutes the TV. "Thank you for telling me. I'm listening."

options.text: "I'm fine, Papa. I'm only a bit tired these days."
options.then: He nods slowly. "Okay. My door is open if that changes."

options.text: "It's nothing. Everyone is stressed before boards."
options.then: "True," he says. "Don't overthink it." He turns back to the news.

options.text: "Please don't tell Mummy. She'll only worry about me."
options.then: He frowns. "Let me understand what's going on first, beta."

steps.why: Telling a parent plainly lets them help, and it is never your fault.

steps.prompt: The next morning, your father knocks and says: "I've been thinking about last night. How are you today?"

options.text: "Still heavy. I'd like to talk to someone."
options.then: "Then we'll find someone," he says. "I'm glad you said that."

options.text: "Fine. Please forget about last night."
options.then: He nods, unconvinced. "All right. The offer stands."

options.text: "Better after sleep. I'll just keep pushing on."
options.then: "If you say so," he says. He watches you leave for school.

options.text: "Maybe I'm just being dramatic."
options.then: He shakes his head. "Weeks of feeling heavy isn't dramatic."

steps.why: Naming that you want to talk to someone is how you let help in.

steps.prompt: A few days later, your father says: "There's the school counsellor, and Tele-MANAS 14416 is free to call. What would feel okay?"

options.text: "I'd like to see the counsellor. Please come along."
options.then: "Of course," he says. "I'll check the timings today."

options.text: "Counsellors are for people who can't cope."
options.then: "That's not true," he says gently. "Many capable people see one."

options.text: "Let's wait until the boards are over."
options.then: "Weeks is a long time to carry this," he says, but lets it rest.

options.text: "If I see a counsellor, everyone at school will find out."
options.then: He shakes his head. "They usually keep it private, beta. We can ask them first."

steps.why: A school counsellor and Tele-MANAS 14416 are real support, with a parent nearby.

steps.prompt: At dinner, your aunt notices the quiet talks and asks: "What's wrong with you lately?"

options.text: "Nothing's wrong. Talking to someone helps when stress is heavy."
options.then: She blinks. "Hm. My neighbour's son talked to someone too. I remember now."

options.text: "Nothing. Please drop it."
options.then: She shrugs. The question stays in the room.

options.text: "Maybe something is wrong. Maybe I am just weak."
options.then: Your father puts his hand on yours. "No," he says quietly.

options.text: "Mind your own business, Aunty. It is not your life."
options.then: The table goes quiet. Your mother frowns at you.

steps.why: Talking to someone when stress is heavy is a strength, not a sign that something is wrong with you.

scenarios.relearn: Naming that you're struggling and need support is how you let your people in.

scenarios.hook: A friend has seemed down all week, and today they ask to talk.
scenarios.setup: You're sitting together on the school steps after class.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "I feel hopeless. I don't see the point of anything lately."

options.text: "I'm really glad you told me. I'm here. Let's talk."
options.then: Your friend exhales. "I didn't think anyone would listen."

options.text: "You'll be fine. Don't think like that."
options.then: They nod and look away. "Yeah. Sure."

options.text: "Everyone feels like this. Just sleep it off."
options.then: A thin smile. "Maybe." They pick up their bag, then put it down again.

options.text: "Don't tell anyone. They'll think you're crazy."
options.then: They nod and zip their bag, but they don't leave. The silence stretches.

steps.why: Listening and staying close tells them they matter, and none of this is their fault.

steps.prompt: After a pause, your friend says: "I can't even say why I feel like this."

options.text: "You don't have to explain. It's not your fault."
options.then: Their eyes fill. "Thanks. I keep thinking it is."

options.text: "Think about the good things you have."
options.then: They nod. "I know. That makes me feel worse."

options.text: "Is it your marks, or your family? Tell me."
options.then: They shake their head. "Please don't ask."

options.text: "Come on, there must be a reason. Just say it."
options.then: They tense up. "Forget it. I shouldn't have said anything."

steps.why: They don't need a reason. They need you to listen without pushing.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "I don't want you telling anyone."

options.text: "I care too much to keep this alone. Can we tell an adult together?"
options.then: They go quiet. "Together?" they ask. "Okay. Maybe."

options.text: "I won't tell anyone. I promise."
options.then: They relax. You now hold a heavy secret by yourself.

options.text: "Fine, but call me if it gets worse."
options.then: They agree. You wait for a call that may or may not come.

options.text: "I'll tell everyone in the class group so they can help."
options.then: Messages pile up in the group. Your friend feels exposed and goes very quiet.

steps.why: Telling a trusted adult is right even if they say no, and doing it together keeps them safe.

steps.prompt: Later that day, your friend texts: "I looked up the school counsellor. What would I even say?"

options.text: "Say what you told me. We'll tell an adult and call Tele-MANAS 14416 together."
options.then: They breathe out. "Okay. Could you stay while I do?"

options.text: "Just say you're stressed and leave it at that."
options.then: They nod. The real words stay unsaid.

options.text: "Maybe skip it and see how you feel tomorrow."
options.then: They shrug. Tomorrow comes, and the feeling is still there.

options.text: "I'll call and tell them everything for you."
options.then: They look relieved, then uneasy. "They'll want to hear from me."

steps.why: Going along while they speak for themselves, and using Tele-MANAS 14416, gives real support.

scenarios.relearn: For a friend in distress: stay with them and help them reach support like Tele-MANAS 14416.

scenarios.hook: You've studied for hours with your group and badly need a short break.
scenarios.setup: As you stand up, one friend frowns.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Taking a break already? The others are studying right now."

options.text: "I study better after a break. Ten minutes, then I'm back."
options.then: He shrugs. "Fine. Ten minutes, then."

options.text: "Okay, you're right. I'll keep going."
options.then: He nods. Your eyes stay on the page, but nothing sinks in.

options.text: "You're not my boss. Stop nagging me."
options.then: He rolls his eyes. "Wow. Take it easy."

options.text: "I'll take a break, but only after this chapter."
options.then: "Another hour, then," he says. The tiredness stays with you.

steps.why: A short break now helps you study better, and you can say so kindly.

steps.prompt: Later, another friend says: "People who take breaks fall behind the topper."

options.text: "I'm tracking my own progress, not the topper's."
options.then: She raises her eyebrows. "Hm. Fair enough."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. I'll skip the break today."
options.then: She smiles. Your head feels heavy as you reopen the book.

options.text: "Fine. I'll rest, but I'll study all night to catch up."
options.then: She laughs. "Now that's dedication." You feel a knot of dread.

options.text: "Then I'll fall behind. Whatever."
options.then: She goes quiet. "I didn't mean it like that," she says.

steps.why: You can rest without comparing, because your own progress is what counts.

steps.prompt: A friend says: "Let's all study till 2 am tonight."

options.text: "I'll study until ten, then sleep. See you tomorrow."
options.then: "Suit yourself," he says. "Tell us what you remember tomorrow."

options.text: "Okay, I'll stay, even though I'm exhausted."
options.then: "Great!" he says. By one, you're reading the same page again.

options.text: "Count me out. I'm not studying with you anymore."
options.then: The group goes quiet. Someone says, "Wow. Okay then."

options.text: "Sure, I'll see how I feel later."
options.then: "Okay," he says. "See how you feel." By midnight you're still there, drained.

steps.why: Holding your limit kindly keeps you in the group and keeps you rested.

scenarios.relearn: You can hold a healthy break against pressure; rest makes your studying work better.

scenarios.hook: You snapped at your sibling during exam week and want to make it right.
scenarios.setup: Later you find them sitting at their desk, back turned to you.

steps.prompt: Your sibling says, with their back turned: "What do you want?"

options.text: "I'm sorry I snapped. That was stress, not you."
options.then: They turn around slowly. "Okay. Thanks for saying that."

options.text: "Nothing. Just checking if you're still sulking."
options.then: They scowl. "Wow. Go away."

options.text: "Look, I was stressed, so you can't be upset."
options.then: They fold their arms. "I can be upset if I want."

options.text: "Never mind. Forget it."
options.then: They shrug and turn back. The silence stays.

steps.why: A plain apology that names the stress, not the person, starts the repair.

steps.prompt: Your sibling says: "It really hurt when you shouted."

options.text: "That makes sense. I shouldn't have shouted."
options.then: They nod. "Okay. I'd rather you tell me."

options.text: "Everyone gets stressed. What more do you want?"
options.then: They look away. "Nothing." The room feels colder.

options.text: "You always overreact."
options.then: They flinch. "See? That's what I mean."

options.text: "I'll buy you ice cream, and we're even."
options.then: They half smile. "Okay," they say, though they look unconvinced.

steps.why: Listening to how it landed shows you take their feelings seriously.

steps.prompt: Your sibling asks: "What if you shout again?"

options.text: "Tell me it's too much. I'll take ten minutes."
options.then: They nod. "I can do that. Thanks."

options.text: "I won't. Not ever. I promise you that."
options.then: They smile uncertainly. Both of you know it's a lot to promise.

options.text: "Then you'll just have to put up with it, won't you?"
options.then: Their face falls. "Okay," they say quietly.

options.text: "Let's not talk about that now."
options.then: They shrug. "Fine." The question hangs in the air.

steps.why: A real plan for next time helps more than a promise you can't keep.

scenarios.relearn: Owning that stress made you snap, and apologising, repairs it; excuses don't.

scenarios.hook: You're the dependable eldest, quietly drowning, and a cousin senses it.
scenarios.setup: At day's end, she finds you alone in the kitchen.

steps.prompt: Your cousin asks: "You always look after everyone. How are you, really?"

options.text: "Honestly, I'm carrying a lot. I need some support too."
options.then: She sits down. "Thank you for saying that. What's been hardest?"

options.text: "All good. Don't worry about me. I'm used to it."
options.then: She tilts her head. "If you ever want to talk, I'm here."

options.text: "Tired, but someone has to hold everything together."
options.then: "You don't have to do it alone," she says, but you wave her off.

options.text: "Why do you ask? Did someone say something?"
options.then: She blinks. "No. I just noticed. Never mind."

steps.why: Saying you need support too lets the people who love you step in.

steps.prompt: Your cousin says: "You can tell me one thing that's weighing on you."

options.text: "The responsibility for everyone. I need it shared."
options.then: She nods slowly. "That's fair. Let's work out who can take what."

options.text: "Nothing really. I'm just being dramatic."
options.then: "I don't think so," she says. You look at the floor.

options.text: "Everything. It's all my fault things are falling apart."
options.then: "It isn't," she says firmly. "You've been doing so much."

options.text: "My siblings. They never lift a finger."
options.then: She nods carefully. "Hm. Maybe they don't know you need them to."

steps.why: Naming what weighs on you lets someone help you carry it.

steps.prompt: Your cousin asks: "Would it help if I sat with you when you talk to your parents?"

options.text: "Yes, please. I want to ask them for help."
options.then: "Done," she says. "We'll pick a quiet evening."

options.text: "No, I'll manage it by myself."
options.then: "Okay," she says. "The offer stays open."

options.text: "Not now. Maybe after the exams."
options.then: "All right," she says, but her smile is a little worried.

options.text: "Can you just tell them for me? I can't do it."
options.then: "I can come along," she says. "They'll want to hear it from you."

steps.why: Asking a family member to sit beside you makes the first talk easier.

steps.prompt: At breakfast, your mother looks at you and says: "Are you okay? You look worn out."

options.text: "I'm tired. Can we share the chores differently?"
options.then: She puts the spoon down. "Yes. Let's sit down and sort it out."

options.text: "I'm fine, just a bit tired."
options.then: She hesitates. "Okay. But tell me if it gets too much."

options.text: "You'd know that if you ever really looked at me."
options.then: Her face tightens. "That's not fair," she says.

options.text: "I'll manage. The family needs me."
options.then: She sighs. "We do. But you matter too, beta."

steps.why: Asking for a specific change gives your family something they can do.

scenarios.relearn: Even the strong one is allowed to say they're struggling and need support.

scenarios.hook: You're behind on your syllabus and haven't told anyone, and you feel embarrassed.
scenarios.setup: After class, your teacher stops you at the door.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says: "I can help you plan your revision. Would that be useful?"

options.text: "Yes, please. I'm behind, and a plan would help."
options.then: "Good. Bring your syllabus tomorrow and we'll start," he says.

options.text: "No, I've got it, Sir. Thank you."
options.then: "All right," he says. "The offer stays open."

options.text: "Maybe. I'm not that far behind though."
options.then: "Hm. Let me know," he says, watching you leave.

options.text: "Could you just give me your notes instead?"
options.then: "Notes alone won't fix a plan," he says, but hands you a few pages.

steps.why: Accepting help when you're behind is smart, not shameful.

steps.prompt: A few days on, your teacher catches you in the corridor and asks: "Which chapters feel the shakiest right now?"

options.text: "Chemistry and Maths. Two chapters in each."
options.then: He writes them down. "Good. That's four chapters we can plan."

options.text: "Everything's fine, mostly. Just a few small things."
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "Mostly?" You look at your shoes.

options.text: "All of it. I'm hopeless at this."
options.then: "You're not," he says. "But let's find the actual gaps."

options.text: "I don't know. You choose."
options.then: "I'd rather hear it from you," he says. "Take a day to list them."

steps.why: Naming the specific gaps lets him help with what actually needs fixing.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says: "Let's check in twice a week. Can you manage Tuesday and Friday?"

options.text: "Yes. Can I bring my own list of topics?"
options.then: "Please do," he says. "That will help me help you."

options.text: "Yes, but I'll probably be late most days."
options.then: "We'll start at the time you can manage," he says, writing it down.

options.text: "Can we just do it once, near the exams?"
options.then: "Once is too late," he says. "Twice a week works better."

options.text: "I'll try. I don't want to waste your time."
options.then: "You're not wasting it," he says. "That's what I'm here for."

steps.why: Regular check-ins keep a plan alive, and you can show up ready.

scenarios.relearn: Accepting offered help when you're behind is smart, not shameful.

scenarios.hook: A group in your class is mocking a student who broke down during an exam.
scenarios.setup: In the corridor, one of them turns to you.

steps.prompt: A classmate says: "Did you see him crying in the exam hall? So weak."

options.text: "Exam stress is normal. Let's not pile on."
options.then: He pauses, then looks away. "I guess he did look really stressed."

options.text: "Ha, yes. He should toughen up."
options.then: The group laughs. You feel a flicker of something uneasy.

options.text: "I didn't see anything."
options.then: He shrugs. The laughter picks up again behind you.

options.text: "You're the weak one for gossiping about it."
options.then: He bristles. "Whoa. Relax." The mood turns cold.

steps.why: Naming exam stress as normal makes it safer for everyone to cope.

steps.prompt: The next day, your classmate cracks another joke about it and says: "It's only banter. Nobody's hurt."

options.text: "Jokes like that stop people asking for help."
options.then: He shifts. "Hm. Never thought of it that way."

options.text: "Fine, fine. Just joking, then."
options.then: He grins. The laughter starts up again.

options.text: "It's not funny to me. Leave me alone."
options.then: He raises his hands. "Okay, okay. Chill."

options.text: "Fine, joke about it, just not when I'm around."
options.then: "Sure," he says, and tells the same joke at the next bench.

steps.why: Explaining why it matters, calmly, can change how a group talks.

steps.prompt: A friend whispers: "He's sitting alone again. Should someone say something?"

options.text: "Let's sit with him, and ask our teacher to check in."
options.then: He looks up, surprised. "Oh. Hi." He moves his bag, and later the teacher quietly checks in.

options.text: "Leave him alone. Talking to him will only make it worse."
options.then: You both watch him from a distance. He keeps looking at his notebook.

options.text: "Not me. They might start laughing at me too."
options.then: Your friend nods slowly. The two of you stay where you are.

options.text: "Let's tell him to get over it."
options.then: Your friend grimaces. "I don't think that'll help," they say.

steps.why: Sitting with someone who's struggling, and looping in a teacher, shows they aren't alone.

scenarios.relearn: Normalising exam stress and refusing to mock it makes it safer for everyone to cope.

scenarios.hook: "If you can't put your strengths in fancy words, you don't really have any."

myth.un: If you can't name your strengths in fancy words, you don't have any.
myth.re: Everyone has real strengths; naming them simply is enough to build on.
myth.why: A strength is shown in what you do, not how impressively you phrase it.

scenarios.relearn: You don't need fancy words; naming a real strength simply is enough.

scenarios.hook: "Changing your mind about who you are means you were fake before."

myth.un: Changing your mind about who you are means you were fake before.
myth.re: Growing and updating who you are is honesty, not fakeness.
myth.why: Self-knowledge unfolds for life, so it naturally keeps changing.

scenarios.relearn: Updating who you are as you grow is honesty, not fakeness.

scenarios.hook: "Real self-awareness means analysing your every flaw, hard."

myth.un: Real self-awareness means picking apart your every flaw, harshly.
myth.re: Kind, honest reflection builds self-knowledge; harsh self-attack just hurts.
myth.why: Self-criticism narrows your view; self-compassion lets you see clearly.

scenarios.relearn: Kind, honest reflection builds self-knowledge; harsh self-attack doesn't.

myth.why: Pushing feelings down loses the signal; reading them builds self-awareness.

scenarios.hook: "Adopt your friends' values, or you'll get left behind."

myth.un: You should adopt your friends' values or you'll be left behind.
myth.re: There are no 'right' values to copy; the work is knowing your own.
myth.why: Borrowed values guide someone else's life, not yours.

scenarios.relearn: There are no 'right' values to copy; know your own.

scenarios.hook: "A confident adult never feels unsure of who they are."

myth.why: Self-knowledge is honesty about yourself, not certainty about everything.

myth.re: Your values are the base of every good decision you'll make.
myth.why: When choices get hard, knowing what matters most points the way.

scenarios.hook: "By 18 you should have your whole personality locked in."

myth.un: By 18 your personality should be fully locked in.
myth.re: Who you are keeps developing for years; you only need to start, not finish.
myth.why: People grow and change across their whole lives, at every age.

scenarios.relearn: Who you are keeps developing; you don't need it locked in by 18.

scenarios.hook: Relatives keep telling you what people like you should want from life.

steps.prompt: At a wedding, an aunt says what you ought to want. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her and say you'll decide for yourself
options.then: She blinks, then smiles. "Well, you've clearly thought about it," she says.

options.text: Tell yourself she must know better than you do
options.then: You smile and nod. Her certainty makes your own thoughts feel small.

options.text: Say they're all outdated and walk off
options.then: A few people gasp. Your mother follows you outside.

options.text: Decide you're ungrateful for wanting something different
options.then: You apologise in your head. The next hour is mostly guilt.

steps.why: Thanking people while keeping the decision yours respects them and you.

steps.prompt: That evening your mother asks what you actually want. What do you say?

options.text: What you value, and what you're unsure of
options.then: She listens. "Honestly, I didn't know you'd thought so much about this," she says.

options.text: That you'll do whatever they think is best
options.then: She looks relieved and slightly worried. The question isn't answered.

options.text: What the relatives said, so she's pleased
options.then: She nods. It sounds like something she's already heard.

options.text: That you'd like to be left alone to think
options.then: She says okay. The evening is quiet and a little distant.

steps.why: Sharing both your values and your doubts lets your family really know you.

steps.prompt: A cousin shows you her list of what she wants. Yours is blank. What do you do?

options.text: Start your own list slowly, even if it's short
options.then: Two lines go down. They look small, and they're yours.

options.text: Copy hers so you're not behind
options.then: Her list looks tidy. It doesn't match anything you feel.

options.text: Skip anything others would find odd
options.then: The list reads well. Two things you care about aren't on it.

options.text: Wait for someone to tell you what to want
options.then: Nobody does. The page stays blank.

steps.why: A short list of your own wants is a start, and it is yours.

scenarios.debrief: Input from others is useful. The final word on who you are is yours, and pressure from others is never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: Hear others, but decide who you are by your own values.

scenarios.hook: You're choosing a path, but you've never sat down to ask what you value.

steps.prompt: Applications close in ten days and everyone has a view. What do you do?

options.text: Set aside a quiet hour to map what you value
options.then: Your page fills slowly. By the end you know three things that matter.

options.text: Pick whatever sounds most impressive
options.then: You choose in two minutes. The choice feels like someone else's.

options.text: Go with whichever option most friends are choosing
options.then: Your friends are happy. The reasons aren't yours.

options.text: Put off thinking about it for a few days
options.then: Three days slip past in other things. The deadline feels closer.

steps.why: A quiet hour of reflection turns noise into a clear starting point.

steps.prompt: Later that week, as you think about what matters to you, you notice it isn't what your family expects. What do you do?

options.text: Stay honest with yourself and note the parts you doubt
options.then: Your picture is honest. Two parts still feel uncertain.

options.text: Change your answers to match what they expect
options.then: Your answers look acceptable. You feel quietly flat.

options.text: Drop the idea of thinking it through because it only creates trouble
options.then: You push the thought away. The little clarity you had fades.

options.text: Decide your values must be wrong because they differ
options.then: The doubt sits heavy. You stop trusting what you wrote down.

steps.why: An honest answer, doubts included, is more use than a tidy one.

steps.prompt: A senior offers advice that doesn't match what you value. What do you do?

options.text: Thank them and check their advice against what you value
options.then: Two of their tips fit. You leave the others without argument.

options.text: Follow their advice because they've been through it
options.then: Their advice is sound for them. It isn't built around what you value.

options.text: Brush it off because they don't really know you
options.then: They look a little hurt. You've missed one useful idea.

options.text: Ask three more people and follow the majority
options.then: The advice splits. You're back where you started.

steps.why: Others' advice is useful when you weigh it against your own values.

scenarios.debrief: A little self-reflection makes every choice that follows truer to you.
scenarios.relearn: Figure out your values first; choices then fit who you are.

scenarios.hook: After a setback, you catch yourself thinking, 'maybe this just isn't who I am.'

steps.prompt: You didn't make the school team, and the thought won't leave you. What do you do?

options.text: Treat it as one event and note what you learned
options.then: You write down two things to work on. The thought quiets a little.

options.text: Decide you're just not good enough
options.then: The label sticks all evening. You skip practice.

options.text: Quit the sport so it can never hurt again
options.then: You put your kit away. The ache is gone, and so is something you liked.

options.text: Pretend you never really wanted a place on the team
options.then: Friends nod. You feel the small lie sitting in your chest.

steps.why: One setback is an event to learn from, not a verdict on who you are.

steps.prompt: A friend asks how you're really feeling about it. What do you say?

options.text: That it hurt, and you're thinking about what's next
options.then: She nods. "That sounds honest," she says. "What are you thinking?"

options.text: That you're fine and it's really nothing to talk about
options.then: She believes you. The hurt stays inside.

options.text: That it proves you're not talented
options.then: She frowns. "I don't think one tryout proves anything," she says.

options.text: That you'd rather talk about anything else
options.then: She changes the subject. You both feel a little awkward.

steps.why: Saying how you feel, honestly, keeps one event from becoming a label.

steps.prompt: A month later, a new tryout is announced. What do you do?

options.text: Think about what you learned and what you miss, then decide
options.then: You weigh what stung against what you enjoyed. You choose, and the choice is yours.

options.text: Sign up at once, just to prove everyone else wrong
options.then: You train hard out of anger. The joy isn't there.

options.text: Skip it because you've been rejected once
options.then: The tryout day passes. You feel a pang you can't quite explain.

options.text: Wait to see whether your friends sign up first
options.then: Your friends don't. The deadline passes while you wait.

steps.why: You decide again, with what you've learned, rather than letting one result decide for you.

scenarios.debrief: You're a pattern over time, not one rough moment.
scenarios.relearn: A setback is an event to learn from, not your identity.

scenarios.hook: You feel free to be yourself in some places and have to hold back in others.

steps.prompt: A classmate asks a personal question in front of the whole group. What do you do?

options.text: Answer briefly and steer the talk away
options.then: The group moves on. You keep your own space and your values steady.

options.text: Decide you're being fake and tell everything
options.then: The group goes quiet. You feel exposed and unsure about what comes next.

options.text: Make up a long story so that nobody asks more
options.then: The story gets bigger. You feel uneasy for the rest of the day.

options.text: Tell yourself it's your fault for being so easy to question
options.then: The thought stays. You spend lunch quietly replaying it.

steps.why: Reading the room for safety isn't fakeness, because your values stay the same.

steps.prompt: That night, you feel tense about the day and what it brought up. What do you do?

options.text: Talk to a trusted adult or friend who has your back
options.then: Your friend listens and says she's glad you told her. The tension eases.

options.text: Type out everything in a message to the whole class
options.then: Your thumb hovers over send, your heart racing, and you put the phone down.

options.text: Bury it and tell yourself it doesn't matter
options.then: You laugh a lot. The tension returns at night.

options.text: Decide you're a fraud for hiding anything at all
options.then: The thought grows. Your head feels heavy at bedtime.

steps.why: A person you trust can share the weight so you don't carry it alone.

steps.prompt: A new friend wants to hang out and asks a lot of questions. What do you do?

options.text: Share a little at a time and see how they respond
options.then: They listen well and don't pry. You feel a bit safer after each chat.

options.text: Tell them everything on the very first day
options.then: They look surprised. You feel quite unprotected afterwards.

options.text: Avoid them completely so nothing slips out
options.then: The invitations stop. You feel lonelier than before.

options.text: Say whatever you think they want to hear
options.then: They seem pleased. You aren't sure they know the real you.

steps.why: Opening up in steps lets trust grow before you share more.

steps.prompt: You feel guilty about not being open everywhere. What do you do?

options.text: Remind yourself that choosing where to open up isn't fakeness
options.then: The guilt softens a little. You notice which places feel safe.

options.text: Decide you're a fraud and keep it to yourself
options.then: The label sticks. You feel worse each time you hold back.

options.text: Open up to everyone to prove you're honest
options.then: Some people take it well. A few don't, and it stings.

options.text: Pull away from everyone to avoid feeling guilty
options.then: The guilt lessens. So does the company you keep.

steps.why: Choosing who you open up to is part of staying safe and being yourself.

scenarios.debrief: Staying true to your values while reading the room is self-knowledge, not fakeness.
scenarios.relearn: Holding your values steady across settings is being yourself.

scenarios.hook: Two things you value, your family and your own dream, seem to pull against each other.

steps.prompt: A decision about a distant college is due, and both pull at you. What do you do?

options.text: Write down both values and what each one needs
options.then: Your page shows that the two needs overlap more than you'd thought.

options.text: Ignore the clash and hope it sorts itself out
options.then: The deadline gets closer. The pull gets sharper.

options.text: Choose whichever answer ends the argument fastest
options.then: The argument stops. You aren't sure the answer is yours.

options.text: Pick your dream and stop talking to your family about it
options.then: The silence at home grows. You feel the distance in every meal.

steps.why: Naming both values honestly lets you decide with clarity.

steps.prompt: A week later, your parents ask what you're thinking. What do you say?

options.text: Share both values and ask what they're worried about
options.then: Your father says he worries about cost. It's the first time he has said it.

options.text: That you haven't decided anything yet
options.then: They nod and wait. The unspoken tension stays.

options.text: That your dream matters more, and nothing else
options.then: Their faces tighten. The conversation stops there.

options.text: That family matters most, so you'll do as they say
options.then: They look relieved. You feel your dream shrink a little.

steps.why: Sharing both sides gives your family a way to understand and help.

steps.prompt: You find a middle path, but it costs something. What do you do?

options.text: Weigh what each option gives and costs, then choose and own it
options.then: The choice has a cost. You can say plainly why you made it.

options.text: Pick whichever feels least risky and don't explain
options.then: The choice is easy. Nobody knows your reasons, including you.

options.text: Keep looking for a perfect option with no cost at all
options.then: The weeks pass. Every option you find has a cost of its own.

options.text: Let a friend decide so it isn't your fault
options.then: She picks one. You feel relieved and strangely unmoved.

steps.why: A good decision weighs the costs honestly and then is owned.

scenarios.debrief: Seeing two of your values pull against each other is deep self-knowledge.
scenarios.relearn: Noticing when your values clash helps you decide thoughtfully.

scenarios.hook: Everyone's posting a five-year plan, and you have no idea what yours is yet.

steps.prompt: A friend asks you to share your plan in a joint post. What do you do?

options.text: Say you're starting with your values and the next step
options.then: She nods. "Honestly, that's more real than my plan," she says.

options.text: Copy someone else's plan to look sorted
options.then: The plan looks great on the screen. It has nothing to do with you.

options.text: Skip the post and feel behind everyone else
options.then: Your phone buzzes with their posts. You feel further behind.

options.text: Make up a big plan that you don't really believe in
options.then: You write a confident page. You feel like an imposter.

steps.why: Starting from your values and one real step is more honest than a borrowed plan.

steps.prompt: A relative asks what you'll be doing in five years. What do you say?

options.text: That you're working it out, and will pick a next step soon
options.then: He nods. "Fair enough. That's more than I knew at your age," he says.

options.text: A confident answer you've just made up on the spot
options.then: He's pleased. You feel the pressure of living up to it.

options.text: That you have no idea and you're hopeless at it
options.then: He frowns. "Don't say that," he says.

options.text: That you'll do whatever he suggests
options.then: He smiles. You feel the plan slip out of your hands.

steps.why: You can be honest about not knowing yet while still working toward a next step.

steps.prompt: A month on, you still don't know what the future holds. What do you do?

options.text: Pick a next step, using your values
options.then: The step is small and clear. You feel steady.

options.text: Panic that you're behind everyone
options.then: The feeling is loud. Your sleep suffers.

options.text: Wait until you know everything before moving
options.then: The days pass. Nothing has changed except the time.

options.text: Switch plans because someone else's looks better
options.then: The new plan is shiny. You lose the progress you'd made.

steps.why: Self-knowledge unfolds as you go, so choose a next step, then another.

scenarios.debrief: Few people truly know at your age. You only need to start, not finish.
scenarios.relearn: Self-knowledge unfolds for life; start with your values and the next step.

scenarios.hook: You catch yourself measuring your worth against a classmate's highlight reel.

steps.prompt: A classmate posts about winning an award. What do you do?

options.text: Be happy for them, then turn back to your own work
options.then: You send a quick congratulation. Your own page feels more welcoming.

options.text: Decide you're simply not good enough
options.then: The thought grows. Your own work feels pointless.

options.text: Scroll through all their posts for an hour
options.then: Every post adds to the ache. You feel drained.

options.text: Post your own best moment right away to compete
options.then: A few likes come in. You keep checking for more.

steps.why: Being glad for others while keeping your focus protects your own progress.

steps.prompt: In class, the teacher praises them again. What do you do?

options.text: Note what you could learn and refocus on your own
options.then: You jot down one idea. It helps you for the rest of the lesson.

options.text: Sit sulking in your seat for the rest of the lesson
options.then: The lesson passes without you hearing it.

options.text: Whisper that they're just showing off
options.then: A friend laughs. It makes you feel small afterwards.

options.text: Plan to study harder only to beat them
options.then: The plan lights you up. It also ties your mood to theirs.

steps.why: Learning from someone's strength is a use of comparison. Competing with them isn't.

steps.prompt: That night your own progress list looks smaller than theirs. What do you do?

options.text: Check it against your own values and last term
options.then: Against last term, you've come a long way. The list looks different.

options.text: Tear it up because it's too small
options.then: The page is gone. So is the record of what you did.

options.text: Add extra things so it looks bigger
options.then: The list grows. You know which items are padding.

options.text: Decide you'll never be able to catch up with them
options.then: The thought sits heavy. You close your notebook.

steps.why: Your own progress against your own past shows what's real.

scenarios.debrief: Coming back to your own values beats comparing yourself to others.
scenarios.relearn: Your own values and progress matter more than a comparison.

scenarios.hook: You don't know the whole road ahead, but a deadline is forcing a choice.

steps.prompt: A form for a skills course closes in three days. What do you do?

options.text: List what you value and what you know, then pick
options.then: The page holds three facts and two values. One course fits both.

options.text: Wait for total certainty before moving
options.then: Three days go by. On the last evening you pick in a hurry, still unsure.

options.text: Apply for whatever the first person you ask suggests
options.then: A neighbour names a course and you apply in minutes. It isn't quite what you want.

options.text: Choose the course with the most famous name
options.then: The name looks good on paper. Its content isn't what you want.

steps.why: Facts plus values give you enough to choose, even without the full map.

steps.prompt: At the centre, the counsellor asks what brings you to this course. What do you say?

options.text: What matters to you and what you hope for
options.then: She nods. "That's a clear reason. It'll help you stay on track."

options.text: That someone you trust suggested it to you
options.then: She smiles. "Advice helps. What matters to you about it?"

options.text: That you don't know and didn't think about it
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "Hm. Let's work out why you're here."

options.text: Whatever you think she wants to hear
options.then: She looks puzzled. The reasons don't quite match.

steps.why: Saying what you want from it helps you stay with it.

steps.prompt: Midway through, you doubt your choice. What do you do?

options.text: Check it against your values and talk to a mentor
options.then: The mentor helps you see two parts that still fit. The doubt shrinks.

options.text: Drop out right away
options.then: You leave the course. The doubt leaves with you for a while.

options.text: Hide the doubt and stay quiet about it
options.then: You keep going. The doubt travels with you.

options.text: Blame yourself for choosing wrong
options.then: The thought repeats. It doesn't help you decide.

steps.why: Doubt is a cue to check your values and ask someone, not to quit on impulse or blame yourself.

steps.prompt: A few months on, you still have no job offer. What do you do?

options.text: Take the next step you can, and ask for help
options.then: Someone you trust introduces you to two employers. One agrees to a trial.

options.text: Decide the whole thing was wasted
options.then: The thought lingers. Your course notes sit in a drawer.

options.text: Wait for a job to come to you
options.then: The phone stays silent. A month goes by.

options.text: Start another course without thinking it through
options.then: The new course is similar. You feel the same uncertainty.

steps.why: Even without the full map, you can take the next step with help.

scenarios.debrief: You can decide well by your values, even without the full map.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing your values lets you decide even without the whole picture.

scenarios.hook: A relative has opinions about your future, and you want to answer honestly.
scenarios.setup: She raises it again at the family gathering.

steps.prompt: Your aunt says: "A girl your age should be thinking of marriage, not a career."

options.text: "I hear you. I'm deciding by my own values."
options.then: She tilts her head. "Hm. You sound sure," she says.

options.text: "Maybe I'm not allowed to say no to an elder."
options.then: She smiles and nods. Your mother looks at you, unconvinced.

options.text: "You're so old-fashioned. You just don't get it."
options.then: She stiffens. "Is that how you speak to your elders?"

options.text: "Maybe I only think this way because I'm young."
options.then: She nods knowingly. "You'll understand when you're older," she says.

steps.why: You can hear her out and keep the choice yours. This pressure is not your fault.

steps.prompt: Your aunt says: "We only want what's best for you. Your parents have given up so much for you."

options.text: "I know you care. I still need to decide this myself."
options.then: Her expression softens. "That's fair," she admits.

options.text: "Then stop pushing me and let me be."
options.then: She puts down her cup. "I'm only trying to help."

options.text: "Maybe I'm ungrateful for wanting something else."
options.then: The guilt settles on you. Your mother says quietly, "Nobody called you ungrateful, beta."

options.text: "You don't care about me. You care what people say."
options.then: Her face goes pale. "That's an unkind thing to say."

steps.why: You can honour her care and still hold your decision.

steps.prompt: Your mother quietly asks: "What do you want, though? Tell me."

options.text: "I want my own plan, and your backing with Aunty."
options.then: She squeezes your hand. "I'll speak to her, beta. Take the time you need."

options.text: "I want to study. I'll handle Aunty on my own."
options.then: She frowns gently. "You don't have to do it alone, beta. I can help."

options.text: "Aunty says wanting this will shame the family."
options.then: She shakes her head. "That is her worry, beta, not the truth. What do you want?"

options.text: "I'm sorry I've made this so hard for everyone."
options.then: "You haven't, beta. This is not your fault. Tell me."

steps.why: Telling someone who loves you what you want, and asking for their backing, means you don't face this alone.

steps.prompt: A cousin whispers: "Aren't you scared of what they'll say about you?"

options.text: "A little. But my life is mine to decide."
options.then: She grins. "I wish I could say that," she whispers.

options.text: "Yes. Everyone says girls who argue end up alone."
options.then: She shrugs. "They do say that," she whispers, unsure.

options.text: "I don't care what anyone thinks of me at all."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. You aren't sure that's true.

options.text: "Maybe I am selfish for wanting this."
options.then: She looks alarmed. "Please don't think that. You haven't done anything wrong."

steps.why: Deciding by your own values takes courage, and others' words don't change that.

scenarios.relearn: You can hear others and still decide who you are by your own values.

scenarios.hook: A friend is sure you should want exactly what he wants from life.
scenarios.setup: You value something different, and today he brings it up again.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Everyone sensible wants this. Why don't you?"

options.text: "I respect that. What matters to me is different."
options.then: He pauses. "Huh. I hadn't thought of it like that."

options.text: "Yeah. I guess I should want that too."
options.then: He grins. You feel unsure about what you just agreed to.

options.text: "Your goals are pointless anyway, honestly."
options.then: His face falls. "Wow. That was unnecessary."

options.text: "Don't ask me that. Can we talk about something else?"
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay. But I'm curious."

steps.why: Respecting their path while stating yours keeps the friendship honest.

steps.prompt: Later that week, your friend says: "I keep thinking about our chat. What do you really want, though?"

options.text: "I'm still working out what works for me."
options.then: He thinks about it. "Fair. I'd rather hear that than a polite yes."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. I should rethink my whole plan."
options.then: He smiles. You feel a little hollow.

options.text: "You only ask because you want me to just copy you."
options.then: He stares. "Where did that come from?"

options.text: "You'll see. I'll prove my way works better than yours."
options.then: He laughs. "Sure." The chat feels like a contest.

steps.why: There are no right values, only the work of knowing your own.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks: "So are we okay? Can we still hang out?"

options.text: "Of course. We can differ and still be friends."
options.then: His shoulders relax. "Good. I'd hate to lose that."

options.text: "Only if you stop going on about it."
options.then: He mutters. "Okay, okay." The mood is stiff.

options.text: "Sure, but I won't be telling you my plans again."
options.then: He nods slowly. "Alright." He looks a bit hurt.

options.text: "Sure. Next time I'll just say yes to everything."
options.then: He grins. Both of you know it isn't a real answer.

steps.why: Friends can want different things and still respect each other.

scenarios.relearn: There are no 'right' values; knowing your own is the work.

scenarios.hook: You've made a mistake, and your first instinct is to call yourself useless.
scenarios.setup: You're walking home together after school.

steps.prompt: A friend asks: "Hey, I saw what happened. How are you doing?"

options.text: "That stung. It's one mistake I can learn from."
options.then: She nods and smiles. "That sounds like a real answer," she says.

options.text: "I'm hopeless. I always mess everything up."
options.then: She frowns. "That sounds really harsh," she says.

options.text: "It wasn't my fault. It never is."
options.then: She hesitates. "Hm. Are you sure about that?"

options.text: "Fine. I don't want to talk about it right now."
options.then: She nods and falls into step beside you. "I'm around if you want," she says.

steps.why: Calling it one mistake, kindly, lets you learn without attacking yourself.

steps.prompt: After a few quiet steps, your friend asks: "If this had happened to me, what would you say to me?"

options.text: "It happens. Let's work out what to do next."
options.then: She smiles. "Then why not say that to yourself?"

options.text: "I'd say you should have known better."
options.then: She winces. "Is that what you'd really say?"

options.text: "I'd say it's nothing and we should move on."
options.then: She tilts her head. "But it clearly isn't nothing."

options.text: "I'd say the same harsh things I say to myself."
options.then: She goes quiet. "That sounds exhausting."

steps.why: Talking to yourself the way you'd talk to a friend builds self-knowledge.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks: "So what's one thing you could do differently next time?"

options.text: "I could check the details early and ask for help."
options.then: She nods. "That's a real plan. I like it."

options.text: "Nothing. It's just who I am."
options.then: She shakes her head. "I don't think that's true."

options.text: "Be perfect, so it never happens again."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "That's a tough one to keep."

options.text: "Make sure nobody sees me try next time."
options.then: She laughs, then stops. "Wait, are you serious?"

steps.why: A kind, specific next step beats a harsh judgement.

scenarios.relearn: Kind, honest self-talk builds self-knowledge; harsh self-attack doesn't.

scenarios.hook: You have no five-year plan yet, and grown-ups keep asking.
scenarios.setup: At a neighbour's house, a visitor turns to you.

steps.prompt: A visitor asks: "So what's your big five-year plan?"

options.text: "I'm still working it out. I know what I value."
options.then: He smiles. "Honest. I like that."

options.text: "Oh, I've got it all mapped out. Totally sorted."
options.then: He raises his eyebrows. "Wow. Tell me more." You scramble, then admit it isn't all mapped out.

options.text: "I have no idea. I'm probably just useless."
options.then: His smile fades. "Oh. I didn't mean to upset you."

options.text: "Whatever my parents decide for me, I guess."
options.then: He chuckles. "That's easy, at least."

steps.why: Being honest about not knowing yet is better than faking certainty.

steps.prompt: The visitor says: "At your age, I knew exactly what I wanted."

options.text: "That's great. I'm working on my next step."
options.then: He nods. "Good. Steps are what count."

options.text: "Then I must be behind everyone. I'm sorry."
options.then: He looks taken aback. "No, no. That isn't what I meant."

options.text: "Times were different then, weren't they?"
options.then: He gives a dry laugh. "I suppose they were."

options.text: "Maybe I should just copy your plan."
options.then: He chuckles. "Mine wouldn't fit you. I'm afraid not."

steps.why: You can respect someone's path without measuring yourself against it.

steps.prompt: The visitor asks: "Have you spoken to a mentor about it?"

options.text: "Not yet. I'll ask my teacher to map next steps."
options.then: He nods. "Teachers know more than they get credit for."

options.text: "No. I don't need anyone's advice."
options.then: He shrugs. "Suit yourself." The talk goes cool.

options.text: "No. I'm too embarrassed to ask anyone about it."
options.then: He smiles kindly. "Most people feel that way. It passes."

options.text: "Yes, and they said it's all completely fine."
options.then: He looks pleased. You feel the small fib in your throat.

steps.why: Asking a mentor for help is part of working out a path.

scenarios.relearn: Self-knowledge unfolds for life; starting honestly beats faking certainty.

scenarios.hook: A friend keeps comparing marks with yours to needle you.
scenarios.setup: In the corridor, he holds up his paper.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "I got 84. What did you get?"

options.text: "We run different races. I'm focused on mine."
options.then: He blinks. "Huh. Okay." He lowers the paper.

options.text: "You're right. I'm just worse than you."
options.then: He grins. "Well, I wasn't going to say it."

options.text: "At least I'm not a show-off like you are."
options.then: His grin fades. "What's your problem?"

options.text: "I got more than you did. Obviously."
options.then: His eyebrows rise. "Show me, then." You freeze.

steps.why: Staying calm and focused on your own path stops the comparison game.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks: "Come on. What's it all for, if not to be the best?"

options.text: "I care about improving on my own scores."
options.then: He shrugs. "Fine. That's something, I guess."

options.text: "To beat you next time. Watch me."
options.then: He smiles. "Bring it." You feel the race start.

options.text: "It's for nothing. I don't care about any of it."
options.then: He frowns. "Wait. Are you okay?"

options.text: "Stop asking me that. It's annoying."
options.then: He raises both hands. "Alright. Relax."

steps.why: Measuring against your own past is the comparison that helps.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "I'm just trying to push you."

options.text: "Thanks. Asking how I'm doing helps more."
options.then: He considers it. "Okay. How are you doing, then?"

options.text: "Then push yourself, not me."
options.then: He mutters. "Wow." He walks off.

options.text: "Okay. Sorry I was short with you."
options.then: He nods. "No worries." The comparison stays unspoken.

options.text: "Fine. Let's compare every test from now on."
options.then: He grins. "Deal." You feel the weight of it already.

steps.why: You can say what helps you, kindly, and still be friends.

scenarios.relearn: Your own values and progress matter more than a comparison.

scenarios.hook: At a youth event, someone you've only just met makes you feel unsure.
scenarios.setup: By the snack table, he leans in.

steps.prompt: He says: "Come on. Tell me who you really are."

options.text: "I share that with people I know well. Not yet."
options.then: He pauses. "Fair enough. I didn't mean to push."

options.text: "Maybe it's rude to keep my answers to myself."
options.then: He tilts his head and waits. You feel guilty for a moment.

options.text: "My friend says opening up fast is how you make friends."
options.then: He nods eagerly. "Your friend's right. So go on."

options.text: "I'm exactly who you think I am. Nothing more."
options.then: He smiles. He doesn't seem to believe it.

steps.why: Choosing who you open up to is part of being yourself, and part of staying safe.

steps.prompt: He says: "Everyone else here told me. Don't you trust us?"

options.text: "Trust takes time. I'll share when I'm ready."
options.then: He shrugs. "Alright. No pressure."

options.text: "Maybe I'm being rude by not answering."
options.then: He raises his eyebrows. "Everyone else managed," he says, and you feel worse.

options.text: "If everyone else told you, it must be safe to tell."
options.then: He smiles. "Exactly," he says, and waits for you to start.

options.text: "Maybe something is wrong with me."
options.then: He frowns. "No. I didn't say that."

steps.why: Pressure to share is a reason to be careful, and it's never your fault.

steps.prompt: As you head for the exit, he follows and says: "You can tell me anything. I'll keep it between us."

options.text: "I need to find the organiser."
options.then: He steps back. You walk to the organiser and tell her what happened. She listens and stays with you.

options.text: "Okay. But promise me it stays between us."
options.then: He nods. You feel the secret already starting to weigh.

options.text: "Maybe you're just friendly. Maybe I'm overreacting."
options.then: He smiles warmly. "Exactly. You can trust me," he says.

options.text: "My cousin says adults only make a fuss about things."
options.then: He nods. "Smart. Adults overreact," he says. You feel more alone.

steps.why: A trusted adult can help when someone keeps pressing, and a secret that worries you is always worth telling.

scenarios.relearn: Being yourself includes choosing who you open up to and when.

scenarios.hook: You're not fully sure what you want to do after school, and it weighs on you.
scenarios.setup: In the staff room, your teacher looks up from his papers.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks: "So what do you want to do after school?"

options.text: "I'm still exploring. I'm starting from my strengths."
options.then: He nods. "That's a good place to begin."

options.text: "I'll do whatever you think is best, Sir."
options.then: He smiles. "I'd rather hear what you think."

options.text: "Doesn't matter. I'll never figure it out anyway."
options.then: He frowns. "I wouldn't be so sure of that."

options.text: "I've got it all planned, Sir. Nothing to worry about."
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "Really? Tell me what the plan is."

steps.why: Starting from your strengths is an honest answer when the path isn't fixed.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks: "What would you say you're good at?"

options.text: "Explaining things, and staying calm when busy."
options.then: He writes it down. "Those are useful strengths."

options.text: "Nothing really. I'm not special."
options.then: He shakes his head. "I've watched you. That isn't true."

options.text: "Everything, Sir. I'm honestly good at all of it."
options.then: He smiles. "Everyone has a few things that stand out."

options.text: "Whatever my marks say I'm good at."
options.then: He nods. "Marks show part of it. What else?"

steps.why: Knowing your strengths gives you something to build on.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says: "Would you like to try something small to find out more?"

options.text: "Yes. Maybe I can shadow someone for a day."
options.then: He smiles. "I know someone. I'll ask her."

options.text: "No. I'd rather wait until I'm sure."
options.then: He shrugs. "Certainty comes slowly. But okay."

options.text: "Yes, if you choose something for me."
options.then: He chuckles. "I'll suggest. You'll choose."

options.text: "Not now. I'll look at it after the boards."
options.then: He nods. "All right. The offer stays open."

steps.why: Trying something small is how self-knowledge grows, one step at a time.

scenarios.relearn: Starting from your strengths is a fair answer when the path isn't fixed.

scenarios.hook: Your friends plan to use leaked answers for the unit test and want you in.
scenarios.setup: At the canteen, Imran leans over.

steps.prompt: Imran says: "Everyone's in. Just open the file and use it."

options.text: "Okay fine. I'll look so you don't get annoyed."
options.then: He grins and sends the file. Your stomach feels tight.

options.text: "It goes against what I value. No hard feelings."
options.then: He shrugs. "Your loss. Fine."

options.text: "You lot have no morals, honestly. Do what you like."
options.then: Imran's face hardens. "Wow. Okay."

options.text: "I'll look at it, but I won't use it."
options.then: Imran laughs. "That's the same thing, yaar."

steps.why: A calm no that names your own values keeps the friendship open.

steps.prompt: Next day, Riya asks: "Imran says the file's going round. Where do you stand?"

options.text: "I'm not judging you. It's just not for me."
options.then: Riya nods slowly. "Okay. At least you're honest."

options.text: "Fine. If everyone's using it, count me in."
options.then: Riya relaxes. You feel your own view slip away.

options.text: "You're all cheating and you know it."
options.then: Riya snaps. "Wow, preach more."

options.text: "Let's talk about something else, please."
options.then: Riya lets it go. The question is still hanging.

steps.why: Saying it is about you, not them, lets the line hold without an attack.

steps.prompt: Imran asks: "Are we still on for cricket on Sunday?"

options.text: "Let's skip it. I'm done with this whole group."
options.then: Imran goes quiet. "Right. Okay."

options.text: "Sure. And I'll join the next plan too, to make up."
options.then: He says great. You wonder what you've signed up for.

options.text: "I don't know. Ask the others and tell me."
options.then: He shrugs, and the plan fades out without anyone deciding.

options.text: "Still on. Count me in, but not for the answers."
options.then: He grins. "Good. Bring the bat."

steps.why: Holding one line while staying warm keeps the friendship and your values.

steps.prompt: A week later, Imran asks: "Can I copy off you in tomorrow's test? Please?"

options.text: "Okay, but only this once. Don't tell anyone."
options.then: He agrees fast. Your stomach tightens.

options.text: "No. And honestly, you should be ashamed of yourself."
options.then: He flinches. "Wow. Okay, then."

options.text: "Let's revise together tonight. I won't let you copy."
options.then: He thinks. "Fine. Tonight at six?"

options.text: "Sorry, I'll be sitting far away. Can't help."
options.then: He sighs. "Okay." You've avoided saying what's true.

steps.why: Offering another way to help keeps your value and the friendship.

scenarios.relearn: Deciding by your own values, kindly, keeps your life yours.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that confuse harsh self-criticism with real self-awareness.

scene.text: Noticing how a setback made you feel
Calling yourself a failure for one mistake
Asking kindly why a thing got to you
Listing every flaw to 'toughen up'
Reflecting on what you value

scenarios.why: Tearing yourself down isn't self-awareness; kind, honest reflection is what builds it.
scenarios.relearn: Harsh self-criticism isn't self-knowledge; kind reflection is.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that hand your identity to other people.

scene.text: Hearing advice, then deciding by your own values
Becoming whoever the loudest relative wants
Knowing what matters most to you
Copying a friend's whole life to fit in
Listening, but keeping the final say yourself

scenarios.why: Letting others author your identity isn't self-knowledge; you keep the final say.
scenarios.relearn: Hear others, but decide who you are by your own values.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two myths about identity hiding among the truths.

scene.text: Self-knowledge unfolds across your whole life
By 18 you must have yourself fully figured out
There are no 'right' values to copy
Feeling unsure of yourself means you've failed
Knowing your values guides good decisions

scenarios.why: Both flagged lines are myths the game flips: self-knowledge unfolds for life, and doubt is normal.
scenarios.relearn: You don't need it all figured out; self-knowledge unfolds for life.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that treat feelings as something to bury.

scene.text: Naming a feeling to understand it
Pushing every feeling down to look strong
Asking what a feeling is telling you
Numbing out so you never have to feel it
Noticing your reactions without judging them

scenarios.why: Burying or numbing feelings loses the signal; noticing them builds self-awareness.
scenarios.relearn: Feelings carry information; noticing them builds self-awareness.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that copy values instead of knowing your own.

scene.text: Asking what genuinely matters to you
Adopting a trend's values to fit in
Naming a line you won't cross
Wanting something only because relatives do
Choosing what sits right with your conscience

scenarios.why: Borrowed values steer someone else's life; the work is knowing your own.
scenarios.relearn: There are no 'right' values to copy; know your own.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that tie your whole worth to one result.

scene.text: A setback is one event you can learn from
One bad result means you're a failure for good
Your worth isn't decided by a mark sheet
If you slip once, you've ruined everything
You're a pattern over time, not one day

scenarios.why: Tying your worth to a single result is the myth; you're far more than one event.
scenarios.relearn: One result doesn't define your worth or who you are.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that pretend self-knowledge means being perfect.

scene.text: Being honest with yourself about a weak spot
Hiding every flaw so you seem flawless
Owning a mistake and learning from it
Believing real adults never feel unsure
Treating yourself with everyday kindness

scenarios.why: Self-knowledge is honesty, not perfection; hiding flaws and faking certainty get in the way.
scenarios.relearn: Self-knowledge is honesty with yourself, not perfection.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that let comparison decide who you are.

scene.text: Measuring your progress against your own past
Judging your worth by a classmate's reel
Coming back to what you actually value
Deciding you're behind because others post wins
Running your own race at your own pace

scenarios.why: Comparison is a thief, not a measure of you; your own values and progress are what count.
scenarios.relearn: Your own values and progress matter more than a comparison.
