scenarios.hook: School's nearly over and adulthood feels huge.

steps.prompt: You stare at a long list of things to learn. What do you do?

options.text: Pick one tool and use it this month
options.then: You pick the one-next-step habit and stick a note on your desk.

options.text: Wait until I feel fully ready
options.then: The list grows. The feeling of ready doesn't come.

options.text: Start everything on the first of next month
options.then: The date arrives and the list is as big as ever.

options.text: Ask everyone what to do and add it all
options.then: You have forty tips and no clear place to begin.

steps.why: Starting small gets you moving, and ready doesn't arrive by waiting.

steps.prompt: Two weeks on, starting still feels awkward. What do you do?

options.text: Give up and wait for an easier way in
options.then: The next way in feels awkward too, and you stop again.

options.text: Decide I'm just bad at this
options.then: You feel small, and the list looks even bigger.

options.text: Start three more things to make up for it
options.then: A pile of half-started things grows on your desk.

options.text: Try a smaller first step and keep at it
options.then: It fits a little better. You notice one thing it helps.

steps.why: Awkward at first is normal, and small changes help it fit.

steps.prompt: A relative asks how you're getting ready for life after school. What do you say?

options.text: Say I'm totally sorted
options.then: She's pleased. You feel the pressure to stay perfect.

options.text: Say I'm not ready for any of it
options.then: She frowns and worries about you. You feel worse.

options.text: Say I'm still working it out and learning as I go
options.then: She nods. "That's more honest than most grown-ups."

options.text: Say it's too early to think about
options.then: She laughs and changes the subject, and the worry stays with you.

steps.why: An honest answer shows being life-ready means learning, not having it all done.

scenarios.debrief: A tool used once becomes a habit you keep.
scenarios.relearn: Don't wait to feel ready; put one tool into practice to begin.

scenarios.hook: Results are out and yours aren't what relatives wanted.

steps.prompt: Your aunt calls to say how disappointed the family is. What do you do?

options.text: Agree it's a disaster and apologise
options.then: She sighs and says to work harder. You feel smaller after the call.

options.text: Listen, then say marks are not all of me
options.then: Aunty goes quiet, then says she only wants the best for you.

options.text: Say relatives have no right to comment
options.then: She says "Is this how you talk?" and the call ends.

options.text: Say nothing and hand the phone to Mummy
options.then: Your mother takes it. You hear your name and a long sigh from the next room.

steps.why: You can hear concern without agreeing that a rank is your worth.

steps.prompt: That night, you keep staring at the marksheet. What do you do?

options.text: Write what went well and what I'd change
options.then: The list shows effort you'd forgotten. One subject needs a plan.

options.text: Compare my marks with everyone in my class
options.then: The numbers pile up. You feel worse and no clearer.

options.text: Scroll my phone until I'm too tired to think
options.then: The marksheet is still there in the morning.

options.text: Decide this has closed every door
options.then: The night feels very long. Your worth was never in that number, but it's hard to see tonight.

steps.why: Looking at what went well and what to change keeps the result in proportion.

steps.prompt: Your cousin says to take whatever course will have you now. What do you do?

options.text: Take whichever course accepts me fastest
options.then: A seat is yours by evening. You aren't sure it's the one you want.

options.text: Let the relatives pick so it's on them
options.then: The family agrees quickly. The choice is no longer yours.

options.text: Refuse to talk about it for months
options.then: Weeks pass and the deadlines get closer.

options.text: Look up courses and weigh them by my values
options.then: You list three that fit what you care about, and where each leads.

steps.why: Many paths stay open, and your own values help you pick one.

steps.prompt: A neighbour asks in front of everyone what you scored. What do you do?

options.text: Joke that it's too embarrassing to say
options.then: A few people smile. The question follows you home.

options.text: Make up a higher number
options.then: They congratulate you. You spend the evening worried about being found out.

options.text: Say calmly I'd keep that private, and I'm working out my next step
options.then: The room is quiet, then someone asks about your plan.

options.text: Say it was a bad result and look away
options.then: The neighbour says sorry. The number feels stuck to you.

steps.why: You can keep a number private. A rank is one exam, not a verdict on you.

scenarios.debrief: Worth isn't a rank; many good paths remain.
scenarios.relearn: Results matter but don't define your worth; decide your next step by your values.

scenarios.hook: Board prep is piling up and you're carrying it alone.

steps.prompt: It's 11 pm and the syllabus feels endless. What do you do?

options.text: Push on through the night
options.then: You read till 3 am and can't recall the last chapter.

options.text: Break it into days and start with tomorrow
options.then: The pile becomes a list of small days. Your chest loosens a little.

options.text: Scroll for ten minutes to calm down
options.then: Ten minutes becomes an hour. The pile is still there.

options.text: Tell myself a topper would be done by now
options.then: Everyone's marks swirl in your head and the page blurs.

steps.why: Splitting a big load into days makes it something you can start.

steps.prompt: Days later, your head feels heavy and sleep is off. What do you do?

options.text: Tell one trusted person I'm stretched
options.then: Your elder cousin listens and offers to quiz you on Saturday.

options.text: Tell no one so I don't worry them
options.then: You keep going. The heaviness sits quietly with you.

options.text: Post about it on the class group chat
options.then: Replies pile up, mostly jokes, and some of the posts stress you more.

options.text: Say "I'm fine" whenever someone asks
options.then: They believe you. You feel more alone.

steps.why: Telling one person you're stretched is strength, and shrinks the load.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks how prep is really going. What do you do?

options.text: Say it's all fine
options.then: He nods and moves on. The stuck spots stay stuck.

options.text: Say I'll probably fail
options.then: He worries, and the talk is about your fear, not your plan.

options.text: Ask for extra work to prove myself
options.then: He gives you more. The load grows.

options.text: Say what's going well and where I'm stuck
options.then: He sits with you and shows how to plan past papers.

steps.why: Being honest with a teacher gets you real help for the real gaps.

steps.prompt: The mock results come back lower than you hoped. What do you do?

options.text: Hide the paper from everyone
options.then: The paper sits in your bag. The worry grows.

options.text: Decide there's no point revising more
options.then: You close the books and drift. The gaps stay exactly where they were.

options.text: Look at where marks slipped, and tell a friend
options.then: Your friend nods. "Okay. Let's make a plan for those."

options.text: Study through the night to fix it
options.then: You study till 4 am. The morning is a blur.

steps.why: A mock result is feedback, and sharing it keeps the load lighter.

scenarios.debrief: Break big stress down and lean on someone; that's strength, not weakness.
scenarios.relearn: Break the big stuff down and lean on people; don't carry it alone.

scenarios.hook: You've been skipping sleep and meals to power through.

steps.prompt: Your head is foggy and you've skipped dinner again. What do you do?

options.text: Drink more tea and keep going
options.then: The tea buzz fades by nine. You re-read the same page.

options.text: Promise to eat properly after the test
options.then: You gain forty minutes. You spend them staring at the book.

options.text: Eat something, then study a shorter stretch
options.then: You finish less, but what you read stays in your head.

options.text: Take a long break and promise to catch up
options.then: The break stretches. Guilt builds as the pile grows.

steps.why: You can't think well on an empty stomach, so food comes first.

steps.prompt: A friend says you look exhausted. What do you do?

options.text: Say I'm fine and I'm just tough
options.then: She frowns, then lets it go. The cycle continues.

options.text: Tell her I've been skipping sleep and ask her to nudge me
options.then: She laughs, relieved. "Deal. Lights out by eleven."

options.text: Joke that sleep is for the less ambitious
options.then: She forces a smile. You both change the subject.

options.text: Say tired is what exams cost
options.then: She nods. You feel slightly proud, and slightly worse.

steps.why: Naming the problem and asking for a nudge makes the habit stick.

steps.prompt: It's the night before a test. What do you do?

options.text: Revise for an hour, then sleep
options.then: You wake rested and the answers come easier than you feared.

options.text: Study till 2 am and sleep an hour
options.then: You blur through the paper. The facts won't come up.

options.text: Skip revision and go straight to sleep
options.then: You sleep well. Parts of the paper feel like a surprise.

options.text: Stay up and sleep after the test
options.then: You arrive jittery and watch the clock all morning.

steps.why: Rest is part of preparing, so sleep belongs in the plan.

scenarios.debrief: The basics are part of the toolkit, not a weakness.
scenarios.relearn: Self-care keeps you able to cope; you can't run well on empty.

scenarios.hook: Things are fine now, but you've no one you'd call if they weren't.

steps.prompt: Your school's mentor evening is on Saturday. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it because I'm fine right now
options.then: Saturday goes by. You meet nobody new.

options.text: Go, but stay at the back and leave early
options.then: You see a few mentors from a distance and leave without speaking.

options.text: Go only if a friend does
options.then: Your friend can't make it, so you stay home too.

options.text: Go and talk to one mentor about my goals
options.then: A mentor gives you her email and says "write any time".

steps.why: Meeting a mentor while things are calm means someone knows you when it counts.

steps.prompt: A classmate you barely know offers to share notes. What do you do?

options.text: Say no so I don't owe anyone
options.then: She shrugs. The door stays shut.

options.text: Say yes, then never talk to her again
options.then: You use the notes and the contact fades.

options.text: Say yes, and offer something in return
options.then: She smiles. "Great. Maybe we could revise together."

options.text: Say yes, but keep it all business
options.then: The notes help. You still know nothing about each other.

steps.why: Small trades build people you can lean on later.

steps.prompt: You scroll your contacts and name only two people to call on a bad day. What do you do?

options.text: Decide two is plenty and stop
options.then: The list stays small. On a bad day it might feel thin.

options.text: Add a teacher or mentor and a relative I trust
options.then: The list now has four names, and you know which for what.

options.text: Wait until I actually need more
options.then: You tell yourself you'll build it when it's needed.

options.text: Collect fifty numbers so I'm covered
options.then: Most of them wouldn't know how to help.

steps.why: A few people matched to different needs make a support network.

steps.prompt: A classmate you've been chatting with looks upset one day. What do you do?

options.text: Ask quietly if she wants company or to talk
options.then: She nods. "Company would be nice."

options.text: Pretend not to notice and move on
options.then: She sits alone. You see her in the corridor later.

options.text: Ask loudly in front of everyone what's wrong
options.then: She turns red and says nothing.

options.text: Tell her everyone has bad days
options.then: She nods, and goes quiet.

steps.why: A network works both ways, so you show up for others too.

scenarios.debrief: A network built early is there when you need it.
scenarios.relearn: Build your support network before you need it, not in the middle of a crisis.

scenarios.hook: A younger cousin is scared of leaving home for college.

steps.prompt: Meera says she's terrified of hostel life. What do you do?

options.text: Listen, and say I felt nervous too
options.then: She relaxes a little. "You did? I thought it was only me."

options.text: Tell her to toughen up
options.then: Meera's smile fades. She stops talking about it.

options.text: Say hostels are great and she's worrying over nothing
options.then: She nods politely and the knot in her stomach stays.

options.text: Offer to pack and sort all her forms
options.then: She says thanks. She still doesn't feel ready.

steps.why: Listening and sharing your own nerves tells her she isn't alone.

steps.prompt: Days later, Meera brings it up again and asks what she can actually do before she goes. What do you do?

options.text: Hand her a long list of hostel rules
options.then: She reads half and feels more nervous.

options.text: Say she'll work it out once she's actually there
options.then: She nods, and the nervous feeling goes with her.

options.text: Tell her to keep busy so she doesn't think about it
options.then: She nods. The worry waits for her at night.

options.text: Share two tools that helped me
options.then: She jots down naming the change and staying in touch. "I'll call Sunday."

steps.why: One or two tools she can use are more helpful than a pile.

steps.prompt: Before she leaves, Meera says she doesn't want to bother anyone with her feelings. What do you do?

options.text: Say she's right and should keep it to herself
options.then: She nods. The week of her leaving feels heavy.

options.text: Promise to sort every problem that comes up for her
options.then: She feels safe for now, and wonders what happens when you can't.

options.text: Say she's not a burden, and offer a weekly call
options.then: She smiles. "Okay. Sundays, then."

options.text: Tell her to message the whole family group instead
options.then: She winces. She doesn't want the whole family reading it.

steps.why: Reminding her she's not a burden gives her a way to reach out.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, Meera calls to say she's homesick and it's harder than she thought. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her to stop crying and focus
options.then: She goes quiet. "Okay. Bye."

options.text: Listen, say it's normal, and ask what helps
options.then: She sniffs. "Mostly calls. And my notes from home."

options.text: Book her a ticket home before she decides
options.then: She's startled. "I didn't say I wanted to leave."

options.text: Say it'll pass and hurry off the call
options.then: She says okay. She still feels homesick and alone.

steps.why: Listening and asking what helps keeps her supported and in charge.

scenarios.debrief: Passing the toolkit on is how the thread keeps going.
scenarios.relearn: Share the toolkit and remind others they're not alone.

scenarios.hook: You don't know how the next year will go and it's unsettling.

steps.prompt: At night, the unknowns of next year loop in your head. What do you do?

options.text: Try to plan every unknown
options.then: Your list grows to three pages and the worry gets bigger.

options.text: Write down one thing I can do tomorrow
options.then: The loop quiets. You have one small job for the morning.

options.text: Ask a friend to tell me how it will go
options.then: She doesn't know either, and you end up more anxious.

options.text: Tell myself not to think about it
options.then: The thought comes back louder around 2 am.

steps.why: One step you can control makes the unknown smaller.

steps.prompt: A relative asks what your plan is for next year. What do you do?

options.text: Say what I know, what I don't, and my next step
options.then: He nods. "That's honest. Let me know how it goes."

options.text: Make up a confident plan
options.then: He's impressed. You spend the evening hoping he won't ask more.

options.text: Say I have no idea and leave it there
options.then: He frowns and starts suggesting plans of his own.

options.text: Say whatever will end the questions fastest
options.then: He's satisfied. You feel your plan slip further from you.

steps.why: Saying what you know and your next step is honest and enough.

steps.prompt: A form you needed is delayed by a month. What do you do?

options.text: Wait and do nothing until it arrives
options.then: The month drags. You feel more stuck than before.

options.text: Panic and tear up the whole plan
options.then: You start again and feel even less sure.

options.text: Blame myself for not applying sooner
options.then: You replay the missed date over and over. The month goes to guilt, not the plan.

options.text: Pick the next step I can still control
options.then: You start a short course and ask a teacher what else helps.

steps.why: When plans shift, one controllable step keeps you moving.

scenarios.debrief: You don't need the whole map; just the next step.
scenarios.relearn: For uncertainty, focus on the next step you can control.

scenarios.hook: A classmate tells you the pressure has felt heavy and constant for weeks.

steps.prompt: She says she's tired of feeling like this. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her to just relax and wait it out
options.then: She nods and goes quiet. The next day she looks even more tired.

options.text: Say everyone is stressed in exams
options.then: She tries to smile. She feels even less seen.

options.text: Listen, and say I'm glad she told me
options.then: She breathes out. "I thought you'd think I was being dramatic."

options.text: Offer study tips to fix the pressure
options.then: She thanks you. The tips don't touch how she feels.

steps.why: Listening and saying you're glad she told you opens the door.

steps.prompt: Later she asks if she's overreacting. What do you say?

options.text: Say maybe she is, and exams will end soon
options.then: She shrinks back. "Yeah. Probably."

options.text: Say it's not her fault, and weeks of heavy stress deserve support
options.then: Her shoulders drop. "Okay. Thanks for not brushing it off."

options.text: Say she'll feel fine once the results are out
options.then: She nods, but the weight is still on her face.

options.text: Say it's her problem to sort out
options.then: She nods. She's left on her own with it.

steps.why: Heavy, constant stress deserves support, and it's never her fault.

steps.prompt: The counsellor, Mr. Reddy, is on campus this week. She says she'd be too embarrassed to go to him. What do you do?

options.text: Say it's normal. Offer to go along, or call Tele-MANAS 14416
options.then: She thinks, then nods. "Would you sit outside?"

options.text: Say that's fine and she can skip it if she's embarrassed
options.then: She looks relieved, and the weight stays.

options.text: Tell Mr. Reddy everything before she's agreed
options.then: Mr. Reddy is kind, but she's startled and wishes she'd had time to get ready.

options.text: Tell her she has to see him today, no excuses
options.then: She feels pushed and says she needs to think.

steps.why: Asking for support is normal, and doing it with her say makes it easier.

steps.prompt: A week later she's laughing again and says she's fine now. What do you do?

options.text: Drop it since she says she's fine
options.then: You stop asking. If it returns, she may not say.

options.text: Ask how she's feeling every single day
options.then: She starts avoiding you, as it feels like surveillance.

options.text: Tell the class she's doing better
options.then: She finds out and feels exposed.

options.text: Say I'm glad, and keep checking in
options.then: She smiles. "Thanks. I'll tell you if it comes back."

steps.why: Staying in touch keeps help within reach. It was never her fault.

steps.prompt: At a school session, Mr. Reddy asks how students can look out for each other. What do you say?

options.text: People should keep their problems to themselves
options.then: He tilts his head. "Do you think that helps?"

options.text: Only teachers can really handle these things
options.then: He says teachers help, and so do friends.

options.text: I'd listen, stay in touch, and point to help like Tele-MANAS 14416
options.then: He nods. "Staying in touch matters, and so does knowing where to turn."

options.text: I'd make a joke so it isn't awkward
options.then: A few classmates laugh. The real point slips by.

steps.why: Looking out for each other and pointing to real help is real support.

scenarios.debrief: Persistent distress routes to help; it isn't waited out alone.
scenarios.relearn: Heavy, persistent stress: reach a trusted adult or Tele-MANAS 14416.

scenarios.hook: Part of you feels you should have every answer before adulthood starts.

steps.prompt: A relative asks if you've got life figured out. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes just to make the questions stop
options.then: He nods, pleased. You feel a little fake.

options.text: Say no because I'm behind everyone else my age
options.then: He frowns, and starts listing what you should be doing.

options.text: Say I'll let you know when I finally do
options.then: He laughs, and nothing is really said.

options.text: Say I know my values and who I'd ask
options.then: He smiles. "That sounds like enough to start."

steps.why: Knowing your values and your people is what being ready means.

steps.prompt: A friend shows off her detailed five-year plan. What do you do?

options.text: Make up a five-year plan of my own too
options.then: Your plan sounds good, and you spend the night trying to believe it.

options.text: Feel behind and avoid her for a few weeks
options.then: You skip her calls, and the distance grows.

options.text: Admire it, and say mine is a next step
options.then: She grins. "That's actually kind of smart."

options.text: Tell her that plans never really work out
options.then: She looks hurt. You feel you've been unfair.

steps.why: A plan is useful, but so is a next step and people you trust.

steps.prompt: A seat opens in a summer course you'd only half planned for. What do you do?

options.text: Say no until I'm completely sure I'm ready
options.then: The chance passes. You're still not fully ready.

options.text: Weigh facts and values, and ask someone I trust
options.then: They ask good questions. You decide with a clearer head.

options.text: Say yes straight away so I don't lose it
options.then: You start in a rush and find questions you hadn't asked.

options.text: Ask my friends to decide for me
options.then: Each friend says something different.

steps.why: Readiness means using your tools and your people, not waiting for certainty.

scenarios.debrief: No one has every answer; tools and people are enough to start.
scenarios.relearn: Life-ready is having the tools and your people, not all the answers.

scenarios.hook: A real choice with a deadline is in front of you, and your old habit says to guess.

steps.prompt: The form asks you to choose a course by Friday. What do you do first?

options.text: Gather facts on fees, eligibility and where each leads
options.then: A senior at college explains the real fees and what the course leads to.

options.text: Guess and hope it works out
options.then: You pencil in a box. You feel lighter, and a bit uneasy.

options.text: Pick what my friends picked
options.then: Two friends say different things, and neither knows your marks.

options.text: Wait and hope the deadline gets extended
options.then: The days go by and Friday doesn't move.

steps.why: Facts come first, so the choice rests on something solid.

steps.prompt: The form is still open and you've narrowed it to two courses. What do you do next?

options.text: Pick the one with the higher pay alone
options.then: The pay is better. It leaves out things you told yourself mattered, so you keep wavering.

options.text: Pick the one my uncle likes
options.then: Your uncle is delighted. You aren't sure it's what you'd have chosen, and you keep wavering.

options.text: Choose by gut feeling with no more facts
options.then: Your gut says one thing on Monday and another on Tuesday.

options.text: Check each against what I value
options.then: One course keeps matching what you wrote down as important.

steps.why: Your values turn a list of facts into a choice that fits you.

steps.prompt: Friday is close. Your two courses differ: one costs less now, the other leads further. What do you do?

options.text: Pick the cheaper one without looking ahead
options.then: It feels safe now, and the later years go unexamined.

options.text: Pick the one that leads further whatever it costs
options.then: It looks ambitious. The money question stays open.

options.text: Weigh the long term against what my family can afford
options.then: You map both paths and find where the money works.

options.text: Ask a friend to choose for me
options.then: She picks quickly. You aren't sure why she chose that one.

steps.why: Weighing the long game with real limits is how adults decide well.

steps.prompt: You submit. A friend says you picked wrong. What do you do?

options.text: Reopen the whole choice and worry for days
options.then: The doubts return, and you can't make any plans.

options.text: Explain my reasons, and learn from how it goes
options.then: She listens. You feel steady, and ready to adjust if needed.

options.text: Blame the confusing form
options.then: You feel better for a minute. The choice is still yours.

options.text: Say I only guessed
options.then: Your friend sighs. It makes the choice sound like it wasn't yours.

steps.why: Owning a choice means you decided it and will learn from it.

scenarios.debrief: The toolkit's method works on real choices, not just in theory.
scenarios.relearn: Use the method on real choices: facts, values, the long term, then own it.

scenarios.relearn: Values, how you treat people and your effort are your worth; a result, rank or approval don't define you.

scenarios.hook: You're stuck on a project and a capable friend could help.
scenarios.setup: After class, Anaya zips up her bag.

steps.prompt: Anaya asks: "You look stuck. What's going on?"

options.text: "Nothing, really. I've got it all under control."
options.then: She nods and leaves. You stay stuck.

options.text: "I'm stuck. Could you help me think it through?"
options.then: She puts her bag down. "Of course. Show me where you got to."

options.text: "Don't worry about it. You'd find it boring anyway."
options.then: She shrugs. "Okay, if you say so."

options.text: "Everyone else gets it. I must just be slow."
options.then: "That's not true," she says. The talk turns to comfort, not the problem.

steps.why: Saying "I'm stuck" plainly is how a capable friend gets to help.

steps.prompt: A day later, Anaya asks: "Still stuck on that? I have ten minutes."

options.text: "Yes. I follow the first part but not the second."
options.then: "Okay, let's start there."

options.text: "Honestly, all of it. Can you just do it for me?"
options.then: She hesitates. "I can show you, but I can't do it for you."

options.text: "No, it's fine. Forget I said anything."
options.then: She looks puzzled. "Okay. The offer's open."

options.text: "Maybe later. I don't want to waste your time."
options.then: She smiles. "You wouldn't be. I offered."

steps.why: Naming exactly where you're stuck makes ten minutes enough.

steps.prompt: Later that week, Anaya says: "If you're ever stuck again, just ask me sooner."

options.text: "Sorry for bothering you. I'll try not to again."
options.then: "You weren't bothering me," she says, and it feels a little stiff.

options.text: "I didn't want to look needy in front of you."
options.then: She shakes her head kindly. "It doesn't look that way."

options.text: "Okay. But I'd rather do it alone next time, honestly."
options.then: She shrugs. "Fine. Your call."

options.text: "I will. And tell me if you ever need a hand."
options.then: She smiles. "Deal."

steps.why: Asking for help is a strength, and offering it back keeps friendship fair.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, Anaya asks: "I'm stuck on my own project. Could I ask you?"

options.text: "I'm too busy. Ask someone else, sorry."
options.then: She nods. "Sure. No problem." She sounds let down.

options.text: "Only if you help me with mine again first."
options.then: She pauses. "Okay. It's a trade, then?"

options.text: "Of course. Show me where you're stuck."
options.then: She exhales. "Thanks. It's the second part."

options.text: "Sure, but I'm not great at this, so don't expect much."
options.then: She smiles. You've talked yourself down before you began.

steps.why: Helping back keeps the friendship fair, and shows asking is normal.

scenarios.relearn: Asking plainly for help is a strength, not a weakness.

scenarios.hook: A relative keeps asking what you plan to do next.
scenarios.setup: At a cousin's wedding, Aunty catches you by the snack table.

steps.prompt: Aunty says: "You're nearly eighteen. Time to think about settling down, no?"

options.text: "Everyone says girls my age should think about it."
options.then: Aunty nods. "Exactly." She tells another aunty.

options.text: "Why do you even care about my life, Aunty?"
options.then: Her smile freezes. "Is that how you talk to elders?"

options.text: "I hear you. I'll decide that on my own timeline."
options.then: She blinks. "Hm. I only wanted to help."

options.text: "My friend says to smile and change the subject."
options.then: Aunty laughs and lets it pass. It won't be the last time.

steps.why: A calm line about your own timeline is clearer than hinting or rudeness.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Aunty says: "Your mother is worried about you too. We only want what's good for you."

options.text: "Maybe saying no will hurt Mummy too much."
options.then: Aunty softens. "She does worry." You carry the guilt home with you.

options.text: "I know you care. This is my call to make."
options.then: She sighs. "You've got a mind of your own."

options.text: "You're both interfering. Please just stop it."
options.then: She stiffens. "Careful with your words."

options.text: "I'm sorry I've worried everyone, Aunty."
options.then: She pats your arm. You carry the guilt home as if it were yours.

steps.why: You can thank someone for caring and still keep the decision yours.

steps.prompt: Aunty says: "A family is asking about you. Just meet them once, what's the harm?"

options.text: "No, thank you. Please tell them I'm not looking."
options.then: She frowns. "Think about it." You say you already have.

options.text: "Maybe one meeting is harmless. Everyone says so."
options.then: She is delighted. You feel your stomach tighten.

options.text: "Maybe I'm not allowed to say no to an elder."
options.then: Aunty pauses, then says, "Think about it." Your answer stays unclear.

options.text: "My cousin says a polite yes ends it faster."
options.then: Aunty says your cousin is sensible. The questions carry on, and you feel worn down.

steps.why: No one can push you into this, and the pressure is never your fault.

steps.prompt: Later, your mother finds you quiet and asks: "Beta, what's bothering you?"

options.text: "It's probably nothing. I'm just overreacting."
options.then: She nods and moves on. The comments keep coming, and you feel smaller each time.

options.text: "My cousin says I should just shout at Aunty."
options.then: Your mother sighs. "Don't be rude to elders, beta." You feel unheard.

options.text: "Aunty may be right. Maybe I should think about it."
options.then: Your mother pauses. "Is that what you want, beta?" You aren't sure how to answer.

options.text: "Aunty keeps pushing me about marriage. It's stressing me."
options.then: She puts the plate down. "Thank you for telling me. We'll sort this."

steps.why: Pressure is never your fault, and a trusted adult can help you hold the line.

scenarios.relearn: A calm, clear boundary holds your timeline. If pressure grows, tell a trusted adult or call Childline 1098.

scenarios.hook: A friend has sounded low and flat in your chats all week.
scenarios.setup: Tonight Dev answers your call in a quiet voice.

steps.prompt: Dev says: "Hey. Nothing much. Just tired."

options.text: "Okay. Message me if you need anything."
options.then: "Sure," Dev says, and the line goes quiet.

options.text: "Cheer up. It's really not that bad."
options.then: "Yeah," Dev says, flatly. "Maybe."

options.text: "You always say that. What's wrong? Tell me."
options.then: Dev goes silent. "Forget it."

options.text: "I'm here. Want to talk, or just hang out for a bit?"
options.then: Dev lets out a breath. "Can you just stay on the line?"

steps.why: Offering company without pushing tells a friend they aren't alone.

steps.prompt: Later, Dev says: "I don't want to make it a big thing. It's probably nothing."

options.text: "Okay. Then let's forget it."
options.then: Dev says okay. Nothing more is said.

options.text: "Just go for a run. You'll feel better."
options.then: Dev says okay in a flat voice. Nothing changes.

options.text: "It's not nothing to me. I'm not going anywhere."
options.then: Dev's voice cracks a little. "Okay."

options.text: "Everyone gets low sometimes. You'll be fine."
options.then: Dev mumbles agreement. He sounds further away.

steps.why: Showing the feeling matters to you helps him stop hiding it.

steps.prompt: Days later, Dev asks: "Do you think I should tell my mum? I've felt like this a long while."

options.text: "Only if you're sure. Otherwise it stays between us."
options.then: Dev relaxes. The weight stays with him.

options.text: "Yes. I can sit with you when you tell her."
options.then: Dev is quiet. "Okay. Maybe Saturday."

options.text: "Let's wait until you feel better first."
options.then: Dev agrees. The weight stays another week.

options.text: "Let me tell her for you."
options.then: Dev panics. "No, please don't. I'll do it myself."

steps.why: Getting a trusted adult involved helps, and it is never his fault.

steps.prompt: Dev says he's feeling a bit better. He asks: "If it gets heavy again, what do I do?"

options.text: "Tell me or your mum, and call Tele-MANAS 14416."
options.then: He writes the number down. "Okay. That helps."

options.text: "Just wait it out. It always passes."
options.then: He nods. The heavy feeling stays with him alone.

options.text: "Text me only if it gets really, really bad."
options.then: He nods. He'll wait until it does.

options.text: "Try to handle it yourself first, then tell someone."
options.then: He agrees. He's alone with it for longer.

steps.why: Knowing who to reach early keeps help close, and it's never his fault.

scenarios.relearn: Reaching out warmly tells a friend they're not alone.

scenarios.hook: Your younger brother is anxious about adulting.
scenarios.setup: Late in the evening, Rohan sits down on your bed.

steps.prompt: Rohan says: "Everyone says I'll be an adult soon. I have no idea how."

options.text: "You don't need every answer. You've got tools and people."
options.then: Rohan looks up. "Like who?" You say, "Like me."

options.text: "Just figure it out, like everyone else does. It's fine."
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay." He goes quiet.

options.text: "Don't think about it. You've got years yet, honestly."
options.then: He nods, and the worry sits there anyway.

options.text: "Listen. I'll tell you exactly what to do, step by step."
options.then: He relaxes. He's no clearer on how to decide anything himself.

steps.why: Telling him he has tools and people shows he doesn't need it all solved.

steps.prompt: Rohan asks: "So what do I actually do? Where do I even start?"

options.text: "There's a long list. I'll send it, read everything."
options.then: He opens it later and feels more buried.

options.text: "Hard to explain. You'll see when you get there."
options.then: He nods. He still has nothing to try.

options.text: "You don't need a plan. Just be confident."
options.then: He tries to look confident and still feels scared.

options.text: "Pick one small thing to try, and tell someone."
options.then: He nods. "Okay. I could try that tomorrow."

steps.why: One small thing he can try beats a whole list.

steps.prompt: A week later, Rohan says: "I'm still scared about all of it, even when I try to do something."

options.text: "Then it's not working. Forget it and move on, okay?"
options.then: His face falls. He doesn't mention it again.

options.text: "Stop being scared. You'll be fine, so relax."
options.then: He nods. Being told to stop doesn't make it stop.

options.text: "That's normal. Scared and trying is how it starts."
options.then: He laughs a little. "Okay. Can we try something together?"

options.text: "I'll take over from here. Just give it all to me."
options.then: He hands it over. He learns nothing new.

steps.why: Scared and trying is real progress, and you're beside him.

scenarios.relearn: Sharing the toolkit and reassurance is real support.

scenarios.hook: Exam load is heavy and you've been quiet for days.
scenarios.setup: At lunch, your cousin Neha notices you pushing food around.

steps.prompt: Neha asks: "How are you holding up with the exams?"

options.text: "I'm fine. It's just the usual exam stuff, honestly."
options.then: She nods, unconvinced. You both go back to eating.

options.text: "I'm stretched. I'm breaking it down and asking for help."
options.then: She puts her fork down. "Thanks for telling me."

options.text: "I'm doing great. I'm studying eighteen hours a day."
options.then: Neha blinks. She looks more worried than impressed.

options.text: "I'll fail everything. My whole future is gone."
options.then: Neha looks worried. "That sounds heavy. It's not as final as it feels."

steps.why: Saying "I'm stretched" and what you're doing about it is honest and strong.

steps.prompt: Later, Neha catches up with you. She says: "I've noticed you skipping lunch. What would actually help right now?"

options.text: "A quiz partner, and a proper break on Sunday."
options.then: "I can do both. Sunday we go to the park."

options.text: "Nothing really. I just needed to say it out loud."
options.then: She nods. The load is exactly as heavy tomorrow.

options.text: "Tell me I'll definitely score well. Promise me."
options.then: She says she can't promise. You feel the pressure grow.

options.text: "Take over my hardest chapters for a few days."
options.then: She laughs. "I can't sit your exam, you know."

steps.why: A specific ask gets you real help, and a break counts.

steps.prompt: Neha asks: "If it gets heavier, who else could you talk to?"

options.text: "Nobody. I'll handle it."
options.then: She frowns. "You don't have to do it all alone."

options.text: "Only you, and only if you swear not to tell."
options.then: She hesitates. "I'll listen. I can't promise to stay silent if it's serious."

options.text: "My friends. But I don't want to bother them."
options.then: She says they'd probably want to know.

options.text: "My teacher, or Tele-MANAS 14416 if it gets heavy."
options.then: "Put that number in your phone now."

steps.why: Knowing who to reach before it's heavy means help is close by.

steps.prompt: On exam morning, Neha texts: "How are you feeling? Any last-minute wobbles?"

options.text: "Fine. No wobbles at all."
options.then: She replies with a thumbs up. You still feel your pulse.

options.text: "I'm going to blank out and fail. It's over."
options.then: She texts back fast: "You've prepared. Breathe. I'm here." The dread stays.

options.text: "Nervous, but ready. I ate, slept, and I'm breathing."
options.then: She sends a heart. "Go get it."

options.text: "Fine. I'll stay up cramming till morning."
options.then: She's alarmed. "You'll be exhausted."

steps.why: Naming nerves and using the basics is steadier than hiding or panicking.

scenarios.relearn: Naming that you're stretched and using tools beats bottling it up.

scenarios.hook: A friend has seemed heavy and hopeless for weeks.
scenarios.setup: On Sunday night, Tanvi calls you.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says: "I just feel heavy all the time. Nothing seems to matter."

options.text: "Just cheer up. It'll pass."
options.then: She goes quiet. "Right. Sure."

options.text: "Everyone feels like that before exams."
options.then: She mumbles agreement and feels more alone.

options.text: "That sounds heavy. I'm glad you told me."
options.then: She breathes out. "I thought you'd say I was exaggerating."

options.text: "Come out tomorrow. That'll fix it."
options.then: She says she'll see. You can hear she won't come.

steps.why: Hearing her out first shows you take her seriously.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says: "Please don't tell anyone. I'd feel so stupid."

options.text: "Okay. I promise I won't tell anyone, not ever."
options.then: She relaxes, and the weight stays with just the two of you.

options.text: "It's not your fault. I can't keep this to myself."
options.then: She's quiet. "Okay. Maybe not alone."

options.text: "Then I'll check on you myself every single day."
options.then: She says okay. It's a lot for one friend to carry.

options.text: "Then you have to tell someone tonight, no excuses."
options.then: She stiffens. "I can't. Not tonight."

steps.why: Caring too much to keep it secret is how a friend helps safely.

steps.prompt: Tanvi asks: "Who would I even talk to?"

options.text: "Tele-MANAS 14416, your mum or Mr. Reddy. Call together?"
options.then: She exhales. "Maybe your phone? Could you stay?"

options.text: "Maybe look it up online and see what it says first."
options.then: She scrolls for an hour and feels worse.

options.text: "Sleep on it and see how you feel tomorrow, maybe."
options.then: Tomorrow arrives. Nothing is any different.

options.text: "I'll find someone and send you their name later."
options.then: She says thanks. She hasn't had to decide a thing.

steps.why: Heavy for weeks deserves real help, and it's never her fault.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Tanvi's mother stops you at the gate and asks gently: "Beta, Tanvi seems so quiet. What is it? You can tell me."

options.text: "It's nothing, Aunty. We're just a bit tired today."
options.then: Her mother nods and lets it go. You think of Tanvi, alone with it.

options.text: "Ask Tanvi. I don't think I should say anything."
options.then: Her mother waits, then nods slowly. The moment passes with nothing said.

options.text: "Tanvi's been a bit dramatic about exams, honestly."
options.then: Her mother frowns and stops asking. Tanvi's heaviness gets waved away.

options.text: "I'm worried about her. She's felt heavy for weeks and needs support."
options.then: Her mother's eyes fill. "Thank you for telling me, beta. I'll sit with her tonight."

steps.why: Telling a trusted adult, kindly, gets her real help. It is never her fault.

steps.prompt: A week later, Tanvi asks: "Do I still need Tele-MANAS, or is that only for emergencies?"

options.text: "No, you've got me now. You don't need anyone else."
options.then: She nods. She doesn't know where else to go.

options.text: "Only if things get really, really bad again."
options.then: She nods. She'll wait until then.

options.text: "It's there whenever you want. Calling is strength."
options.then: She smiles faintly. "Okay. I'll save the number."

options.text: "Yes, you absolutely must call them tonight."
options.then: She stiffens. "Don't tell me what to do."

steps.why: Support can have many parts, and it's never too early to reach for help.

scenarios.relearn: Heavy, persistent distress routes warmly to real help like Tele-MANAS 14416.

scenarios.hook: A scholarship form has codes and steps you've never seen.
scenarios.setup: After assembly, Mr. Das, who mentors students, is free.

steps.prompt: Mr. Das asks: "You look puzzled. Can I help?"

options.text: "No, I'm fine. I'll figure it out myself, thanks sir."
options.then: He nods. "My door's open." You stay confused, and he notices.

options.text: "It's probably a silly question. Never mind, sir."
options.then: He frowns. "No questions are silly."

options.text: "Could you just fill it in for me, sir? Please?"
options.then: He shakes his head kindly. "I'll show you, but you'll do it."

options.text: "I haven't done this. Could you walk me through it?"
options.then: He smiles. "Of course. Sit down."

steps.why: Saying you haven't done it before gets you the map.

steps.prompt: Mr. Das says: "That scholarship form has tricky codes. First, do you have your documents ready?"

options.text: "Yes, all ready."
options.then: He says good. You feel the knot in your stomach.

options.text: "I'll bring whatever I find later."
options.then: He sighs. "That may not be enough."

options.text: "I have two. Which others do I need?"
options.then: He ticks a list. "You need three more. Here's how to get them."

options.text: "Doesn't matter. I'll submit it now."
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "Slowly, let's check."

steps.why: Being honest about what you have helps him point to what's missing.

steps.prompt: Mr. Das asks: "Before you submit, who could you ask if you get stuck?"

options.text: "No one at all. I'll manage this on my own."
options.then: He looks at you gently. "That's a lot to carry alone."

options.text: "You, the office and the scholarship help desk."
options.then: He writes the desk's hours on your form. "Use them."

options.text: "My friends. They'll probably know the answer."
options.then: He tilts his head. "They may not know this form's rules."

options.text: "I'll guess at the parts I can't work out."
options.then: He shakes his head. "Guessing is how mistakes happen."

steps.why: Knowing who to ask before you're stuck keeps you moving.

steps.prompt: Mr. Das says the office reports that one document is missing. He asks: "What will you do?"

options.text: "Ask the office what's needed and by when."
options.then: He nods. "Write it down."

options.text: "Hope they accept it without it."
options.then: He frowns. "That's a risk."

options.text: "Wait until they chase me for it."
options.then: He taps the form. "Then the deadline may be close."

options.text: "Ask a friend to handle it for me."
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "It's your form."

steps.why: Asking exactly what's needed, and by when, keeps the form moving.

scenarios.relearn: Asking a mentor to walk you through it beats guessing in silence.

scenarios.hook: You want this to stick, not just be nice to know.
scenarios.setup: On the way home, your friend Aman asks what you got from the toolkit.

steps.prompt: Aman asks: "So what are you actually going to do with it?"

options.text: "Start someday, once things calm down a bit."
options.then: "Mm. When's that?" Neither of you knows.

options.text: "Everything. I'll use every tool starting tomorrow."
options.then: He grins. You both suspect it won't last a week.

options.text: "Probably nothing. It's mostly just good to know."
options.then: He laughs. The toolkit goes back in your bag.

options.text: "One tool this week. I'll tell you which, so I do it."
options.then: "Deal. I'll ask you on Sunday."

steps.why: One named tool and a person who'll ask makes it real.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Aman asks: "So did you pick a tool yet, or what?"

options.text: "I'll decide when the week begins, I suppose."
options.then: He nods. Monday arrives and you haven't chosen.

options.text: "Whichever sounds best. I'll work it out as I go."
options.then: He shrugs. By Wednesday you've forgotten.

options.text: "Break it into days. I'll plan Monday tonight."
options.then: He nods. "Monday night, then. I'll check on Sunday."

options.text: "All of them, in some order that makes sense."
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "That's a lot."

steps.why: A specific tool and a time to use it is easy to follow through.

steps.prompt: On Sunday, Aman texts: "Did you do your tool this week?"

options.text: "I forgot, and I'm just bad at this."
options.then: He tries to cheer you up. The tool stays on the shelf.

options.text: "Partly. I slipped, and I'll start again tomorrow."
options.then: He sends a thumbs up. "Good. Same time next week."

options.text: "Yes, perfectly. Every single day this week."
options.then: He's impressed. You feel you can't admit a slip.

options.text: "Not really. So the toolkit doesn't work."
options.then: He frowns. "One missed week isn't the toolkit."

steps.why: A slip is normal, and starting again counts as using the tool.

steps.prompt: A month later, Aman says: "I'm starting a tool too. Any tips?"

options.text: "Pick one, set a day, tell someone. I'll ask you."
options.then: He grins. "Deal. Thursday?"

options.text: "Start with all of them, like everyone should."
options.then: He looks daunted. "All of them?"

options.text: "Don't bother. It's a lot of work."
options.then: His face falls. "Oh. Okay."

options.text: "Just copy my tool exactly as I do it."
options.then: He tries. It doesn't fit his week.

steps.why: Passing on one tool and a check-in is how a habit spreads.

scenarios.hook: Arjun: under all the input, the final call is yours by your own values. Own that?
scenarios.affirm: You weigh what others say, then decide by your own values; that's yours.

scenarios.relearn: Asking how something works is smart, not weakness.
scenarios.hook: Vijay: asking how a system works isn't weakness, it's smart. Believe it?
scenarios.affirm: Asking the way forward is how everyone learns adult systems; no shame in it.

scenarios.relearn: Reaching out for support is normal, smart and strong; stigma is the only myth.
scenarios.hook: Mr. Reddy: reaching out for mental-health support is normal, smart and strong. Hear that?
scenarios.affirm: Reaching for support is normal and strong; stigma is the only thing that says otherwise.

scenarios.relearn: For uncertainty, focus on the next step you can control.
scenarios.hook: Lensy: when the future's unclear, the next step you control is enough. Feel steadier?
scenarios.affirm: You don't need the whole map; the next controllable step is always enough.

scenarios.relearn: Change being hard doesn't mean you're failing at it.
scenarios.hook: Lensy: change being hard doesn't mean you're failing at it. Take that in?
scenarios.affirm: Hard and survivable can both be true; finding it hard isn't failing.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: if you leave home, you can name it, prepare, and stay connected. Feel doable?
scenarios.affirm: Name the change, prepare a little, stay connected; big transitions get smaller that way.

scenarios.relearn: A good decision is made well, not guaranteed to turn out perfectly.
scenarios.hook: Lensy: a good decision is one made well, not one guaranteed to turn out perfectly. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: You can decide wisely and still face an uncertain result; the process is what's yours.

scenarios.relearn: Support is reciprocal: lean on people, and be there for them too.
scenarios.hook: Lensy: support runs both ways, you lean and you show up for others too. Feel right?
scenarios.affirm: Being there for others, and letting them be there for you, is what a network is.

scenarios.relearn: Self-knowledge is honesty with yourself, not perfection.
scenarios.hook: Lensy: knowing yourself is honesty, not perfection. Feel the difference?
scenarios.affirm: Honesty with yourself, not having it all sorted, is what real self-knowledge is.

scenarios.relearn: A clear, respectful boundary beats a resentful yes.
scenarios.hook: Lensy: a clear, respectful boundary beats a resentful yes. Carry that into adult life?
scenarios.affirm: A calm, clear boundary protects you and the relationship better than a resentful yes.

scenarios.relearn: People skills are learnable, not innate.
scenarios.hook: Lensy: people skills are learnable, not something you're just born with. Believe it?
scenarios.affirm: Listening, boundaries and repair are all practised; no one is born finished at them.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: owning a choice means you made it and you'll see it through. Feel that agency?
scenarios.affirm: Choosing on purpose, rather than drifting, is what adult agency feels like.

scenarios.affirm: A clear sense of what you value quietly orients you when a choice gets hard.
