scenarios.affirm: Being ready never meant never stumbling; it means you can recover and learn each time.

scenarios.relearn: You've come full circle, from naming feelings to running your own life.
scenarios.hook: Lensy: the small friend who began this journey has grown, like you. Feel the bookend?
scenarios.affirm: From a small friend to a near-adult ready for life, you've come the whole way.

scenarios.hook: Your classmate Tanvi keeps borrowing your notes and never returns them.
scenarios.setup: You meet her at the school gate this morning.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says: "Hi! Can I borrow your chapter 5 notes again?"

options.text: "Again? You never return anything, do you? Honestly."
options.then: Tanvi reddens. "That's not fair. I just forget. That's all."

options.text: "Sure, take them. I'll manage somehow."
options.then: Tanvi waves happily. You can't revise properly that night.

options.text: "My notes are getting really worn out lately."
options.then: Tanvi laughs. "Mine too!" and takes them anyway.

options.text: "I need my notes back by tomorrow. I'm revising."
options.then: She blinks. "Oh. Sorry, I'll bring them in the morning."

steps.why: A clear, direct ask is easier to act on than a hint.

steps.prompt: Tanvi arrives empty-handed the next morning and says: "Your notes are still at home. Sorry!"

options.text: "Please bring them by lunch. I'll wait."
options.then: She looks guilty. "I'll get them by lunch. I'm really sorry."

options.text: "It's okay. Bring them whenever you remember them."
options.then: She nods happily. Your test is in four days.

options.text: "Fine. I'll just copy from someone else. Forget it."
options.then: She shrugs, relieved. Your notes stay at her house.

options.text: "That's what you always say, every single time. Always!"
options.then: Tanvi's face crumples. "I said sorry. Why are you shouting?"

steps.why: A specific time gives her something she can actually do.

steps.prompt: A week later Tanvi says: "Can I borrow your science notes now? I'll be careful."

options.text: "Sure, no problem. Keep them as long as you need them."
options.then: She thanks you and walks off. Friday comes and goes.

options.text: "Yes, if I get them back on Friday."
options.then: Tanvi writes "Friday" on her hand. "Deal."

options.text: "Let me think about it and tell you a bit later."
options.then: Tanvi nods. By the time you decide, she has found someone else's notes.

options.text: "No. You've lost your chance to borrow anything from me."
options.then: Tanvi looks hurt. "I only asked once this week."

steps.why: Lending with a clear return day keeps the kindness and the boundary.

scenarios.relearn: A clear, direct ask beats hinting and hoping someone reads your mind.

scenarios.hook: At a family function, Aunty keeps praising your cousin's marks and skips yours.
scenarios.setup: Then she turns to you with a smile.

steps.prompt: Aunty says: "And you, beta? Not as good as Rohan, I heard."

options.text: "Hm." Smile, then slip out of the room for a while
options.then: Aunty laughs. "Shy, no?" When you return, she's on marks again.

options.text: "At least I don't brag about marks all day, Aunty!"
options.then: The room goes quiet. Your mother gives you a long look.

options.text: "I'm working hard in my own way. I'm okay with my path."
options.then: Aunty blinks. "Hmm. Well, hard work is good."

options.text: "Haha, yes, Rohan is much better." Walk away quickly
options.then: Aunty nods, satisfied. You return to find her on marks again.

steps.why: Calm, honest self-respect doesn't need to attack her or to agree with her.

steps.prompt: Aunty says: "But marks decide everything these days, no? What will you do?"

options.text: "Marks matter, but they're not everything. There are many paths."
options.then: Aunty pauses. "Hmm. My neighbour's son found one, true."

options.text: "You're right, Aunty. I'll try much harder next time."
options.then: She approves. You feel a little smaller, and your marks feel like your worth.

options.text: Change the subject: "Is there more of that halwa?"
options.then: Aunty laughs and serves you. The question hangs around the table.

options.text: "That's old-fashioned, Aunty. Nobody believes that anymore."
options.then: Aunty bristles. "Old-fashioned? I raised three children."

steps.why: Marks matter, but they don't decide your worth or your whole future.

steps.prompt: Later your mother says quietly: "Aunty means well, you know. How are you feeling?"

options.text: "I know she does. It stung, and I'd like the comparing to stop."
options.then: Your mother nods slowly. "I'll mention it to her gently."

options.text: "Aunty is always like this. I'm never coming to these again."
options.then: Your mother sighs. "Let's not decide that tonight."

options.text: "I don't care at all. It didn't bother me one bit."
options.then: She studies you. "Okay," she says, not quite believing it.

options.text: "You never stand up for me. You just let her talk."
options.then: Your mother stiffens. "That's not true. I was trying to keep calm."

steps.why: Saying how it felt gives your mother something she can act on.

scenarios.relearn: Calm, honest self-respect lands better than reacting in anger.

scenarios.hook: A friend vents about her sister, and you want to listen, not fix it.
scenarios.setup: You sit with her on the school steps.

steps.prompt: Zara says: "My sister read my messages and told Mummy. I'm so done."

options.text: "Siblings are like that. She'll forget it by evening."
options.then: Zara's mouth tightens. "You don't get it."

options.text: "That sounds hard. Want ideas, or just to be heard?"
options.then: Zara exhales. "Just listen first. Please."

options.text: "Change your password and confront her."
options.then: Zara blinks. "I haven't even told you the whole thing."

options.text: "Oh my god, how awful! She's the worst sister ever."
options.then: Zara nods hard. You both spiral, and it feels louder, not lighter.

steps.why: Asking what she needs lets her say it, and that is real listening.

steps.prompt: Zara says: "And Mummy took her side. I feel like nobody's on mine."

options.text: "Maybe Mummy had a point, though. Have you thought about that?"
options.then: Zara goes stiff. "Wow. Okay."

options.text: "That sounds lonely. I'm here. Tell me more."
options.then: Her eyes fill. "Thank you. I needed someone to say that."

options.text: "Just talk to your Mummy tonight and sort it out properly."
options.then: Zara says maybe, but she looks away.

options.text: "Don't worry about it. It's honestly not worth your energy."
options.then: She nods, but the weight stays right where it was.

steps.why: Naming the lonely feeling shows her she is heard, not managed.

steps.prompt: Zara says: "I don't know what to do. Part of me wants to talk to her. Part of me wants to scream."

options.text: "Talk to her tonight. Waiting only makes things worse."
options.then: Zara's shoulders tighten. "I'm not ready for tonight."

options.text: "Both make sense. What would help you most right now?"
options.then: She breathes out. "A walk first. Then help finding the words."

options.text: "Ignore her for a week. She honestly deserves the silence."
options.then: Zara goes quiet. It doesn't sound like the sister she misses.

options.text: "Scream first, then talk. I'd do exactly the same thing."
options.then: Zara half-laughs, but she is no clearer about what she wants.

steps.why: Asking what would help most lets her find her own next step.

scenarios.relearn: Asking whether they want help or just an ear is real listening.

scenarios.hook: At your weekend shop job, a senior named Mr. Kapoor snaps at you in front of customers.
scenarios.setup: Your coworker Rekha is nearby.

steps.prompt: Mr. Kapoor says: "Wrong labels again! Pay attention!"

options.text: "I'm useless at this. Sorry, sir. I'll redo them tonight."
options.then: He mutters and walks off. You stay late redoing labels that were fine.

options.text: "I didn't! You gave me the wrong sheet!"
options.then: Customers turn to look. His face goes dark red.

options.text: "I'll fix them. But a boss shouldn't shout at staff, Mr. Kapoor."
options.then: His jaw tightens. "Don't tell me how to run this shop."

options.text: "Okay. Rekha, could you check these labels with me?"
options.then: Rekha steps over. Mr. Kapoor huffs and goes back to the till.

steps.why: Asking a colleague to help keeps it calm, and you are not left facing him alone.

steps.prompt: Later Rekha says quietly: "He snapped at you in front of everyone. How are you doing?"

options.text: "Shaken. Is it okay for him to shout like that?"
options.then: Rekha shakes her head. "No. It isn't okay, and it isn't your fault. Tell someone you trust."

options.text: "I deserved it. I'm just bad at this job."
options.then: Rekha frowns. "A mistake needs a correction, not shouting." You still feel small.

options.text: "Could you go and tell him off for me?"
options.then: Rekha winces. "I'm not his boss. The owner or your parents are who to ask."

options.text: "It's fine. Bosses can shout at the youngest staff."
options.then: Rekha shrugs. "Strict is fine. Shouting in front of customers isn't." The knot stays.

steps.why: Saying how it felt gets you support, and being shouted at is never your fault.

steps.prompt: A week later Mr. Kapoor says in a tight voice: "That shelf is wrong. Fix it."

options.text: "Okay. Can I finish this customer, then check with you?"
options.then: He pauses. "Yes. Come find me after."

options.text: "You didn't say that last time!"
options.then: A customer glances up. His voice rises to match yours.

options.text: "Whatever. I'm just doing what I'm told."
options.then: He frowns. "That attitude won't help you here."

options.text: Roll your eyes and mutter about him once he turns away
options.then: He hears the mutter. The shop feels tense all afternoon.

steps.why: Staying calm and giving a clear next step keeps things professional.

steps.prompt: That evening your mother says: "You've seemed tense after work lately. I'm here if you want to talk."

options.text: "Mr. Kapoor keeps shouting at me. Can you help?"
options.then: Your mother holds your hand. "I'm glad you told me. This is not your fault. We'll talk to the owner together."

options.text: "Bosses shout at everyone. That's just how jobs are."
options.then: She frowns but lets it go. The next time he shouts, it lands just as hard.

options.text: "Maybe I'm just too sensitive for a real job."
options.then: Your mother frowns. "Sensitive? Has something happened?" The shouting stays unsaid.

options.text: "Don't worry. I'll sort it out with Mr. Kapoor myself."
options.then: Your mother looks worried. "Please don't face him alone. Let's tell the owner together."

steps.why: Telling a trusted adult gets real help, and being shouted at is never your fault.

scenarios.relearn: Stay calm and professional, ask a coworker to help, and tell a trusted adult if the shouting keeps happening.

scenarios.hook: Your friends plan to copy answers for a group assignment, and you don't want to.
scenarios.setup: They all look at you to agree.

steps.prompt: Aman says: "We'll copy last year's file. Everyone does it."

options.text: "I'd rather we split the work and each do our part."
options.then: Aman groans, "More effort." Sana nods slowly.

options.text: "Sure, whatever the group does is fine with me."
options.then: Aman cheers. You feel uneasy but say nothing.

options.text: "Copying is cheating. It's dishonest, and I'm not doing it."
options.then: Aman rolls his eyes. "Relax, boss. It's one assignment."

options.text: "Okay, fine." Then quietly plan to do only your own part
options.then: Aman thinks you agreed. The group plan stays exactly as it was.

steps.why: Naming what you will do instead is a clear, respectful boundary.

steps.prompt: Sana says: "It's due in two days. We need to decide how to do this."

options.text: "Okay, copying is faster. Let's do it just this once."
options.then: Aman high-fives you. Your stomach drops.

options.text: "Let's divide sections tonight and meet again tomorrow."
options.then: Sana checks the list. "Okay. That's actually doable."

options.text: "I'll tell the teacher you two planned to copy."
options.then: Aman's face hardens. "Seriously? Over a file?"

options.text: "You two do it your way. I'll do mine alone."
options.then: Aman shrugs. The group splits quietly, and the mood sours.

steps.why: A practical plan answers the deadline and keeps you in the group.

steps.prompt: A week later, on the next assignment, Aman says: "I've left it late again. Can you help me?"

options.text: "I'll send my answers so you can copy mine."
options.then: Aman thanks you, and the shortcut turns into a habit.

options.text: "Not my problem if you left it late."
options.then: Aman's smile vanishes. "Wow. Okay."

options.text: "I'll go over your notes with you, but you write it."
options.then: Aman sighs, then grins. "Deal."

options.text: "Sure, I'll just rewrite your part for you."
options.then: He relaxes. You've taken on the work he skipped.

steps.why: Offering help with the work, not doing it for him, keeps the boundary kind.

scenarios.relearn: Naming what you'll do instead is a clear, respectful boundary.

scenarios.hook: You forgot your friend Mehak's birthday, and she is hurt.
scenarios.setup: She sits quietly beside you at lunch.

steps.prompt: Mehak says: "You forgot my birthday. Yesterday. I waited all day."

options.text: "Happy belated! Look at this funny video."
options.then: She doesn't laugh. She goes back to her food.

options.text: "I forgot, and I'm sorry. Let me make it up to you."
options.then: Mehak looks up. "Thank you for just saying it."

options.text: "You could have reminded me. I had a lot going on."
options.then: She stares. "So it's my fault?"

options.text: "I was just so busy. It's not a big deal."
options.then: Her face closes. "It was to me."

steps.why: Owning it without excuses is what lets her trust you again.

steps.prompt: Mehak says: "It's not only the birthday. I feel like I'm last on your list."

options.text: "That hurts to hear. Tell me more."
options.then: She takes a breath. "It's the little things adding up."

options.text: "You're being dramatic. It's just one birthday, Mehak."
options.then: Her eyes fill. "You haven't listened to a word."

options.text: "I said sorry already. What more do you want from me?"
options.then: She looks away. "Never mind."

options.text: "That's not true. I always make time for you, Mehak."
options.then: Mehak shakes her head. "Not lately."

steps.why: Listening to the bigger hurt matters more than defending yourself.

steps.prompt: Mehak says: "So what are you going to do about it?"

options.text: "I'll try to be better. That's all I can promise."
options.then: "Try how?" she asks. You have no answer.

options.text: "Let me buy you a really nice gift to make up for it."
options.then: She shakes her head. "It's not about a gift."

options.text: "I'll give you some space until you feel better."
options.then: She nods. The space stretches into a week.

options.text: "Can we plan a day this weekend? I'll note the dates."
options.then: She half-smiles. "Okay. I'd like that."

steps.why: A specific, kept promise repairs trust better than a gift or a vague one.

scenarios.relearn: Owning your impact without excuses repairs trust faster.

scenarios.hook: In your shared hostel room, your roommate Pallavi keeps leaving the dishes for you.
scenarios.setup: She walks in while you scrub the sink again.

steps.prompt: Pallavi says: "Oh, you're doing dishes? You're so good at it!"

options.text: "Mm." Keep scrubbing with your jaw tight.
options.then: She hums and flops on her bed. The sink is full again tomorrow.

options.text: "No problem! I actually like doing them."
options.then: She thanks you and settles in. The pile is yours again tomorrow.

options.text: "Yeah, someone has to, right?" with a sharp smile
options.then: Pallavi's smile fades. "What's that supposed to mean?"

options.text: "Can we set a turn-by-turn plan for the dishes?"
options.then: She blinks. "Oh. Am I not doing my share? Hmm, let me think."

steps.why: Naming the problem and proposing a fix works better than silent resentment.

steps.prompt: Two days later Pallavi sees the full sink and says: "Ugh, the dishes again. I have classes all day, so I never get time for them."

options.text: "Then I'll only clean my own plate from now on."
options.then: She shrugs. By Friday the sink is a bigger mess.

options.text: "Everyone's busy. That's no excuse."
options.then: Pallavi's face closes. "Fine. I'll do it when I can."

options.text: "Let's try alternate days and swap if one of us is stuck."
options.then: She nods. "Swapping helps. Let's try it."

options.text: "Okay, you're busy. I'll take most of them."
options.then: She beams. She does a few now and then, but the old pattern mostly goes on.

steps.why: A flexible plan fits her schedule without leaving the work all on you.

steps.prompt: A week later the sink is full again. Pallavi says: "Oops, I'm too tired tonight."

options.text: "Fine, I'll do it. Just this once again."
options.then: She thanks you cheerfully. Your resentment grows.

options.text: "I get tired too. Please do them before breakfast."
options.then: She nods. "Fair. I'll do them first thing."

options.text: "You always do this! I'm so done with you."
options.then: Pallavi steps back. "I said I was tired. Why shout?"

options.text: "Okay." Say nothing more, and wash only your own things from now on
options.then: The dishes pile up. A silent standoff takes over the room.

steps.why: A calm, specific ask keeps the plan alive and the room friendly.

scenarios.relearn: Naming the problem and proposing a fix beats silent resentment.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Kavya is telling people you spread her secret, but you didn't.
scenarios.setup: You catch her after class.

steps.prompt: Kavya says: "I know what you did. Everyone knows. How could you?"

options.text: "People who know me will know the truth." Walk away
options.then: Kavya's story keeps spreading while you wait it out.

options.text: "That's not what happened. Can we sort it out, just us?"
options.then: She hesitates, then nods. "Fine. Not here though."

options.text: "I never said it!" Post a long explanation in the class group
options.then: Everyone reads it. Kavya feels attacked and digs in.

options.text: "Fine, then I'll tell people things about you too."
options.then: By evening her friends turn cold toward you. The rumours multiply.

steps.why: Going straight to her, calmly and privately, gives the truth a chance.

steps.prompt: The next day Kavya finds you alone and says: "Priya told me you said it. Why would she lie?"

options.text: "I'm done explaining. Think what you like."
options.then: Kavya's face closes. "Fine."

options.text: "Maybe she misheard. I won't argue about it."
options.then: Kavya shrugs, unsure. The doubt stays between you.

options.text: "I don't know why. Let's ask Priya together, calmly."
options.then: Kavya nods slowly. "Okay. I'd like to hear her say it."

options.text: "Priya's a liar. Everyone knows that about her."
options.then: Kavya frowns. "You're attacking her now?"

steps.why: Asking Priya together fixes the facts without blaming anyone.

steps.prompt: Later that week Priya tells the group: "I'm not sure who said it. I may have mixed things up."

options.text: "Thanks for saying that. Let's clear it up with Kavya."
options.then: Priya nods, relieved. Kavya looks over, listening.

options.text: "You should apologise to everyone, Priya, right here."
options.then: Priya flushes. The group goes silent.

options.text: "I told you all I was innocent!"
options.then: A few people shift. It feels like winning, and not much else.

options.text: Say nothing and let people draw their own conclusions
options.then: The story fades slowly. Kavya still hasn't heard it from you.

steps.why: Thanking Priya and repairing it with Kavya ends the rumour, not just wins it.

steps.prompt: Kavya says: "I'm sorry I believed it so fast. Are we okay?"

options.text: "No. You doubted me so fast, so we're done here."
options.then: Kavya's eyes fill. She turns and walks away.

options.text: "Yeah, we're fine. Let's just say it's all forgotten."
options.then: She smiles, but neither of you mentions it again.

options.text: "I was hurt, but glad we talked. Let's check first next time."
options.then: She nods, relieved. "Deal."

options.text: "I'll forgive you if you tell everyone you were wrong."
options.then: She flinches. "That's not fair to ask."

steps.why: Naming the hurt and agreeing to check first rebuilds trust.

scenarios.relearn: Going straight to the person, calmly, beats fighting rumour with rumour.

scenarios.hook: At your new college, a group is planning a weekend outing and hasn't mentioned it to you.
scenarios.setup: You overhear them near the canteen.

steps.prompt: Rhea says: "We're all going to the lake on Saturday. Oh, hi! Didn't see you."

options.text: "Hey, mind if I join? I'd like to be part of this."
options.then: Rhea blinks, then smiles. "Of course! The more the better."

options.text: "Hi." Wait quietly, hoping someone invites you
options.then: They finish planning. Nobody turns toward you.

options.text: "Wow, not even an invite for me?" with a sharp edge
options.then: The group laughs awkwardly. Someone looks down.

options.text: "Oh, I'm busy that day anyway." Smile and leave.
options.then: "Okay, next time!" Rhea says. The plan is locked in.

steps.why: Asking to be included is a small, brave step, and it works more often than you fear.

steps.prompt: Later Rhea walks over and says: "You're welcome on Saturday, really. It's mostly people from our hostel."

options.text: "Actually, never mind. I'll skip it."
options.then: Rhea shrugs. "Okay, your call."

options.text: "I'll come, but I'll stay near the back."
options.then: She nods. You spend the outing watching from the edges.

options.text: "Okay." Say yes, then check your phone the whole time.
options.then: The group chats around you. Nobody can quite reach you.

options.text: "Yes, I'd like to meet everyone. Can you introduce me?"
options.then: She waves you over. "Come, meet Meera and Dev."

steps.why: Saying yes and asking for an introduction makes it easy for others to include you.

steps.prompt: On Monday Dev says in class: "Hey, you're in my section, right? Want to study physics together?"

options.text: "Sure, but I'll just listen."
options.then: You sit through the session without speaking. Dev doesn't ask again.

options.text: "Maybe. Message me sometime."
options.then: Dev nods. The message never comes.

options.text: "Yes, I'd like that. When works for you?"
options.then: He grins. "Tomorrow after lunch?"

options.text: "Nah, I study alone. It's easier."
options.then: Dev shrugs. "Okay." The door quietly closes.

steps.why: Saying yes with a time turns a small offer into a real friendship.

scenarios.relearn: Asking to be included is a small, brave people skill worth practising.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Nikhil keeps interrupting you in the middle of a sentence.
scenarios.setup: You are telling him about your weekend plan.

steps.prompt: Nikhil cuts in: "Oh, I did that last year. Let me tell you what happened."

options.text: "Let me finish my thought, then I want to hear yours."
options.then: He grins sheepishly. "Oh. Sorry. Go on."

options.text: "You always do this! You never listen to anyone."
options.then: Nikhil frowns. "Always? That's harsh."

options.text: "Never mind." Stop mid-sentence
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay!" and tells his story. Then you try to start again.

options.text: "As I was saying..." Talk louder until he stops
options.then: He raises his voice too. You both talk at once.

steps.why: Calmly saying what you need keeps the talk fair and doesn't make it a contest.

steps.prompt: Two minutes later Nikhil cuts in again: "Wait, wait, one more thing."

options.text: "Mm-hm." Give up and just nod along without finishing
options.then: He chatters happily. Your plan never gets said.

options.text: "One sec. I'll finish, then it's your turn."
options.then: He zips his lips. "Okay, okay."

options.text: "Fine, go ahead. You'll talk anyway."
options.then: He grins, missing the edge. You feel smaller.

options.text: "Seriously? I was in the middle of a sentence!"
options.then: Nikhil winces. "Whoa. Okay, sorry."

steps.why: A short, steady reminder works better than giving up or snapping.

steps.prompt: At lunch Nikhil asks: "Did I do the thing again? Interrupt you?"

options.text: "A little. It helps when you wait till I'm done."
options.then: He nods. "Okay. I'll try. Tell me if I forget."

options.text: "No, no, it's fine. Don't worry about it."
options.then: He smiles, relieved. The habit carries on.

options.text: "Yes, constantly. It's honestly exhausting."
options.then: Nikhil's face falls. "I didn't know it was that bad."

options.text: "Don't worry. You can't help it."
options.then: He shrugs. "True, I can't." Nothing changes.

steps.why: Honest, kind feedback gives him something he can actually change.

scenarios.relearn: Calmly naming the interruption keeps the talk fair, not a contest.

scenarios.hook: You think your English teacher marked you unfairly, and you want to ask, not argue.
scenarios.setup: You wait until the class empties out.

steps.prompt: Mrs. Menon looks up from her desk and says: "You wanted to see me?"

options.text: "This is unfair, and honestly you're just wrong."
options.then: She stiffens. "That is not how we discuss marks."

options.text: "Rhea wrote the same thing and got more marks."
options.then: Mrs. Menon raises an eyebrow. "We are talking about your paper."

options.text: "Could you help me understand this mark?"
options.then: She nods. "Of course. Show me which answer."

options.text: "Never mind. It's fine." Leave without asking.
options.then: You reach the door, but she calls, "Wait. Sit down a minute." The mark still nags at you.

steps.why: Asking to understand opens the door, and attacking closes it.

steps.prompt: Mrs. Menon says: "I took marks off because the argument had no example."

options.text: "Could you show me a good example?"
options.then: She pulls out a model answer. "Look at the second line."

options.text: "But I did put an example in there. I think you missed it."
options.then: She frowns. "Please don't tell me what I missed."

options.text: "I don't think that rule is even in our syllabus, Mrs. Menon."
options.then: "It's in the marking guide," she says coolly.

options.text: "Okay. Sorry to have wasted your time, Mrs. Menon."
options.then: She shakes her head. "Not at all. The marking guide is on my desk if you want to compare."

steps.why: Asking for an example helps you learn why, not just argue.

steps.prompt: Mrs. Menon says: "If you still disagree after comparing with the marking guide, you can ask for a recheck. Do you want that?"

options.text: "Yes, please recheck it right now. I know I'm right."
options.then: She sighs. "Let's not rush it."

options.text: "I'll ask the principal to recheck it for me instead."
options.then: Her face tightens. "You might have asked me first."

options.text: "No, forget it. I don't want to cause any trouble here."
options.then: She nods. The doubt stays with you.

options.text: "Let me compare first, then I'll tell you."
options.then: She smiles. "Good. Take your time."

steps.why: Comparing first lets you decide from facts, not feelings.

scenarios.relearn: Asking to understand, not attacking, keeps a disagreement constructive.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Ritu asks to copy your project the night before submission.
scenarios.setup: She messages you at nine.

steps.prompt: Ritu texts: "Please send me yours. I'll change a few words and nobody will know."

options.text: "Okay, here are some pages. Please don't tell anyone."
options.then: She sends hearts, then goes quiet. You lie awake worrying.

options.text: "I can't share mine. I'll sit with you while you do yours."
options.then: Ritu hesitates, then types: "Okay. Can you come at ten?"

options.text: "No way. That's cheating and you know it, Ritu."
options.then: Ritu goes offline. The seen tick stares at you.

options.text: "I'm busy tonight. Why don't you ask someone else instead?"
options.then: She says okay. You hear later she asked Neel.

steps.why: A kind no plus a real offer keeps the boundary and the friendship.

steps.prompt: A week later Ritu texts: "Another project is due tomorrow and I'm panicking. What do I do?"

options.text: "Stop panicking. You should have started earlier than this."
options.then: Ritu sends nothing. The chat sits silent.

options.text: "Just copy a bit of mine. I won't tell anyone about it."
options.then: She thanks you. The worry you tried to avoid comes back.

options.text: "Tell sir you were ill and ask him for more time."
options.then: Ritu sends the excuse. Sir asks for a doctor's note, and she has none.

options.text: "Open the question sheet. I'll call you."
options.then: She answers fast. "Okay. Opening it now."

steps.why: Helping her start the work herself is real help, and it keeps your line clear.

steps.prompt: The next day Ritu texts: "I wish I'd asked sooner. How do I not end up here again?"

options.text: "Ask me earlier and I'll send you mine to look at then."
options.then: She agrees quickly. The same shortcut waits for next time.

options.text: "Do a little each day. I'll check in on you."
options.then: She sends a thumbs up. "Deal. Starting Monday."

options.text: "Just copy from the class topper next time, honestly."
options.then: She laughs. The pattern stays exactly where it is.

options.text: "I don't know. Maybe you could just try harder next time."
options.then: Ritu replies with a sad face. It isn't a plan.

steps.why: Small daily chunks and a check-in build the habit that fixes the real problem.

scenarios.relearn: A boundary plus a genuine offer of help beats a resentful yes.

scenarios.hook: In a project team, one member did almost nothing but wants equal credit.
scenarios.setup: You pull Imran aside after the meeting.

steps.prompt: Imran says: "We're all in this together, right? Put all four names on it."

options.text: "Let's each say what we did so credit's fair, no blame."
options.then: He shifts. "Uh. Okay. Fair enough."

options.text: "Okay." Then tell the teacher privately
options.then: She asks if you talked to him. Word reaches Imran, who finds you.

options.text: "You did nothing, so your name isn't going on it."
options.then: His face hardens. "Say that louder, why don't you?" He looks away.

options.text: "Fine, put all four names and move on from it."
options.then: He nods. The other two are annoyed at lunch, and Imran overhears.

steps.why: Naming contributions calmly and privately is fairer than blame.

steps.prompt: Imran says: "Okay, I didn't do much. I had exams, and I was embarrassed."

options.text: "Exams? We all had exams. That's a poor excuse."
options.then: He looks away. "I know. Forget I said it."

options.text: "It's fine. The rest of us will do your part."
options.then: He relaxes. The other two stay quietly resentful.

options.text: "Next time, just tell us at the start."
options.then: He nods. The slides are still undone, with two days left.

options.text: "Thanks for being honest. What can you take on now?"
options.then: He thinks. "I can do the slides by Thursday."

steps.why: Honest thanks plus a clear task turns an excuse into a fair share.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says: "Please tell me each member's contribution, so I can mark fairly."

options.text: "We all did equal work, ma'am."
options.then: She frowns. "That's not what I asked."

options.text: "I'll let the others answer first, ma'am."
options.then: Someone says "Equal." The teacher raises an eyebrow.

options.text: "Imran did nothing, ma'am. Only three of us worked."
options.then: Imran's face falls. The team goes quiet.

options.text: "I did the research. Imran did less, and we've talked."
options.then: She notes it down. "Thank you. That's clear."

steps.why: An honest account of each person's part is fairer than blame or a vague "equal."

scenarios.relearn: Naming contributions calmly is fairer than public blame.

scenarios.hook: You misread your friend Anaya's text and replied harshly.
scenarios.setup: The next morning you find her at her locker.

steps.prompt: Anaya says: "That message hurt, you know. I only meant it as a joke."

options.text: "Hey! What's up?" Act like nothing happened.
options.then: Anaya's smile slips. "So we're not talking about it?"

options.text: "I was upset, so I said what I felt. Don't be so sensitive."
options.then: Anaya steps back. "That's not an apology."

options.text: "The joke wasn't clear. You should word things better."
options.then: She blinks. "So it's my fault?"

options.text: "I read that wrong and snapped. Sorry. What did you mean?"
options.then: She softens. "I was joking about the photo, not you."

steps.why: Naming your misread and asking again repairs the moment.

steps.prompt: Anaya says: "Honestly, you could have just asked before replying like that."

options.text: "Texting is tricky. It could happen to anyone."
options.then: She half-agrees. You haven't said what you'll change.

options.text: "I'm so bad at this. I'm the worst friend ever."
options.then: Anaya rushes to comfort you. The repair becomes about you.

options.text: "Can we not go over this again? It's done."
options.then: Anaya looks down. "Okay. Sure."

options.text: "You're right. Next time I'll ask before I reply."
options.then: She nods. "Thank you. That's all I wanted."

steps.why: Owning what you'll do differently makes the apology real.

steps.prompt: Anaya says: "Okay. Are we good? Want to sit together at lunch?"

options.text: "Only if you promise never to joke like that again."
options.then: Anaya frowns. "I can't promise that."

options.text: "Yes. And I'll slow down before replying when I'm upset."
options.then: She smiles. "Good plan. Come on."

options.text: "Maybe. I need some time to cool off first."
options.then: She shrugs. The lunch table has one empty seat.

options.text: "Sure, but let's never mention it again."
options.then: She nods. The topic sits there unspoken.

steps.why: Saying yes and naming one habit rebuilds trust.

scenarios.relearn: Naming your misread and asking again repairs the moment.

scenarios.hook: Two friends, Isha and Dhruv, are fighting and each wants you on their side.

steps.prompt: Isha messages her side and asks you to agree. What do you do?

options.text: Agree with her so she calms down

options.text: Hear her out, but say I won't take a side
options.then: She sighs. "Okay. At least you listened."

options.text: Tell her what Dhruv said about her

options.text: Reply tomorrow and avoid it for now

options.text: Pass it on, but soften the words so it won't sting

options.text: Pass it on and add what she said about him

options.text: Tell both of them I'm done with them

options.text: Say Isha is, since she asked first

options.text: Say it's complicated and hint at details

options.text: Say it's between them, and I care about both
options.then: She nods and drops it. Word gets back that you stayed fair.

steps.why: Staying caring but neutral helps a fight cool down.

scenarios.debrief: A fight cools when you listen to both and let them speak to each other.
scenarios.relearn: You can support both friends without taking sides or carrying messages.

scenarios.hook: A group chat turns into pile-on jokes about one classmate.

steps.prompt: The jokes about Rishi keep coming and others are laughing. What do you do?

options.text: Add one joke so I'm not the odd one out
options.then: Everyone reacts with laughing faces. Rishi will see it.

options.text: Leave the chat quietly and say nothing
options.then: The jokes keep going without you.

options.text: Steer the chat to a different topic

options.text: Screenshot it and mock it on another chat

steps.prompt: Rishi has seen the chat and goes quiet at school. What do you do?

options.text: Ignore it, since it isn't my business

options.text: Message him privately to check in

options.text: Confront the ringleader loudly in class

steps.prompt: A teacher asks the class about messages that hurt someone. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her what happened and ask for her help
options.then: She thanks you, and says she'll handle it without naming you.

options.text: Say I didn't see anything

scenarios.relearn: You can interrupt a pile-on without a public fight, and check on the person.

scenarios.hook: A friend keeps cancelling last-minute, and it's wearing you down.

steps.prompt: Meghna cancels again an hour before you meet. What do you do?

options.text: Quietly stop inviting her, with no reason given

options.text: Cancel on her next time to teach her a lesson
options.then: She feels hurt, and now both of you are cancelling.

options.text: Say it's fine every time and sulk later
options.then: She believes you. You feel more resentful each time.

options.text: Say how it lands and ask what's going on
options.then: She types for a while. "I know. I'm sorry. Can I explain?"

steps.why: Saying how it lands, and asking, gives her a chance to explain.

steps.prompt: Meghna says she's had a lot going on at home. What do you do?

options.text: Say everyone has problems so she should show up
options.then: She goes quiet and feels unheard.

options.text: Say it's okay, but quietly keep resenting it
options.then: She feels the chill and can't tell why.

options.text: Ask what would make plans easier for her
options.then: She thinks. "Shorter plans, maybe. I get tired."

options.text: Offer to fix whatever is happening at her home
options.then: She's touched and unsettled. You can't really fix it.

steps.why: Asking what helps respects her situation without taking over.

steps.prompt: Meghna suggests a Saturday plan. What do you do?

options.text: Say yes but expect her to cancel anyway
options.then: The day comes. You're cold before she's said a word.

options.text: Say yes and agree how we'll tell each other if plans change

options.then: The plan is vague, and Saturday slips by.

steps.prompt: A month later, Meghna cancels again, but this time she warns you early. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her for telling me early, and rebook
options.then: She sounds relieved. "Thanks. Saturday?"

options.text: Say it's always the same with her
options.then: She's quiet. "I thought I did better."

options.text: Say fine and block the day anyway
options.then: You wait on the day, hoping she'll turn up.

options.text: Cancel the plan with her entirely
options.then: She's left puzzled, and wonders what she did.

steps.why: Noticing the new habit encourages it to stick.

scenarios.debrief: Honest, curious feedback beats silent withdrawal or revenge.
scenarios.relearn: Saying how something lands, and asking why, beats going cold.

scenarios.hook: You and a teammate clash on how to do a presentation.

options.text: Insist my way is the only right way to do it

options.text: Take turns, with hers this time and mine the next

steps.prompt: On the day, Farah forgets part of her section. What do you do?

options.text: Point out her mistake in front of the class
options.then: The class gasps. Farah goes red.

options.text: Say nothing now, then complain about it later
options.then: The talk goes on, and you bring it up angrily afterwards.

options.text: Take over her entire section without asking

scenarios.debrief: Looking for the shared goal turns a clash into a better plan.
scenarios.relearn: Finding what you both want can turn a clash into a stronger result.

scenarios.hook: A relative scoffs at your career choice at the family dinner.

steps.prompt: Uncle says your career choice is a waste of your marks. What do you do?

options.text: Argue it out at the table until someone finally wins

options.text: Stay calm, state my view once, change the subject

options.text: Say I'll think about it just to end the talk

options.text: Say he has no idea what he's talking about

options.text: Ask my father to tell Uncle off

steps.prompt: Your cousin asks if you're really sure about your choice. What do you do?

options.text: Say I'm absolutely certain about every single thing

options.text: Say I don't want to be asked about it again

options.text: Say yes, what I know, and what I'm still learning

scenarios.debrief: You can hold your view calmly, thank people for caring, and still keep the bond.
scenarios.relearn: You can hold your view calmly without turning it into a fight.

scenarios.hook: A friend tells you a secret, and you almost repeat it by habit.

steps.prompt: Amrit told you a secret, and the group is gossiping near it. What do you do?

options.text: Share it just with one person

options.text: Hint at it without actually saying it
options.then: Someone guesses it out loud. Amrit's name comes up.

options.text: Catch myself and change the subject

options.text: Say I can't say, but make it obvious

scenarios.debrief: Keeping confidences, and owning a slip, is what makes you trustworthy.
scenarios.relearn: Keeping a confidence, and owning a slip fast, is core to trust.

scenarios.hook: A new junior at your part-time job is struggling and being mocked.

scenarios.hook: You owe a friend money and she hasn't mentioned it.

scenarios.debrief: Naming a money issue first, with a plan, protects the relationship.

scenarios.hook: A friend's advice keeps turning into put-downs.

options.then: He looks surprised. "Oh. I didn't think of it like that."

options.text: Laugh it off and take it, like I always do
options.then: He grins. It happens again the next day.

options.text: Put him down right back to even out the score
options.then: He snaps back. Now it's a fight, not advice.

options.text: Say nothing and start quietly avoiding him
options.then: He doesn't know why you've gone quiet.

steps.why: Naming how it lands gives him a chance to change.

steps.prompt: Next time, Rohit makes another dig about your marks, then says you're too sensitive and he's only being honest. What do you do?

options.text: Apologise for being so sensitive again
options.then: He nods. You feel smaller.

options.text: Laugh loudly to prove I'm not sensitive
options.then: He's satisfied. You feel something sink.

options.text: List his flaws to show how it feels
options.then: He bristles. The talk becomes a trade of insults.

options.text: Say honest is fine, put-downs aren't
options.then: He pauses. "Okay. What do you want from me?"

steps.why: You can accept honesty and still refuse put-downs.

steps.prompt: A week later, Rohit asks how your test prep is going. What do you do?

options.text: Say it's fine and shut the topic down
options.then: He shrugs. Nothing is different.

options.text: Say to ask my other friends about it
options.then: He looks hurt. You've closed a door.

options.text: Tell him the kind of help I'd like
options.then: He listens. "Okay. I'll quiz you, not lecture you."

options.text: Drop him from my group chats
options.then: He notices by evening and is bewildered.

steps.why: Saying what you need turns advice into support.

scenarios.debrief: Naming the pattern and asking for what you need is a clear boundary.
scenarios.relearn: You can name disguised put-downs and ask for real support instead.

scenarios.hook: Your team picked an idea, and you still think yours was better.

steps.prompt: The team picked Neel's idea over yours. What do you do at the next meeting?

options.text: Do my part half-heartedly to prove a point
options.then: The work is thin. The team notices.

options.text: Back it fully and offer to help make it work
options.then: Neel looks surprised and pleased. "Thanks. I could use you."

options.text: Keep bringing up my idea whenever I can
options.then: Meetings drag. Others start sighing.

options.text: Skip the meeting, since it isn't my plan
options.then: The team works without you. You've lost a say.

steps.why: Disagree, then commit once it's decided. That's how teams move.

steps.prompt: Midway, you spot a real problem in Neel's plan. What do you do?

options.text: Raise it with facts and suggest a fix
options.then: The team looks. "Good catch. Let's change it."

options.text: Tell everyone I told them so
options.then: The room goes cold. Neel is stung.

options.text: Stay quiet so the plan fails
options.then: The problem grows, and so does the damage. The team scrambles to patch it later.

options.text: Quietly switch back to my own idea
options.then: Neel finds out. Trust takes a hit.

steps.why: Raising a real problem with a fix is committed teamwork.

steps.prompt: The project is submitted. Your teacher asks who did what. What do you do?

options.text: Say my idea would have been better
options.then: Neel's face drops. The teacher frowns.

options.text: Say nothing about my own part
options.then: The teacher notes it down without you.

options.text: Mention only the places where Neel was wrong
options.then: The teacher notices the edge in your voice.

options.text: Credit the team, including Neel, and say what I did
options.then: The teacher nods. "Sounds like a good team."

steps.why: Crediting the team honestly keeps trust for the next project.

scenarios.debrief: Disagreeing well, then committing once it's decided, is mature collaboration.
scenarios.relearn: You can disagree, then back the group's decision wholeheartedly.

scenarios.hook: A friend asks you to tell her parents she was at your place when she wasn't.

steps.prompt: Kavya asks you to say she was studying at your house. What do you do?

options.text: Lie to her parents to keep her happy
options.then: Her parents believe it. Kavya now knows you'll cover again.

options.text: Refuse coldly and lecture her about honesty
options.then: She walks off, angry, and the talk is over.

options.text: Say I can't lie, but I'll help another way
options.then: She sighs. "Okay. What other way?"

options.text: Say yes, then dodge when her mother calls
options.then: Her mother is puzzled. Kavya is cross with you anyway.

steps.why: A warm no to lying, with another offer, keeps both your values and the bond.

steps.prompt: Later, Kavya asks again, saying real friends cover for each other. What do you do?

options.text: Give in so she won't be angry at me
options.then: She thanks you. You feel the knot in your stomach.

options.text: Say I'm her friend, so I'd help her ask
options.then: She goes quiet. "Maybe I could just ask Mum."

options.text: Say a real friend wouldn't even ask me this
options.then: She stiffens. "Wow. Okay."

options.text: Say it's her problem to sort out
options.then: She turns away. The offer to help is gone.

steps.why: Offering to help her ask keeps honesty and friendship together.

steps.prompt: Kavya's mother calls you and asks where Kavya was last night. What do you do?

options.text: Say Kavya should tell her, and I'll nudge her
options.then: Her mother pauses. "Hm. I'll ask her tonight."

options.text: Make up a quick story on the spot
options.then: Her mother accepts it. You'll have to keep it going.

options.text: Hang up without answering
options.then: Her mother calls back, and she's worried now.

options.text: Tell her mother every detail of Kavya's plans
options.then: Kavya will hear, and trust will be broken.

steps.why: Not lying and not spilling every detail is honest. If she may be unsafe, tell an adult.

scenarios.debrief: A warm 'no' to lying, plus another offer of help, holds both values and the bond.
scenarios.relearn: You can refuse to lie for a friend and still offer real help.

scenarios.hook: Online, someone twists your words to make you look bad.

steps.prompt: A stranger quotes half your post and says you meant it nastily. What do you do?

options.text: Fire back harder to win the thread
options.then: The stranger replies tenfold. The thread explodes.

options.text: Delete everything and tell nobody
options.then: The post vanishes from your page. You sit alone with it, and nobody knows.

options.text: Keep reading every reply to see what they say
options.then: An hour later you're tense and no clearer.

options.text: Post one clear reply saying what I meant
options.then: A few people read it and the thread slows.

steps.why: One clear reply states your point without feeding the argument.

steps.prompt: Screenshots and replies keep spreading, and some are cruel. What do you do?

options.text: Reply to every cruel comment one by one
options.then: Each reply brings two more.

options.text: Read them all and stew over each one
options.then: By midnight your chest feels tight.

options.text: Stop replying, mute the thread and tell a trusted adult
options.then: Your older cousin reads it. "That's not on you."

options.text: Ask my friends to attack them for me
options.then: Your friends pile in. Now there are two fights.

steps.why: Stepping back and telling an adult helps, and it's never your fault.

steps.prompt: A friend says to delete the account and disappear. What do you do?

options.text: Delete everything tonight and tell no one why
options.then: The account is gone. The hurt stays, and you carry it alone.

options.text: Take a break and decide later what to do
options.then: A few days off helps. You feel calmer.

options.text: Keep arguing so they can't have the last word
options.then: The fight continues. You can't sleep.

options.text: Post a long thread explaining every detail
options.then: The thread is long. Few people read it.

steps.why: Taking a break gives you room to decide when you're calm.

scenarios.debrief: One clear reply, then stepping back, beats a war or silent spiralling.
scenarios.relearn: State your point once and disengage; you don't owe an endless reply.

scenarios.hook: A close friend gives you honest feedback that stings.

steps.prompt: Ira says your essay draft is confusing and rushed. What do you do?

options.text: Take a breath, thank her and ask for an example
options.then: She points to one paragraph. "Here. This part lost me."

options.text: Get defensive and list her mistakes back
options.then: She stiffens. "I was only trying to help."

options.text: Agree instantly and say I'm hopeless at this
options.then: She says you're not hopeless. The talk stops being about the essay.

options.text: Say "fine" and hide the draft from her
options.then: She senses it. She stops giving you feedback.

steps.why: Asking for an example turns a sting into something you can use.

steps.prompt: That night, her comments keep replaying in your head. What do you do?

options.text: Rewrite the whole essay in a panic
options.then: You're up till 2 am and the essay is messier.

options.text: Decide she's just jealous of me
options.then: You feel better for ten minutes and no better after.

options.text: Beat myself up for every flaw she found
options.then: The flaws grow bigger. The essay doesn't improve.

options.text: Sit with it, then note what's fair to use
options.then: You write three notes. One is easy to fix.

steps.why: Weighing what's fair is how you grow without self-blame.

steps.prompt: Ira asks if her feedback helped. What do you do?

options.text: Say it was harsh and leave it at that
options.then: She nods, hurt. She won't offer next time.

options.text: Say it was all useful and say no more
options.then: She smiles. You skip the points you doubted.

options.text: Say what helped and what I disagreed with
options.then: She grins. "Fair. You're not just agreeing."

options.text: Say I won't ask her for feedback again
options.then: She's startled. "Okay. That's up to you."

steps.why: Honest replies keep honest feedback coming.

steps.prompt: Ira shows you her own draft and asks for honest feedback. What do you do?

options.text: Say it's perfect and don't mention anything
options.then: She smiles. The weak parts stay.

options.text: Say what works first, then one thing to fix
options.then: She nods. "That's something I can use."

options.text: Say it's confusing and rushed, like she told me
options.then: She stiffens. It lands as payback.

options.text: List everything that's wrong with it
options.then: She goes quiet, and the draft goes into her bag.

steps.why: Honest feedback with kindness is the kind you'd like to receive.

scenarios.debrief: Taking feedback openly, then weighing it, is a quiet, powerful skill.
scenarios.relearn: Taking honest feedback in, then weighing it, is how you grow.

scenarios.hook: A friend keeps over-sharing your business with others.

steps.prompt: Jiya has told others something you told her privately. What do you do?

options.text: Stop telling her anything, with no explanation
options.then: She feels the chill and doesn't know why.

options.text: Tell her what's private and ask her to keep it
options.then: She blushes. "Oh. I'm sorry. I'll keep it."

options.text: Share her business with others as payback
options.then: The word gets back to her fast.

options.text: Laugh it off and let it keep happening
options.then: She shares more, and you feel more exposed.

steps.why: Saying clearly what's private is fairer than silence or payback.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Jiya says she never really knew which things were private. What do you do?

options.text: Say what counts as private so she doesn't have to guess
options.then: She nods. "That helps. Thanks for telling me."

options.text: Say she should just know by now
options.then: She goes quiet. "I don't think that's fair."

options.text: Say it's fine and nothing more
options.then: She relaxes. It happens again next month.

options.text: Make a long list of what she can never say
options.then: She feels policed, and she's defensive.

steps.why: Saying what's private takes the guesswork out for both of you.

steps.prompt: Jiya says she wants to tell you something private about herself. What do you do?

options.text: Say I'd better not hear it in case I slip
options.then: She feels dismissed. "Okay. Never mind."

options.text: Promise to keep anything she tells me, whatever it is
options.then: She relaxes and starts. You wonder what you'd do if it were serious.

options.text: Say only if I can tell one other person
options.then: She shakes her head. "Then no."

options.text: Say I'll keep it, unless she's not safe, and thank her
options.then: She smiles and tells you. You keep it, and she knows the one limit.

steps.why: Keeping her confidence, with one honest limit about safety, shows what trust means.

scenarios.debrief: Say what's private clearly, and keep a friend's confidence in return.
scenarios.relearn: You can name what's private and ask a friend to keep it, plainly.

scenarios.hook: At a family gathering, an elder asks you to do all the serving.

steps.prompt: Dadi says you'll do all the serving, as always. What do you do?

options.text: Do it all silently and fume
options.then: The evening drags. You feel your face getting hot.

options.text: Refuse loudly and walk out of the room
options.then: A hush falls. Dadi says you're being dramatic.

options.text: Calmly ask everyone to share it, as fair
options.then: Dadi blinks. Your cousin nods. "That's fair."

options.text: Do it with a smile and vent to a friend later
options.then: Dadi is pleased. Nothing changes next time.

steps.why: Calmly calling it unfair, and asking for a share, is fair and clear.

steps.prompt: Later, your brother is on his phone as the trays pile up. He shrugs: "It's tradition." What do you do?

options.text: Say I'll go and tell Mummy on him right now
options.then: He rolls his eyes. The tray stays with you.

options.text: Say tradition can be shared, and hand him a tray
options.then: He sighs and gets up. "Fine. Give it here."

options.text: Do his share and mine so it all ends quietly
options.then: You feel the load on your back. He thanks you.

options.text: Tell him he's useless and storm off to the kitchen
options.then: He shouts back. Aunty frowns at both of you.

steps.why: Asking for fairness without a fight lets him do his share.

steps.prompt: Later, your mother says to let it go for the sake of peace. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her it matters to me, and ask her help
options.then: She sits down. "Okay. Tell me what happened."

options.text: Let it go and agree with her to keep the peace
options.then: She smiles, relieved. You feel it again at the next gathering.

options.text: Say she never once stands up for me, ever
options.then: She's hurt, and the talk turns to the past.

options.text: Plan to avoid every family gathering from now on
options.then: The gatherings go on without you. You miss some of it.

steps.why: Telling someone you trust why it matters gives you support for next time.

scenarios.debrief: Naming an unfair split calmly, as a shared job, is agency without a scene.
scenarios.relearn: You can name an unfair split calmly and ask for it to be shared.

scenarios.hook: You realise you were wrong in a debate you argued hard.

steps.prompt: The next morning, you find a fact that proves the other side right. What do you do?

options.text: Keep defending it so I don't look weak
options.then: You lose some trust with each defended point.

options.text: Go quiet and pretend it never happened
options.then: The point stays hanging between you.

options.text: Say it was basically a draw
options.then: She frowns. "It wasn't, though."

options.text: Tell the other person plainly I changed my mind
options.then: She raises her eyebrows. "Wow. Thanks for saying that."

steps.why: Saying "I changed my mind" plainly earns more respect than defending.

steps.prompt: A friend teases that you argued so hard. What do you do?

options.text: Say I was only playing devil's advocate
options.then: He smirks. It rings hollow.

options.text: Say the facts are actually unclear
options.then: He frowns. You both know that isn't true.

options.text: Laugh, and say I was wrong and glad to know
options.then: He laughs too. "Respect."

options.text: Snap at him for teasing me about it
options.then: He backs off, and the mood turns sour.

steps.why: Laughing at your own mistake shows it doesn't threaten you.

steps.prompt: Later, the person you debated asks for your view on something else. What do you do?

options.text: Say I'll never argue with anyone again
options.then: She's puzzled. She wanted your view.

options.text: Share it, and say how sure I am
options.then: She listens. "That's useful."

options.text: Agree with whatever she says
options.then: She suspects you aren't being honest.

options.text: Hold back in case I'm wrong again
options.then: She's left without your view, and the conversation stalls.

steps.why: Saying how sure you are keeps you honest and approachable.

scenarios.debrief: Changing your mind out loud is a strength, not a loss.
scenarios.relearn: Saying 'you're right, I've changed my mind' is a strength, not a defeat.

scenarios.hook: In your project group, Riya has good ideas, but louder members talk over her.

steps.prompt: Riya starts to share an idea and Karan talks over her. What do you do?

options.text: Message Riya later to say her idea was actually good
options.then: She thanks you warmly. The group still never hears the idea.

options.text: Tell Karan he is far too loud and should stop interrupting
options.then: Karan bristles and the room tenses. Riya shrinks into her seat.

options.text: Say Riya had a point and ask to hear it
options.then: Karan pauses. Riya picks her idea back up, a little shyly.

options.text: Let the meeting move on, since Karan's plan sounds fine anyway
options.then: Karan's plan wins on volume. Riya goes quiet and checks her phone.

steps.why: Making space in the moment lets the group hear the idea and tells Riya she belongs.

steps.prompt: A few days later the group must pick one idea to present. Riya has a plan in her notebook. What do you do?

options.text: Tell Riya she needs to speak up a lot more next time
options.then: Riya nods, a little stung, and puts the notebook away.

options.text: Ask Riya to walk everyone through her plan
options.then: She explains it clearly, and the others ask real questions.

options.text: Back whichever idea the group can agree on the fastest
options.then: It is settled in two minutes. Riya's notebook stays closed in her bag.

options.text: Present her plan yourself, since you know she gets nervous
options.then: The group likes it. Riya studies the table and says nothing.

steps.why: Inviting her to share lets the group hear Riya in her own words.

steps.prompt: On presentation day the teacher asks who contributed what, and Riya sits quietly. What do you say?

options.text: Say Riya worked on it too and ask her to describe her part
options.then: Riya blushes. The teacher turns to her and asks a follow-up question.

options.text: Say it was mostly yours, since you led the final push
options.then: The teacher smiles at you. Riya's face falls, and she stays quiet afterwards.

options.text: Let the louder members answer on behalf of the group
options.then: Karan says it was a team effort. Riya looks at her shoes.

options.text: Say the whole group thought of it together, as a team
options.then: The teacher nods and moves on. Riya's part is never named.

steps.why: Crediting Riya by name shows the group values every voice and builds trust.

scenarios.debrief: Pulling a quiet voice in, and crediting them, is leadership.
scenarios.relearn: Making space for a quieter teammate, and crediting them, lifts the group.

scenarios.hook: "Setting a boundary means you're being rude or selfish."

myth.un: A boundary makes you rude or selfish.
myth.re: A clear, respectful boundary protects the relationship and is fair to both.
myth.why: Saying your limit kindly prevents the resentment that quietly wrecks bonds.

scenarios.relearn: A respectful boundary protects a relationship; it isn't rudeness.

scenarios.hook: "Saying sorry first means you lose the argument."

myth.un: Apologising first means you lost.
myth.re: Owning your part repairs trust and often unsticks the whole conflict.
myth.why: Naming your share lets the other person lower their guard too.

scenarios.relearn: Apologising for your part repairs trust; it isn't losing.

scenarios.hook: "Avoiding conflict keeps relationships healthy."

myth.un: Avoiding all conflict keeps a relationship healthy.
myth.re: Handled calmly, working through a disagreement makes a bond stronger.
myth.why: Issues you never raise don't vanish; they build up as quiet distance.

scenarios.relearn: Working through conflict calmly strengthens a bond; avoiding it builds distance.

scenarios.hook: "Good listeners just stay quiet and let the other person talk."

myth.un: Listening is just staying quiet.
myth.re: Real listening is reflecting back and asking, so they feel understood.
myth.why: Silence can be drifting; checking 'so you mean…?' proves you're with them.

scenarios.relearn: Real listening reflects back and asks; it's more than staying quiet.

scenarios.hook: "To be a leader you have to be the loudest in the room."

myth.un: Leading means being the loudest.
myth.re: Strong leaders listen, include quieter voices, and share the credit.
myth.why: People follow someone who makes the group better, not just the loudest one.

scenarios.relearn: Leadership is including and crediting people, not being the loudest.

scenarios.hook: "If a friendship takes effort, it isn't a real one."

myth.un: A real friendship never takes effort.
myth.re: Every close bond needs honest talk, repair after fights, and showing up.
myth.why: Effort isn't a sign it's wrong; it's how closeness is actually built.

scenarios.relearn: Real friendships take honest effort, repair and showing up.

scenarios.hook: "Being assertive is just a polite word for being aggressive."

myth.un: Assertive is the same as aggressive.
myth.re: Assertive states your need clearly while respecting the other person; aggressive runs them over.
myth.why: You can be firm and kind at once; that's the whole skill.

scenarios.relearn: Assertive means clear and respectful; aggressive means running people over.

scenarios.hook: You have felt low for days, and your friend Sara texts "you good?"

steps.prompt: Sara's text lands while you're still feeling low. What do you do?

options.text: Send back a funny meme so she won't ask more
options.then: She laughs back. You feel more alone than before.

options.text: Leave it on read until you feel less low
options.then: Her text sits there. By morning she hasn't tried again.

options.text: Reply honestly: "Actually, not really. Can we talk?"
options.then: Sara calls within a minute. "Of course. I'm here."

options.text: Reply "fine" and put the phone down
options.then: Sara sends a heart. The opening closes quietly.

steps.why: An honest answer opens a door that "fine" keeps shut.

steps.prompt: A day later Sara texts that she's still thinking about you and asks for a walk after school. What do you do?

options.text: Say yes, then cancel at the last minute
options.then: Sara says it's fine. She doesn't suggest another day.

options.text: Say you're busy, since you don't want to drag her down
options.then: She replies "okay". She sounds disappointed.

options.text: Say yes, then talk about homework the whole way
options.then: The walk is pleasant. Nothing real gets said.

options.text: Say yes and tell her it's been a heavy few days
options.then: She walks beside you and doesn't hurry you.

steps.why: Saying yes and being honest gives her a way in to support you.

steps.prompt: A few days later Sara can see you are still low. She says it might help to tell your mother or the school counsellor. What do you do?

options.text: Agree, and ask her to be there when you tell your mother
options.then: She squeezes your hand. "I'll be right there."

options.text: Ask her to promise not to tell anyone, ever
options.then: She frowns. "I'll keep you company, but I'm worried."

options.text: Say having her is enough, so you don't need anyone else
options.then: She smiles, though she looks a little worried.

options.text: Say you'll think about it, and then let it slide
options.then: A week passes. Nothing is any lighter.

steps.why: More support is stronger, and feeling low is never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: An honest answer to 'you good?' is a small, brave doorway to real support.
